items.title: [FEATURE] Multi-tenancy of the SPEC-002 capabilities: tenant-scoped subject and column-encryption keys, per-tenant credentials, sequences, senders and storage, tenant-aware background cycles, two-tenant isolation tests on the 10 providers and Marten

items.body:
## Summary

Every capability SPEC-002 adds or changes is tenant-aware on every store and provider it ships on; this issue owns the cross-cutting pieces no single child covers and the two-tenant isolation suite on the 10 providers and Marten.

Tracks SPEC-002 requirement(s) REQ-061; acceptance criteria AC-043; reference scenario(s) S11. Tracking id in SPEC-002 §13.2: **P-54**, priority **P0**. Part of #1186.

## Motivation

- SPEC-002 DEC-009 (b): multi-tenancy is required in 1.0 even if the first deployment runs one tenant, because adding a tenant key to persisted records, sequence keys, key stores and credential stores after 1.0 breaks the API and the schema on the 10 providers and Marten.
- Each practice is its own controller (GDPR Art. 28 with the operator as processor), so records of processing, consents, processor registers and retention policies belong to the tenant.
- `Encina.Tenancy` already resolves tenants (`src/Encina.Tenancy/Abstractions/ITenantProvider.cs`); `Encina.Marten.GDPR` (subject keys) and `Encina.Security.PII` carry no tenant; the audit and ABAC stores do not filter by the current tenant (#798); the outbox, inbox, saga and scheduled-message entities have no tenant column (#737, #738, #739, #760).

## Proposed Solution

- Tenant id from the request context (#1147) on every record SPEC-002 adds or changes; restored from persisted context in background processing (#1164); never two tenants in one unit of work.
- Credentials (OAuth tokens P-32, outbound credentials and client certificates P-31/P-44, webhook secrets #731/#734) stored and resolved per tenant; a missing tenant configuration fails closed, never falls back to another tenant's.
- Sequences and chains keyed by tenant (P-36, P-38); notification senders (P-33) and blob storage (P-37) per tenant.
- Subject keys (P-04) and column-encryption keys (P-46) scoped per tenant.
- Pacing (#469) and rate limits (P-31) per tenant.
- With tenancy off, a fixed default tenant applies and no tenant configuration is needed (pay-for-what-you-use).
- The two-tenant isolation suite of AC-043 across all stores.

## Alternatives Considered

1. **Tenancy after 1.0.** Breaks persisted shapes on 10 providers and Marten (DEC-009). Rejected.
2. **Database-per-tenant only.** Does not cover shared key stores, credential stores and background cycles; kept as one `Encina.Tenancy` strategy, not the only one.

## Affected Packages

- [x] Encina (core)
- [x] Encina.EntityFrameworkCore
- [x] Encina.Dapper.*
- [x] Encina.ADO.*
- [ ] Encina.AspNetCore
- [x] Encina.MongoDB
- [ ] Encina.OpenTelemetry
- [ ] Encina.Caching.*
- [x] Encina.Messaging
- [ ] Encina.Polly
- [ ] Encina.Cdc
- [x] Other: `Encina.Tenancy`, `Encina.Marten.GDPR`, `Encina.Security.PII`, `Encina.Security.Audit`, the compliance modules and the new packages of SPEC-002 §5.11

## Provider Implementation Matrix

The 10 database providers apply (CLAUDE.md, Multi-Provider Implementation Rule).

| Provider | Tenant column and filter | Background cycle isolation | Two-tenant test | Notes |
|----------|:-:|:-:|:-:|-------|
| ADO-SqlServer | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |  |
| ADO-PostgreSQL | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |  |
| ADO-MySQL | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |  |
| Dapper-SqlServer | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |  |
| Dapper-PostgreSQL | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |  |
| Dapper-MySQL | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |  |
| EFCore-SqlServer | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |  |
| EFCore-PostgreSQL | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |  |
| EFCore-MySQL | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |  |
| MongoDB | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |  |

Marten: tenant id on every compliance stream and read model SPEC-002 adds or changes, two-tenant test on PostgreSQL.

## Cross-Cutting Integration

| # | Function | Status | Notes |
|---|----------|--------|-------|
| 1 | **Caching** (`ICacheProvider`, decorator, `[Cache]`) | ✅ | Cache keys include the tenant id |
| 2 | **OpenTelemetry** (`ActivitySource`, `Meter`) | ✅ | `ActivitySource` and `Meter` per SPEC-002 REQ-062; tenant id as attribute; no payloads or subject identifiers |
| 3 | **Structured Logging** (`[LoggerMessage]`, `Log.cs`) | ✅ | `[LoggerMessage]` with EventIds in a range registered in `EventIdRanges` (ADR-021) |
| 4 | **Health Checks** (`IEncinaHealthCheck`) | ✅ | Tenant store health (#596) |
| 5 | **Validation** (`IValidationProvider`, pipeline) | ✅ | Options validated at start-up |
| 6 | **Resilience** (retry, circuit breaker, timeout) | ❌ N/A | No call to an external system |
| 7 | **Distributed Locks** (`IDistributedLockProvider`) | ❌ N/A | No shared state updated by concurrent hosts |
| 8 | **Transactions** (`IUnitOfWork`, atomicity) | ❌ N/A | Single-operation writes |
| 9 | **Idempotency** (`InboxPipelineBehavior`, dedup) | ❌ N/A | Not a message or request entry point |
| 10 | **Multi-Tenancy** (`TenantId`, `ITenantContext`) | ✅ | Tenant-aware per SPEC-002 REQ-061 (AC-043); fixed default tenant when tenancy is off |
| 11 | **Module Isolation** (`ModuleId`, `IModuleContext`) | ❌ N/A | SPEC-002 requires no module scoping; `ModuleId` in messaging stays with #747 |
| 12 | **Audit Trail** (`IAuditStore`, audit events) | ✅ | Tenant configuration changes audited (#752) |

### Observability Details (if applicable)

Names are proposals; the implementation plan fixes them.

| Metric Name | Type | Description |
|-------------|------|-------------|
| `encina.tenancy.missing_tenant_config` | Counter | Operations refused because the tenant has no configuration (fail closed) |

| Span Name | Attributes | Description |
|-----------|------------|-------------|
| `encina.tenancy.resolve` | `encina.tenant_id` | Tenant resolution for background work |

## Test Matrix

| Test Type | Required? | Scope | Notes |
|-----------|:---------:|-------|-------|
| **UnitTests** | Required | Every new type and branch |  |
| **GuardTests** | Required | Public constructors and methods |  |
| **ContractTests** | Required | Tenant filtering contract per store |  |
| **PropertyTests** | Required | No generated query or export returns another tenant's record |  |
| **IntegrationTests** | Required | 10 providers and Marten, two tenants |  |
| **LoadTests** | Required | Tenant isolation under concurrent access | CLAUDE.md LoadTests guidelines (Multi-Tenancy) |
| **BenchmarkTests** | Justify | Not a hot path | `.md` justification per CLAUDE.md |

## Implementation Tasks

### Core Abstractions

- [ ] Tenant resolution for background processing from persisted context
- [ ] Fail-closed tenant configuration lookup for credentials, senders, storage and keys
- [ ] Single-tenant default with no configuration
- [ ] Two-tenant isolation suite

### Provider Implementations (if applicable)

- [ ] ADO.NET providers (3): SqlServer, PostgreSQL, MySQL
- [ ] Dapper providers (3): SqlServer, PostgreSQL, MySQL
- [ ] EF Core providers (3): SqlServer, PostgreSQL, MySQL
- [ ] MongoDB provider (1)
- [ ] Marten streams and read models

### Observability

- [ ] OpenTelemetry metrics
- [ ] Traces / spans
- [ ] Health checks: tenant store (#596)
- [ ] EventId range registered in `EventIdRanges.cs` and the assembly added to `EncinaEventIdAllocationTests`

### Testing

- [ ] UnitTests
- [ ] GuardTests
- [ ] ContractTests
- [ ] PropertyTests
- [ ] IntegrationTests (Docker)
- [ ] LoadTests (if applicable, otherwise `.md` justification)
- [ ] BenchmarkTests (if applicable, otherwise `.md` justification)

### Documentation

- [ ] XML doc comments on all public APIs
- [ ] README updates
- [ ] Configuration guide
- [ ] Architecture Decision Record (if applicable)

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC-043: P-54, #737, #738, #739, #760, #798 and #596 closed; S11 passes
- [ ] AC-043: on each of the 10 database providers and on Marten, an integration test writes, under two tenants, the records of every store SPEC-002 adds or changes and shows that a query, an export, a DSR request and a background cycle (outbox, inbox, saga and scheduler dispatch, retention sweep, purge) run for tenant A never return, act on or export a record of tenant B
- [ ] AC-043: a subject key or a column-encryption key of tenant A cannot decrypt tenant B's data; crypto-shredding a subject in tenant A leaves the same subject id in tenant B readable
- [ ] AC-043: two tenants get independent gapless sequences and chains for the same series key
- [ ] AC-043: OAuth tokens, gateway and channel credentials, client certificates and webhook secrets resolve per tenant, with a missing tenant configuration failing closed
- [ ] AC-043: with tenancy off, the same tests pass with no tenant configuration
- [ ] Core abstractions implemented and tested
- [ ] All applicable providers have implementations
- [ ] All test types per Test Matrix implemented (or justified with `.md`)
- [ ] OpenTelemetry instrumentation in place
- [ ] Tenant-aware (SPEC-002 REQ-061, AC-043): every record this issue adds or changes carries the tenant id from the request context; queries, exports and background cycles filter by it; a two-tenant test shows tenant A never reads, acts on or exports tenant B's data; with tenancy off, a fixed default tenant applies and no tenant configuration is needed.
- [ ] Instrumented (SPEC-002 REQ-062, AC-044): a test with an in-memory exporter shows the main operations emit their activity and metric with the tenant as an attribute; log messages use `[LoggerMessage]` with EventIds inside a range registered in `src/Encina/Diagnostics/EventIdRanges.cs` and the assembly is covered by `tests/Encina.UnitTests/Testing/Architecture/EncinaEventIdAllocationTests.cs`; a health-check test covers each checkable dependency; a test asserts that no activity attribute, metric tag or log message carries a payload, a response body or a direct identifier of a data subject.
- [ ] The pull request records the ADR-018 evaluation of the 12 transversal functions and its outcome for tracing, metrics, logging and health checks.
- [ ] Documentation complete
- [ ] Zero build warnings
- [ ] Every applicable coverage flag reaches its target in `.github/coverage-manifest/` (per-flag obligations model)

## Documentation

- [x] Package README
- [x] Configuration guide in `docs/`
- [x] ADR in `docs/architecture/adr/` (for architectural decisions)
- [x] Scaling/usage guidance
- [x] Changelog fragment under `changelog.d/` (see `changelog.d/README.md`)
- [ ] ROADMAP.md update (if applicable)
- [x] Implementation plan under `docs/plans/` generated with `docs/engineering/prompts/implementation-plan-prompt.md` and linked here before work starts (CLAUDE.md, Feature plans)

## Related Issues

- #1186 - [EPIC] EU regulatory readiness (SPEC-002), parent
- #737, #738, #739, #760 - `TenantId` in outbox, saga, scheduled and inbox messages
- #798 - Tenancy for Security.Audit and ABAC

milestone.title: RS<->TS Feature Parity
milestone.description:
Close the Rust<->TS gap so the Rust API (forge-server and the browser runtime) serves everything the TS server does, then the non-API surfaces.

Status on 2026-10-12 (main d39c5fe): the endpoints the default wasm UI calls are covered. Of the 175 endpoints the SDK can call, 6 have no Rust route, and the web UI does not appear to call any of them (found by comparing the SDK with the registered routes): PATCH /industries/:id and /role-types/:id (#18, #19), GET /alignment/score and /alignment/match (#76, #77), GET /resumes/:id/entries, POST /templates/:id/create-resume.

Remaining:
- API parity: the six above; tagline regeneration on JD link and unlink and its parity gate (#66: #71, #72); JD input validation and list pagination in Rust (#43, #141); #142.
- Non-API surfaces: JD parser, embeddings and alignment, MCP, CLI, PDF contract, migration ownership, ELM lifecycle hooks, the DB decision.
- Housekeeping (#117), for example the 125 dead todo!() stubs in forge-sdk (#118).

Deferred until the TS-to-Rust migration is complete: Extension work (#44, #107-#109, #115, #116, #129).

Keep widening `just parity-tier0` as routes gain tests.

items.body:
## Motivation

Two open beads were written for a storage stack that never shipped.

- **`forge-8rzs`** places the CRDT operation log in the browser's database and exposes it through wasm-bindgen (`get_sync_ops`, `apply_sync_ops`). That puts capture in one host only. What actually ships is the same `forge-sdk` stores running natively and in the Worker, so capture belongs at the store layer, where both hosts get it.
- **`forge-j9by`** (multi-user auth and tenant isolation) says it needs the DB strategy first (`forge-58ht`) and feature-flag infrastructure (`forge-mgr2`).

The docs that frame both beads also assume engines the ADR may reject:

- `models/sync.md` and Seam 7 have D1 as the merge target and a "Turso session layer" for diffing.
- The migration plan's Phase 4 provisions a D1 database per tenant namespace, behind a sync endpoint on the Hono API.

If #90 changes the engine, these beads change shape too. They should be updated in the same motion, not discovered later.

## Goals

- `forge-8rzs` and `forge-j9by` are rewritten against the accepted ADR, with the capture point, merge target and tenant model stated.
- The sync design's conflict model is reconciled with whatever sync mechanism the ADR picks.
- The tension between server-side merge and zero-knowledge storage (Seam 9) is resolved on paper.

## Description

### Ideal

A short design note, appended to `models/sync.md` or kept as an ADR follow-up, records:

- where operations are captured (the #93 write path);
- what an operation contains;
- who merges, and where;
- how tenants are isolated (a database per tenant, or a tenant column);
- how auth scopes a request to its tenant;
- how all of this survives zero-knowledge encryption.

`forge-8rzs`, `forge-j9by` and `forge-58ht` are updated to match, and their dependencies point at the new issues.

### Minimal

- `forge-8rzs` and `forge-j9by` are updated: capture moves to the store layer, the merge target and tenant model come from the ADR, and the stale wa-sqlite wording is gone.
- Open questions are listed in each bead.

## Spec

The linkage must answer:

1. **Capture point.** Is every write captured in the `forge-sdk` seam (#93), so both hosts log identically? Lifecycle hooks (#97) must not emit duplicate operations.
2. **Operation shape.** Entity-level operations (`actor_id`, timestamp, entity, id, field, value), as `forge-8rzs` lists. The alternative is engine-level change capture, such as Turso's CDC (an early preview) or Turso Sync's logical statements.
3. **Conflict model.** `models/sync.md` specifies:
   - per-field LWW;
   - Add-Wins OR-Sets for tags and resume entries;
   - LSeq for ordering.

   Turso Sync documents "last push wins". If the ADR picks Turso Sync, say which model wins, and where.
4. **Merge target.**
   - **D1:** many databases per account (50,000 on the paid plan, which can be raised), 10 GB each.
   - **Turso Cloud:** required as the remote by Turso Sync.
   - **Another:** whatever the ADR names.

   Also decide which runtime serves the sync endpoint. The migration plan says the Hono API on a Cloudflare Worker.
5. **Tenant model.** One of the `forge-58ht` options. Then cover how `forge-j9by`'s auth middleware scopes each request, and how migrations reach N tenant databases.
6. **Zero knowledge.** Seam 9 says the server stores encrypted blobs and merges on metadata only. Engine-level sync ships plaintext statements, so state whether it is compatible. If it isn't, state what the server can still compute, such as market-stats contributions, which stay unencrypted.
7. **Self-hosted.** OSS installs run with no sync, or with sync to their own server and no hosted dependency.

## Constraints

- Offline-first: every operation works with no network, and conflicts resolve at merge time (`models/sync.md:113-118`).
- One database owner tab (ADR 0002). Capture happens in the owner's Worker.
- Shared migrations. Any op-log table is a normal numbered migration in `packages/core/src/db/migrations`.
- Forge is SaaS with an OSS distribution. Tenant isolation and auth scoping are required, and the OSS build can't require a hosted service.

## Examples

```text
write path (both hosts)
  route -> store fn -> seam.execute(...)
                         |-> engine write
                         '-> op_log.append({actor, hlc, entity, id, field, value})  [same txn]
sync
  push ops since version_vector -> server -> merge (LWW / OR-Set / LSeq) -> tenant store
  pull remote ops -> apply through the same seam (no re-capture)
```

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] **Given** the ADR is accepted, **when** a reader opens `forge-8rzs`, **then** it names the store-layer capture point, the operation shape and the merge target from the ADR, and no longer mentions wa-sqlite.
- [ ] **Given** the ADR is accepted, **when** a reader opens `forge-j9by` and `forge-58ht`, **then** they state the tenant model and how auth scopes a request, and their dependencies point at the right issues.
- [ ] **Given** the design note, **when** a reviewer checks it against Seam 9, **then** it says what the server can and cannot read, and the merge still works without decrypting payloads.

## Refs

- `docs/src/architecture/models/sync.md:11-84`, `:99-125`
- `docs/src/architecture/seams.md:121-132` (Seam 7), `:147-157` (Seam 9)
- `docs/src/migrations/mvp-2.0-browser-first.md:116-129` (Phase 4)
- `docs/src/architecture/models/deployment.md:148-156`
- `crates/forge-sdk/src/db/backends/mod.rs:1-6`, `crates/forge-api/src/db.rs:9-41`
- `AGENTS.md:6`
- Beads: `forge-8rzs`, `forge-j9by`, `forge-58ht`, `forge-mgr2`, `forge-txdt`
- Turso Sync (push/pull, "last push wins", Turso Cloud remote): https://docs.turso.tech/sync/usage; Turso CDC: https://github.com/tursodatabase/turso/blob/main/docs/manual.md
- D1 limits: https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/limits/
- Related: #90, #93, #97, #107

---
<sub>Beads: generate them from this issue per [`.agents/context/work-tracking.md`](https://github.com/resu-mx/forge/blob/main/.agents/context/work-tracking.md) and label each one `gh:<this issue's number>`.</sub>

items.title: Explore single-process multi-tenant SQLite runtime for shared-schema workloads
items.body:
## Summary

Explore a **shared-schema multi-tenant application runtime** where one server process/orchestrator multiplexes many physically isolated SQLite/libSQL databases, typically one DB per application tenant, while exposing a single Convex-like developer experience.

This is not a proposal to replace Norn's current per-tenant storage direction. Norn already benefits from tenant-isolated databases because organizations may have different ontology, configuration, extensions, placement, and lifecycle. The question here is whether the same underlying primitive becomes even more efficient for conventional SaaS where every customer runs essentially the same schema and application code.

## Core architecture

Instead of shared tables with `tenant_id` + RLS, or one heavyweight database server/process per tenant:

```
                  ONE NODE / PROCESS
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ API / query / function runtime           │
│                  │                       │
│          tenant-aware router             │
│                  │                       │
│      ┌───────────┼───────────┐           │
│      ▼           ▼           ▼           │
│    A.db        B.db        C.db           │
│   SQLite      SQLite      SQLite          │
│                                          │
│ shared runtime, schema, migrations,      │
│ authz, realtime, caches, telemetry       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

SQLite is in-process, so this is not N SQLite server processes. Maintain a bounded/LRU set of open handles for hot tenants; cold tenants remain durable state with essentially no dedicated compute or RAM.

At larger scale:

```
                    Global router
                         │
                tenant → placement
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          ▼              ▼              ▼
        Node A          Node B          Node C
       many DBs        many DBs        many DBs
```

The tenant DB becomes the native shard, isolation, lifecycle, and mobility unit.

## Why this may be efficient for shared-schema SaaS

For something like a todo SaaS:

```
Todo App
schema v42
functions v17
indexes ...
      │
      ├── tenant A.db
      ├── tenant B.db
      ├── tenant C.db
      └── tenant D.db
```

Almost everything can be amortized.

**Shared per application/process**
- SQLite/libSQL engine
- function/runtime code
- schema definition
- generated query code / prepared-query templates
- migration definitions
- authorization engine
- realtime/sync machinery
- telemetry
- handle/cache management

**Per tenant**
- SQLite DB/state
- WAL/replication state
- routing/schema-version metadata
- working-set cache only while active

The hypothesis is that this can achieve very high density for huge numbers of small or mostly-idle tenants while retaining stronger physical isolation than shared-table tenancy.

## Isolation and AuthZ

Do not make RLS the application authorization abstraction.

```
request
→ authenticate
→ resolve application + tenant
→ authorize subject/action/resource/context
→ route to tenant DB
→ execute
```

Normal queries should not require `WHERE tenant_id = ?`: another tenant's rows simply do not exist in the selected database.

Within-tenant permissions remain an AuthZ/policy problem. DB-level mechanisms may still exist as defense in depth.

## Convex-like DX hypothesis

Investigate whether this substrate makes a Convex-like backend much easier without building a storage engine from scratch.

```ts
export const createTodo = mutation({
  args: { text: v.string() },
  handler: async (ctx, args) => {
    return ctx.db.insert("todos", {
      text: args.text,
      completed: false,
    });
  },
});
```

Internally:

```
request
→ identity
→ application
→ tenant
→ authz
→ placement/router
→ tenant SQLite/libSQL DB
→ transaction
```

Developer mental model: one application/database.

Physical model: potentially hundreds of thousands or millions of isolated SQLite DBs sharing one application definition.

## Realtime / Zero

Explore a Zero-style sync layer instead of reproducing Convex's reactive database internals from scratch:

```
client reactive query
        │
local materialized state
        │
      sync
        │
realtime gateway
        │
tenant change stream
        │
tenant.db
```

Tenant DBs are naturally independent synchronization domains.

Research:
- current Zero architecture and DB assumptions
- feasibility over SQLite/libSQL/Turso
- direct adoption vs adaptation vs borrowing protocol/query architecture
- SQLite/libSQL hooks/CDC/change capture
- dependency/invalidation granularity
- optimistic writes and offline operation
- keeping realtime gateways separate from DB compute so WebSockets do not pin tenant runtimes

## Scale to zero

Target lifecycle:

```
HOT
resident handle/runtime/cache
   ↓ idle
WARM
cached handle/placement
   ↓ idle
COLD
durable DB only
CPU ≈ 0
RAM ≈ 0
```

Activation:

```
request
→ route
→ acquire worker
→ open/attach DB
→ execute
→ eventually evict
```

The difficult part is not suspension itself but fast/correct activation: concurrent wakeups, write ownership, WAL/replication catch-up, migration state, cache reconstruction, subscriptions, and routing races.

## Shared schema + fleet migrations

One desired schema:

```
application desired_schema = v58
```

Independent convergence:

```
A.db v58 ✓
B.db v58 ✓
C.db v57 → migrate
D.db cold → potentially migrate on activation
```

Investigate eager vs lazy migration, compatibility windows, canaries, failure isolation, extremely stale cold DBs, schema-version routing, and whether prepared query/schema metadata can be shared across identically shaped DB handles.

## Hot tenant graduation

Application code should remain unchanged as physical placement changes:

```
cold tenant → shared node
active tenant → sticky/warm worker
hot tenant → dedicated worker/node
very large tenant → dedicated replication/resources
```

Explore live tenant movement, draining, replication/copy, router cutover, and useful libSQL/Turso primitives.

## Cross-tenant operations

Cross-tenant queries become fan-out/distributed operations. Treat this as an explicit tradeoff.

Prefer:

```
tenant OLTP DBs
      │
   CDC/events
      ▼
shared analytical plane / lake / OLAP / derived indexes
```

rather than compromising tenant OLTP isolation for global analytics.

## Relationship to Norn

Keep these motivations separate:

**Norn native tenant runtime**
```
organization
→ unique DB/runtime
→ potentially unique ontology/schema/config/extensions
```

Tenant is a genuine computational/data domain.

**Shared-schema application runtime**
```
application definition
→ identical schema/code
→ many isolated tenant DBs
```

Tenant is primarily an isolation/sharding/lifecycle/placement domain.

The latter may reuse Norn infrastructure for routing, placement, SQLite/libSQL lifecycle, backups, replication, migrations, AuthZ, observability, runtime scheduling, scale-to-zero, and realtime.

## Key research questions

- What existing systems implement **one process multiplexing many independent SQLite DBs**, not merely provisioning one remote DB service per tenant?
- How many SQLite/libSQL DBs can one process/node realistically manage?
- Practical open-handle/file-descriptor limits and optimal LRU strategy?
- Filesystem/object-storage metadata cost at 10k/100k/1m DBs?
- WAL and page-cache overhead per hot DB?
- Can prepared statements/query plans/schema metadata be amortized across identically shaped DBs?
- Best write-ownership model?
- Which libSQL/Turso replication components are reusable/embeddable?
- Can a tenant move between nodes with negligible downtime?
- Cold activation latency?
- Failure mode when one tenant exceeds SQLite's preferred write/concurrency envelope?
- Can Zero provide the realtime/client-sync layer?
- What Convex semantics still need to be implemented above SQLite?
- Which remaining pieces are database-engine work versus platform/runtime work?
- Economics vs shared Postgres + RLS, Neon-style serverless Postgres, D1, Turso Cloud database-per-tenant, and conventional sharding?

## Prototype / benchmark

Build a deliberately small benchmark before committing architecturally:

1. Single Rust process.
2. One common schema.
3. Generate 10k–100k small tenant SQLite/libSQL DBs.
4. Tenant-aware request router.
5. Bounded LRU DB-handle cache.
6. Mixed concurrent read/write workload with realistic hot/warm/cold distribution.
7. Measure cold-open latency, warm latency, throughput, RAM, FDs, disk/cache behavior, WAL overhead, and noisy-neighbor effects.
8. Apply one schema migration using eager and lazy fleet strategies.
9. Move a live tenant between two worker processes/nodes.
10. Prototype change capture + realtime subscription for a small todo app.
11. Compare where useful with shared SQLite/Postgres and hosted Turso/D1-style approaches.

## Success criteria

Interesting if evidence shows:
- idle tenant marginal CPU/RAM approaches zero;
- one node can economically host a very large DB fleet;
- activation latency is interactive;
- hot tenants can graduate without app changes;
- shared-schema fleet migration is tractable;
- realtime can be layered on without inventing a storage engine;
- physical tenancy materially simplifies application multitenancy;
- Convex-like DX is plausible while delegating transactions/query planning/storage to SQLite/libSQL.

## Non-goals

- Do not replace Norn's existing tenant-storage direction based on this exploration.
- Do not build a SQL parser, planner, B-tree, WAL, or transactional engine unless evidence requires it.
- Do not assume Turso Cloud is required; distinguish hosted Turso from reusable libSQL/Turso technology.
- Do not assume Zero is the realtime answer until current compatibility is verified.
- Do not optimize for cross-tenant OLTP transactions.

**Deliverable:** research plus a benchmarkable prototype design, not a production implementation.

Migrated from `norn-platform#2662`.

items.title: Implement Effect Cluster sharding and multi-runner recovery in the fresh Eventiva backend
items.body:
## Finding — fresh production core is not yet Effect Cluster-backed

Verified on `Resnovas/Eventiva` `main` (2026-11-15): `apps/server/package.json` includes `@effect/cluster@0.60.5` and `@effect/workflow@0.19.1`, but `apps/server/src/main.ts` constructs only a **local, in-process** `ActionHostLive`, registers `platform.status`, attempts one invocation with fail-closed audit and exits. No current production source file implements or starts SQL-backed Effect Cluster runners, shard ownership/routing, runner registration, load distribution or failover. `@eventiva/runtime` correctly remains provider-neutral and must NOT import Cluster directly. Historical two-runner spike Resnovas/Eventiva#785 used archived pre-rebuild `@effect/cluster@0.56.4` and does not prove the rebuilt workspace is distributed.

### Goal

Make the **current** Effect v3 backend execute eligible Eventiva actions and durable work across multiple independent **Effect Cluster** runner processes with DB-supported shard ownership, observability, graceful drain, crash recovery, idempotent persistence and tenant isolation. Preserve one action/authorization/audit path for UI/API/agents; shard by canonical entity/work identity, **not** by splitting tenant databases or bypassing the authorized ActionHost.

### Scope

1. Reconcile the actual `@effect/cluster@0.60.5` API and `@effect/workflow@0.19.1` with Effect v3 and Resnovas/Eventiva#785's measured legacy behavior. Do **not** copy archived old code by default or assume older `NodeClusterSocket.layer({storage: 'sql'})` signatures still apply. If new dependency/version is needed, request explicit approval first.
2. Define portable action-to-durable-entity/work message envelopes and stable correlation/primary/idempotency keys. Keep contracts/schema/runtime shared packages driver-free; Effect Cluster, Node runner transport, Postgres adapters and infrastructure belong in backend integration/composition roots.
3. Build an actual **2-runner** launch/test harness against isolated PostgreSQL 17 (CI/local); validate compatibility with production target Neon PostgreSQL 17 in London, including direct/pooled connection suitability, advisory locks and tenant database routing. Existing Neon dev project is synthetic-only; no CDC/logical replication needed or permitted for this feature.
4. Confirm shards are assigned only to processes hosting required entity types (avoid the legacy empty 'shard-manager' bug from Resnovas/Eventiva#804), and define configurable shards-per-group, heartbeat/lease/expiry, drain and runner-health visibility per Resnovas/Eventiva#805.
5. Mutating and sensitive operations preserve authorized Effect action invocation, A1 atomic domain+idempotency+history+outbox+audit transaction semantics, and persisted-by-default, per-entity-ordered handling with deduplication under at-least-once delivery (Resnovas/Eventiva#806). Never claim exactly-once execution from transport.
6. Long-running agent, schedule and production jobs use Workflow activities and recoverable checkpoints rather than blocking entity mailboxes (related Resnovas/Eventiva#801/35/36/54), with later feature-specific implementation staged appropriately.
7. Include operational documentation, graphs and test instrumentation; do not confuse compute sharding with database-per-tenant architecture.

### Acceptance

* Two separate Node runner processes demonstrably each own shards and process their relevant entities under load.
* Graceful runner drain and SIGKILL/failure/recovery tests show ownership reallocation, continuity of persisted work, no *double-applied business mutations*, per-entity order, clear measured failover and no false delivery guarantees.
* A deliberate duplicate/replay with identical idempotency key returns one persisted result; volatile behavior is explicitly documented and never used for financial, dispatch or safety-critical effects.
* An empty/non-entity runner cannot silently capture shards it cannot serve.
* Tenant A operations never route into tenant B data; all action, permission and audit policies still enforce with runner relocation.
* Automated checks pass, CI evidence and exact commands are recorded, and code is committed directly to `main` with signed conventional commit after Resnovas/Eventiva#807/Resnovas/Eventiva#809 integration gates.

### Dependencies and coordination

Implementation requires the current Resnovas/Eventiva#807 authorized action host and Resnovas/Eventiva#809 SQL-storage adapter/conformance to land. In the meantime a GPT/Codex **read-only compatibility/design orb** may investigate Resnovas/Eventiva#785 legacy results, current package APIs and tests without editing files owned by Resnovas/Eventiva#807/Resnovas/Eventiva#809. Resnovas/Eventiva#804/38/39 remain useful finding references but require re-scoping for the clean rebuild. No new dependencies, paid services, Neon resource changes or other infrastructure provisioning are approved by this planning issue.

**Source evidence**: Resnovas/Eventiva#779 'Server-side sharding and load distribution', Resnovas/Eventiva#785 S5 tested legacy two-runner setup, Resnovas/Eventiva#804/38/39, Resnovas/Eventiva#821; live `apps/server/src/main.ts`, `apps/server/package.json`, `packages/runtime/src/host.ts` on `main`.

items.title: CDC Polling multiple databases
items.body:
Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.
I'm developing a B2B SaaS application where customer data is segregated at the database level, and requests are routed via the session and database driver. However, the current polling mechanism only allows polling from a single database, which creates a limitation for change data capture (CDC).

I need to track events in real time, such as user actions triggering notifications. Since CDC does not work across multiple databases efficiently, I'm forced to use the v5 LTS version of the GraphQL library, which allows me to handle this at the resolver level. While this works for now, it presents scalability concerns as the application grows.

Describe the solution you'd like
I would like a way to support polling across multiple databases natively, ensuring that events from different databases can be captured and processed efficiently. Ideally, this would be done in a way that minimizes performance overhead and ensures real-time event streaming without requiring resolver-level workarounds.

Describe alternatives you've considered
Polling per database instance – This is inefficient and scales poorly.
Using the v5 LTS GraphQL library – Works at the resolver level but is not sustainable long-term.
Event-driven architecture with a separate event bus – Would require significant changes and additional infrastructure, which may not be feasible in the short term.
Additional context
This is a common challenge for multi-tenant applications that segregate data by database. A more efficient CDC mechanism that supports multi-database polling would benefit many SaaS applications following this model.
