items.title: Externalize security audit logs and application logging

labels.name: type:epic
labels.description: Epic: Parent issue tracking multiple related tasks

items.body:
## Problem

Security audit logs (the tamper-evident SHA-256 hash chain) and general application logs are currently stored in the same PostgreSQL instance that serves the application. This is bad practice for several reasons:

- **Separation of concerns**: An attacker who compromises the application database has access to the audit trail they'd want to tamper with
- **Regulatory risk**: GDPR Article 17 (right to erasure) conflicts with immutable audit logs when they share infrastructure — isolation makes compliance boundaries clearer
- **Operational risk**: Audit log volume (every authenticated API request) competes with application queries for connection pool slots, disk I/O, and vacuum cycles
- **Forensics**: If the application DB goes down, you lose the audit trail at the exact moment you need it most

## Current State

- `security_audit_log` table lives in the main `pagespace` PostgreSQL database alongside user data, pages, drives, etc.
- `SecurityAuditService` (in `packages/lib/src/audit/security-audit.ts`) writes directly via Drizzle ORM using the same connection pool
- Hash chain integrity verification (`cron/verify-audit-chain`) runs against the same DB
- Application logs (`logger-database.ts`) also write to PostgreSQL
- **Audit coverage is now at ~100%** — 248 routes, ~234 directly audited, ~14 genuinely exempt (PRs #876-889)

## Desired State

- Security audit logs ship to a dedicated, append-only store (separate PostgreSQL instance, or a purpose-built log store)
- Application logs go to a structured logging pipeline (stdout → collector → external store)
- SIEM delivery via cursor-based pg-boss worker to external SIEM (Splunk, Datadog, etc.)
- The application DB contains only application data

## Context: Monolith Database Decomposition

This is part of the larger infrastructure roadmap documented in `prototypes/pagespace-endgame` (see `DatabasePane.tsx` for the full migration path and `ObservabilityPane.tsx` for the SIEM delivery architecture).

The endgame envisions breaking the monolithic PostgreSQL into properly isolated containers:

- **Application DB** — users, pages, drives, permissions, tasks
- **Audit/Security DB** — security audit log, hash chain, compliance events (append-only, restricted write access)
- **Session store** — already partially in Redis, but session metadata is still in PG
- **Analytics/Telemetry** — AI usage logs, pulse metrics, activity tracking
- **Per-org isolation** — eventual migration from single VPS (75 tables, ~18-20 tenant cap) to per-org database isolation with global control plane

Each concern gets its own container with appropriate access controls, backup policies, and retention rules. The audit DB in particular should have restricted write access (append-only) and separate credentials from the application.

## Implementation Notes

- `SecurityAuditService` already has a clean interface — swapping the storage backend is a matter of changing the repository layer, not the call sites
- The 248 route-level `logAuditEvent()` calls don't need to change — they're fire-and-forget through the service abstraction
- Hash chain verification needs to move with the audit data
- The endgame prototype already designed the SIEM delivery pipeline (cursor-based pg-boss worker) — this just needs to be built
- Consider whether the audit store should be write-only from the application's perspective (reads only via a separate admin interface)

items.title: eval: consider ClickHouse as primary store for billing analytics
items.body:
## Background

The current stack stores FOCUS 1.2 billing line items in PostgreSQL (`billing_line_items` table, 40+ columns, indexed on `billingPeriodStart/End`). This works for early development but PostgreSQL is an OLTP row-store — as billing data volumes grow into hundreds of millions or billions of rows, full-period aggregation queries will become the dominant performance bottleneck.

ClickHouse is a purpose-built columnar OLAP database with an Apache 2.0 licence that has become the de-facto standard for real-time billing and cost analytics at scale. Its design maps naturally to FOCUS billing data.

## Why ClickHouse fits FOCUS billing data

FOCUS 1.2 uses an **append-only correction model**: when a cloud provider discovers a billing error, it emits a new row with `ChargeClass = 'Correction'` — the original row is never mutated. This means billing data is structurally immutable from ingestion onward, which is a perfect fit for ClickHouse's MergeTree engine (which is designed for immutable sorted parts). ClickHouse's known weakness — expensive async mutations — is irrelevant for correction-model data.

Query patterns (aggregating `EffectiveCost` over time ranges, grouped by `ServiceName`, `ResourceId`, `Provider`, filtered by `BillingPeriod`) are exactly the columnar scan patterns ClickHouse is vectorised to execute.

Published benchmarks and real-world migrations show:
- 10–100x query latency reduction vs PostgreSQL on large billing datasets
- 10–30x storage compression (LZ4/ZSTD per-column codecs)
- Sub-second aggregations over billions of rows on modest hardware

## ClickHouse limitations to evaluate

- **Mutations are expensive and async.** `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE/DELETE` rewrites entire data parts in the background. No transactional consistency during mutation. This is a non-issue for billing data (append-only), but matters for any metadata co-located in ClickHouse.
- **Not suitable for OLTP.** User accounts, tenant configs, cost allocation rules, and workflow state require frequent updates and transactional guarantees — these must remain in PostgreSQL.
- **Operational complexity.** Self-hosting ClickHouse on Kubernetes (via the Altinity operator) requires managing ClickHouse Keeper (the ZooKeeper replacement), replication topology, and shard configuration. ClickHouse Cloud eliminates this at a cost premium.

## Recommended architecture: PostgreSQL + ClickHouse hybrid

| Data type | Store | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Billing line items (FOCUS) | ClickHouse | Columnar, analytical, append-only model, 10–100x query performance |
| App data (users, tenants, rules) | PostgreSQL (managed) | OLTP, full TypeORM/NestJS compatibility, CRUD/ACID |

The split is clean: the billing ingestion service writes directly to ClickHouse (dual-write, not routed through PostgreSQL). NestJS queries PostgreSQL for app state and ClickHouse for cost analytics via separate connection pools. No CDC or cross-system sync required for the core use case.

## Multi-tenancy in ClickHouse

Three patterns are supported; the recommended progression:

1. **Shared table with `tenant_id` in partition and primary key + ClickHouse row policies** — simplest to operate, good for early scale. Row policies transparently append `WHERE tenant_id = ...` at the database layer.
2. **Separate database per tenant** (`billing_acme`, `billing_globocorp`) — per-tenant TTL, partitioning, and data retention policies; clean GDPR deletion story (drop database). Suitable for large or regulated tenants.
3. **Separate cluster per tenant** — only for strict data residency requirements.

## Deployment options

- **ClickHouse Cloud** (recommended for early stage): managed, separated compute+storage, auto-pausing, no ZooKeeper/Keeper management. Note: 2025 pricing revision introduced egress fees — factor this into long-term cost modelling.
- **Altinity Kubernetes Operator** (v0.26, Apache 2.0): production-proven self-hosted K8s deployment, manages `ClickHouseInstallation` CRDs, rolling upgrades, replica management. Appropriate once the team has K8s DevOps capacity.

## Application integration

ClickHouse exposes an HTTP interface and a native TCP protocol. The `@clickhouse/client` Node.js SDK (official, maintained by ClickHouse Inc.) provides a typed query API. Billing queries are analytical SQL — TypeORM is not needed (and not appropriate) for ClickHouse; use the SDK directly in a `ClickHouseBillingRepository` service.

## Alternatives considered

- **TimescaleDB** (PostgreSQL extension with columnar compression and hypertables): viable up to ~100M rows with 10–100x query speedup over vanilla PostgreSQL. Simpler stack (one database). Does not close the performance gap for multi-billion-row datasets or sub-second interactive dashboards. Consider as a fallback if a single-database constraint is hard.
- **PostgreSQL with pg_partman + indexing**: reasonable for the current dataset; will not scale to the analytical query patterns expected in a production FinOps platform.

## Tasks

- [ ] Benchmark current PostgreSQL query performance on a representative billing dataset (1M, 100M rows)
- [ ] Evaluate ClickHouse Cloud vs self-hosted (Altinity operator) based on team capacity and cost
- [ ] Design ClickHouse schema for `billing_line_items` (partition by `toYYYYMM(billingPeriodStart)`, primary key `(tenant_id, billingPeriodStart, provider, serviceCategory)`)
- [ ] Implement `@clickhouse/client` adapter in billing ingestion service (replace/parallel to TypeORM insert)
- [ ] Implement ClickHouse row policies for tenant isolation (or per-database isolation if required)
- [ ] Migrate existing billing ingestion endpoint to write directly to ClickHouse
- [ ] Evaluate whether TimescaleDB is an acceptable interim step before committing to the hybrid stack
- [ ] Decide on multi-tenancy isolation level (shared table vs per-database) and document the decision

---
## Deutsche Fassung

## Hintergrund

Der aktuelle Stack speichert FOCUS-1.2-Abrechnungspositionen in PostgreSQL – Tabelle `billing_line_items` mit mehr als 40 Spalten und Indizes auf `billingPeriodStart/End`. Das funktioniert in der frühen Entwicklung, PostgreSQL ist jedoch ein zeilenorientierter OLTP-Speicher. Wenn das Abrechnungsvolumen auf Hunderte Millionen oder Milliarden Zeilen anwächst, werden Aggregationsabfragen über vollständige Perioden zum dominierenden Leistungsengpass.

ClickHouse ist eine speziell entwickelte spaltenorientierte OLAP-Datenbank unter Apache 2.0 und hat sich als De-facto-Standard für Echtzeit-Abrechnungs- und Kostenanalysen im großen Maßstab etabliert. Ihr Design passt natürlich zu FOCUS-Abrechnungsdaten.

## Warum ClickHouse zu FOCUS-Abrechnungsdaten passt

FOCUS 1.2 verwendet ein **Append-only-Korrekturmodell**: Entdeckt ein Cloud-Provider einen Abrechnungsfehler, erzeugt er eine neue Zeile mit `ChargeClass = 'Correction'`; die ursprüngliche Zeile wird nie verändert. Abrechnungsdaten sind damit ab der Datenübernahme strukturell unveränderlich – ideal für die MergeTree Engine von ClickHouse, die auf unveränderliche sortierte Teile ausgelegt ist. Die bekannte ClickHouse-Schwäche teurer asynchroner Mutationen spielt für dieses Korrekturmodell keine Rolle.

Abfragemuster wie die Aggregation von `EffectiveCost` über Zeiträume, gruppiert nach `ServiceName`, `ResourceId` oder `Provider` und gefiltert nach `BillingPeriod`, entsprechen genau den spaltenorientierten Scans, die ClickHouse vektorisiert ausführt.

Veröffentlichte Benchmarks und reale Migrationen zeigen:
- 10- bis 100-fach niedrigere Abfragelatenzen als PostgreSQL bei großen Abrechnungsdatensätzen,
- 10- bis 30-fache Speicherkompression durch spaltenspezifische LZ4-/ZSTD-Codecs,
- Aggregationen über Milliarden Zeilen in weniger als einer Sekunde auf moderater Hardware.

## Zu bewertende Einschränkungen von ClickHouse

- **Mutationen sind teuer und asynchron.** `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE/DELETE` schreibt ganze Datenteile im Hintergrund neu; währenddessen besteht keine transaktionale Konsistenz. Für Append-only-Abrechnungsdaten unproblematisch, aber relevant für gemeinsam gespeicherte Metadaten.
- **Nicht für OLTP geeignet.** Benutzerkonten, Mandantenkonfigurationen, Kostenverteilungsregeln und Workflow-Zustand benötigen häufige Updates und Transaktionsgarantien; sie müssen in PostgreSQL verbleiben.
- **Betriebliche Komplexität.** Selbst gehostetes ClickHouse auf Kubernetes mit Altinity Operator erfordert Verwaltung von ClickHouse Keeper, Replikationstopologie und Sharding. ClickHouse Cloud vermeidet dies gegen einen Preisaufschlag.

## Empfohlene Architektur: Hybrid aus PostgreSQL und ClickHouse

| Datentyp | Speicher | Begründung |
|---|---|---|
| Abrechnungspositionen – FOCUS | ClickHouse | spaltenorientiertes analytisches Append-only-Modell und 10- bis 100-fache Abfrageleistung |
| App-Daten – Benutzer, Mandanten, Regeln | verwaltetes PostgreSQL | OLTP, vollständige TypeORM-/NestJS-Kompatibilität und CRUD/ACID |

Die Trennung ist klar: Der Ingestion Service schreibt direkt nach ClickHouse – Dual Write, nicht über PostgreSQL. NestJS fragt PostgreSQL für App-Zustand und ClickHouse über getrennte Connection Pools für Kostenanalysen ab. Für den Kernanwendungsfall sind weder CDC noch systemübergreifende Synchronisierung erforderlich.

## Multi-Tenancy in ClickHouse

Drei unterstützte Muster mit empfohlener Entwicklung:

1. **Gemeinsame Tabelle mit `tenant_id` in Partition und Primärschlüssel sowie ClickHouse Row Policies:** einfachster Betrieb, gut für frühe Skalierung. Row Policies ergänzen auf Datenbankebene transparent `WHERE tenant_id = ...`.
2. **Eigene Datenbank pro Mandant** wie `billing_acme` oder `billing_globocorp`: mandantenspezifische TTL, Partitionierung und Aufbewahrung; saubere DSGVO-Löschung durch Löschen der Datenbank. Geeignet für große oder regulierte Mandanten.
3. **Eigener Cluster pro Mandant:** nur bei strikten Anforderungen an Datenresidenz.

## Deployment-Optionen

- **ClickHouse Cloud – für die Frühphase empfohlen:** verwaltet, getrennte Compute- und Storage-Ressourcen, Auto-Pause, keine Verwaltung von ZooKeeper oder Keeper. Die Preisänderung 2025 führte Egress-Gebühren ein; diese in langfristige Kostenmodelle einbeziehen.
- **Altinity Kubernetes Operator – Version 0.26, Apache 2.0:** produktionserprobtes selbst gehostetes K8s-Deployment mit Verwaltung von `ClickHouseInstallation`-CRDs, Rolling Upgrades und Replikaten. Sinnvoll, sobald das Team ausreichende K8s-DevOps-Kapazität besitzt.

## Anwendungsintegration

ClickHouse bietet HTTP und ein natives TCP-Protokoll. Das offizielle Node.js SDK `@clickhouse/client` stellt eine typisierte Query-API bereit. Abrechnungsabfragen sind analytisches SQL; TypeORM wird für ClickHouse weder benötigt noch empfohlen. Das SDK direkt in einem Service `ClickHouseBillingRepository` verwenden.

## Bewertete Alternativen

- **TimescaleDB:** PostgreSQL-Erweiterung mit spaltenorientierter Kompression und Hypertables; bis etwa 100 Millionen Zeilen tragfähig, mit 10- bis 100-facher Beschleunigung gegenüber einfachem PostgreSQL. Einfacherer Stack, aber bei Milliarden Zeilen oder interaktiven Dashboards unter einer Sekunde bleibt eine Leistungslücke. Als Rückfalloption bei harter Ein-Datenbank-Vorgabe erwägen.
- **PostgreSQL mit pg_partman und Indizes:** für den aktuellen Datensatz vernünftig, skaliert aber nicht auf die analytischen Abfragemuster einer produktiven FinOps-Plattform.

## Aufgaben

- [ ] Aktuelle PostgreSQL-Abfrageleistung mit repräsentativen Datensätzen von einer Million und 100 Millionen Zeilen benchmarken.
- [ ] ClickHouse Cloud und selbst gehosteten Altinity Operator anhand Teamkapazität und Kosten vergleichen.
- [ ] ClickHouse-Schema für `billing_line_items` entwerfen: Partition nach `toYYYYMM(billingPeriodStart)`, Primärschlüssel `(tenant_id, billingPeriodStart, provider, serviceCategory)`.
- [ ] Adapter mit `@clickhouse/client` im Ingestion Service implementieren – als Ersatz oder parallel zu TypeORM Insert.
- [ ] ClickHouse Row Policies für Mandantenisolation implementieren oder bei Bedarf Datenbanken trennen.
- [ ] Bestehenden Ingestion-Endpunkt auf direktes Schreiben nach ClickHouse migrieren.
- [ ] Bewerten, ob TimescaleDB als Zwischenschritt vor dem hybriden Stack akzeptabel ist.
- [ ] Isolationsniveau für Multi-Tenancy festlegen – gemeinsame Tabelle oder eigene Datenbank – und Entscheidung dokumentieren.

items.title: Move live memory to Postgres and keep vector search in ClickHouse
items.body:
### Component

Memory and search

### Use case

Loom needs to support frequent point reads and writes alongside tenant-scoped retrieval and scans over billions of records. These workloads should not all use the same write path.

A memory write needs ordered versions, compare-and-set, locks and pin checks. ClickHouse serves retrieval and analytics, but its part creation and merge costs make individual committed inserts a poor fit for this workload. [#129](https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/pull/129) batches several request-path tables; it leaves the main memory tables committed.

The sizing assumptions are 5,000 tenants, 50,000 namespaces, 1,000–50,000 memory writes/sec and up to 10,000 user searches/sec. These are design inputs, not measured capacity or production traffic. If all 50,000 writes need a semantic conflict check, that adds 50,000 retrievals/sec before user search, extra retrieval legs or background work. At a sustained 50,000 writes/sec, the system also produces 4.32 billion write events/day.

Quality is the highest priority: retrieval and admission verdicts must use the right revisions, preserve tenant and access boundaries, and retain the evidence needed for recovery. Scalability and low end-to-end latency are required alongside that quality. Optimize cost and component count only within those guarantees; do not trade away recall, durability or access checks to meet a throughput number.

The goals are point reads without a second database lookup, transactional writes, fresh search results, and bounded ingest and retention costs. Postgres and ClickHouse are the only databases. All stored vectors and vector search stay in ClickHouse. The sizing inputs describe a deployment spread across placement units; they are not a promise that one Postgres primary or one namespace sustains the aggregate peak.

### Describe the solution you'd like

#### Storage ownership

Postgres stores current memory content, not just its latest version and hash.

| Workload | Storage |
| --- | --- |
| Current memory content, metadata, versions, locks, pins and compare-and-set | Postgres |
| Working memory, task state, idempotency and delivery claims | Postgres |
| Identity, grants, revocation and mutable namespace configuration | Postgres |
| Revision journal and enrichment jobs | Postgres, retained until their required deliveries complete |
| Embeddings, lexical and vector retrieval, searchable metadata and derived graph projections | ClickHouse |
| Historical revisions, conversation archives, audit queries, usage and rollups | ClickHouse |
| Large immutable code-index artifacts and compiler graph generations | ClickHouse |

Every live record has one authority. Preserve `(org, namespace, agent, user_id, session_id)`, stable record identity, source revision, actor, source class and attestation through both stores. The server derives provenance from the authenticated writer and operation. Org-wide identifiers must still pass the same scope checks without revealing another tenant's records. A ClickHouse projection cannot grant access to a record Postgres refuses.

The Postgres transaction atomically records current content, the complete immutable revision, required delivery jobs, the idempotency state and a hash-only mutation audit event. Keep mutable delivery progress separate from revision payloads so job updates do not replicate the content again. A search document is a derived serving representation, not the revision journal or the audit record. Required audit events are durable before the audited operation completes; best-effort usage metrics have a separate delivery contract.

Keep the existing ClickHouse-only install path for smaller deployments. This proposal defines the Postgres+ClickHouse path. Record the selected authority and reject replicas configured for a different one; an outage must not silently switch a deployment between them.

#### WalShadow replication and enrichment have different jobs

Use [ClickHouse Managed Postgres](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres) with [WalShadow](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres/sync-to-clickhouse/walshadow) for selected database mirrors and revision events. WalShadow is the first implementation path. Loom should not build a general WAL transport or run two writers into the same destination projection.

Build and test the replication path with WalShadow. Judge it by source load, replication lag, payload correctness and recovery under Loom workloads. Its private-preview status alone is not a reason to defer implementation or choose ClickPipes. A documented or reproduced limitation that blocks a required guarantee is a release blocker, not an accepted reduction in quality. Replication benchmarks are not a latency guarantee for a Loom operation.

Pin the evaluated WalShadow build and replication configuration. Its documented limits include failure to continue after an unplanned primary promotion and unresolved large-value reconstruction cases. Validate complete revision payloads, including large text and JSON values, against source hashes through initial load, updates, cleanup and restart. A selected value mode that can substitute missing or incorrect bytes does not qualify for archival delivery. Keep WalShadow as the first implementation path, resolve blocking limitations, and reconsider the transport if it cannot satisfy the required guarantees ([limits](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/544c340d17039d2b24068897c6f616b9e67e1ac6/docs/limitations.md), [failover protocol](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/544c340d17039d2b24068897c6f616b9e67e1ac6/docs/failover.md)).

Replicate an explicit allowlist of tables and columns. Destination identities must distinguish source placement units, databases and tenants, including during a tenant move. Mutable configuration mirrors serve analytics, not authorization. Account for WalShadow recovery state and large-value mirrors in capacity, access control, backup and erasure inventories.

Loom still needs enrichment jobs. CDC does not generate embeddings or decide when a revision is searchable. These jobs read committed revisions directly from Postgres and publish search documents into ClickHouse without first waiting for the CDC mirror.

A search document carries its source revision, content hash, embedding-model and preprocessing versions, chunk identity, text and filter metadata. Reuse an embedding only when its input and model contract match. A worker can rebuild the document from a retained revision or its confirmed archive. Vectors never pass through Postgres tables or its revision journal.

Readiness is recorded only after every projection required by that operation is delivered and visible. Optional graph or analytics work does not delay a write unless its contract requires it. Lexical publication can precede embedding completion, but it must not mark semantic search ready or weaken ordinary `memory.set` success semantics.

#### Writes and point reads

For a semantic `memory.set`:

1. Validate the value and access scope. Start embedding work and the required search-freshness check concurrently.
2. Check duplicates, conflicts and protected memories against sufficiently fresh state.
3. In a short Postgres transaction, recheck the key version and relevant guards, update current content, and record the complete revision and required jobs.
4. Publish the required search projection directly into ClickHouse.
5. Return success after the operation's promised visibility is satisfied.

Do not hold a database transaction open during inference or ClickHouse queries. Reuse embeddings computed during admission, and reuse existing embeddings for metadata-only changes.

Postgres handles same-key compare-and-set atomically. For cross-key semantic admission, capture a generation for every scope whose state can change the verdict and wait for its required search projections. Every relevant creation, update, pin, blacklist, access-policy or model-manifest change advances the corresponding generation in the mutation transaction. After inference and retrieval, compare those generations again in the short commit transaction and advance them with the write. Checking only returned candidate versions misses a peer created while the check was running. A Postgres isolation level alone does not track predicates evaluated in ClickHouse. Recheck time-based expiry and lock leases at commit; a generation does not track the passage of time.

Enforce pinned and blacklist protections separately from approximate result ranking. A contract that refuses peers above a similarity threshold needs a complete check over eligible protected peers; an ANN or quantized shortlist alone cannot prove that no protected peer matches. Evaluate the false-accept and false-refusal rates of semantic verdicts as well as retrieval recall.

Use a deterministic lock order across affected scopes, bounded retries and one request deadline. Batch admissions within busy conflict scopes, including interactions between writes in the batch; vector comparisons still execute in ClickHouse. A namespace-wide invariant still needs namespace-wide coordination; do not split that scope or omit checks to claim horizontal scalability. Measure its sustainable rate and reject excess work explicitly before queues grow without bound.

`memory.set` and `bulk_set` keep their inline verdicts, including pinned refusals. Deferred ingestion is a separate contract that reports pending enrichment. Ordinary transactional operations that need no semantic work finish at the Postgres commit.

A crash after that commit leaves a durable revision and a repairable job. Scope idempotency to the authenticated caller and operation, bind it to a request digest, and replay it only after current authorization. Reusing a key with different input is rejected. A projection timeout returns the committed revision, operation identity and pending state; a retry resumes that revision instead of admitting a second mutation. Specify status lookup, cancellation after commit, idempotency retention, expired-key behavior and the HTTP, MCP and SDK responses before changing the write path.

`memory.get` reads current content directly from Postgres. Strict current reads, final authorization and admission guards use the primary; replicas serve other reads only when their replay position meets the request's consistency requirement.

#### Retrieval and visibility

Strict search captures a finite committed barrier for its authorized scopes when admitted, including any caller-supplied write dependencies, then checks that the selected ClickHouse reader can serve the required projections. Later writes do not keep moving that barrier. This promises coverage through the captured barrier, not an atomic snapshot across the two databases. Current access and deletion checks still apply, and concurrent content changes can require bounded refill or an explicit incomplete result. Any weaker consistency mode is an explicit API contract, never an automatic timeout fallback.

Several writes share one visibility wait at a dependent search. Track a completed prefix with gaps or an equivalent durable manifest; event allocation order and the largest observed revision do not prove that earlier work committed or finished. A superseded revision can be resolved only when the protocol proves that its required serving effect is covered. An insertion acknowledgement or a readiness row on one replica is not proof for every reader. Bind the proof to the actual tables, serving generation and reader; re-establish it after rerouting or replica changes ([ClickHouse read consistency](https://clickhouse.com/docs/resources/support-center/knowledge-base/data-management/read-consistency)).

Track committed state and searchable readiness separately. Readiness includes the source revision, model version and reader visibility. A replication cursor or `max(event_id)` is not enough. WalShadow documents that different tables from one Postgres transaction can become visible in ClickHouse at different times ([consistency limits](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/main/docs/limitations.md#ordering-and-consistency)).

Retrieve lexical, semantic, entity and temporal candidates in ClickHouse. Apply tenant and known eligibility filters inside every retrieval leg, then batch-check candidate revisions, permissions, expiry and deletion state in Postgres before exposing snippets or sending content to an external reranker or answer model. Never attach current content to a score computed from an older revision. Apply the same checks to graph expansion, context assembly, caches, traces, exports and history APIs; an analytical mirror is not an access authority.

Candidate validation cannot recover a relevant revision absent from the search projection. Discard obsolete candidates, deduplicate by source identity and revision, and refill within bounded rounds, rows, bytes and time. Report readiness failures, refill exhaustion and missing required retrieval legs as explicit unavailable or incomplete outcomes. Do not label a truncated pool a complete empty result or let an answer model present it as complete evidence. Define authorization and revision check points for external dispatch and final response, and revalidate when the relevant access generation changes during a long request.

Tenant policy controls external model use and content egress. Partition result and model caches by access scope, source revisions, model and serving generation. Revocation and erasure invalidate affected entries; raw ClickHouse tables and `pg_clickhouse` must not expose an alternative route around these checks.

Keep the existing retrieval path as the baseline. Small eligible sets use tenant-scoped exact scans or an evaluated quantized shortlist with original-vector rescoring. Large tenants get dedicated placement and serving capacity.

[#131](https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/pull/131) found that the tested HNSW layout did not serve tenant reads and had recall and stale-version problems. Adding the same index is not the solution. Evaluate immutable indexed generations plus recent changes for large tenants, but require evidence that the index is used and that filtered recall holds before making that layout part of the serving path. [ClickHouse documents](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/annindexes) both filter trade-offs and index-building cost during inserts and merges.

Version the complete retrieval contract: embedding input and dimensions, lexical tokenization and ranking, filters, fusion, candidate budgets, reranking and temporal rules. Evaluate exact identifiers and phrases, semantic paraphrases, multilingual queries, negation, conflicting revisions, expiry and sparse tenants. Model size or exact vector-neighbor recall alone is not evidence of better final relevance or agent outcomes. Compare candidate generators, embedding and reranking choices on the same evaluation set; the existing path is a control, not a quality ceiling. Choose the strongest measured end-to-end quality that meets the declared capacity and latency requirements, then optimize p99 without lowering the quality gates. Keep citations tied to the validated source revision and test abstention when evidence is insufficient.

Build model and index changes as separate ClickHouse serving generations. Backfill, replay intervening changes and erasures, compare quality against the baseline, prove reader visibility, then atomically switch the Postgres serving manifest. A request pins one compatible model and generation until completion or timeout; retire a generation only after its readers drain. Never compare vectors from incompatible models. Retain a verified generation for rollback only within erasure and retention rules. Measure concurrent rebuild load and bound the recent-change set so it cannot become an unbounded exact scan.

Use [`pg_clickhouse`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/pg_clickhouse/blob/main/doc/pg_clickhouse.md) for unified SQL and analytical queries where the installed version pushes the work down. Keep native ClickHouse queries for the initial serving path. Check `EXPLAIN` before routing a query through Postgres: unsupported filters can prevent limit pushdown, and SQL compatibility alone says nothing about the cost.

#### Tenant placement and database branching

Tenant placement belongs to this architecture; [#157](https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/issues/157) consumes its routing and isolation contract. A tenant is the customer organization represented by `org`. A contract requiring a separately isolated workspace can register its owned namespace set as an explicit placement unit. Neither a user nor an agent/session automatically creates a new database.

| Boundary | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Tenant or registered workspace placement | Region, capacity, authority epoch, and shared or dedicated Postgres service |
| Namespace and collection | Project/content scope and sharing within the tenant |
| User and agent | Grants, private content and permitted actions within those scopes |

Use shared Postgres shards for ordinary tenants and a dedicated always-on service when measured load, residency or the isolation contract requires it. Dedicated placement means an independently sized service with the required HA configuration, not merely `CREATE DATABASE` inside the same resource pool. Personal accounts may have one user and one tenant; that does not make database-per-user the organization model. Keep users who collaborate on documents and memory within the same transactional placement unless an explicit isolation contract requires otherwise.

Route ordinary tenant transactions to one Postgres shard and colocate their transactional dependencies. Promote large tenants to dedicated services when measured load requires it. Managed Postgres offers vertical scaling and read replicas; horizontal write sharding remains a Loom placement decision ([scaling](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres/scaling)). Keep APIs, authoritative transactions, retrieval and validation in the tenant's home region to avoid inter-region round trips in ordinary requests.

Tenant placement includes a durable authority epoch. A move or shard split copies a consistent state, catches up required deliveries, fences and drains the old writers, verifies the destination and switches the route under a bounded write pause. Stale routers and workers cannot write through the old epoch. Split a large tenant only along independent transaction and admission scopes; cross-scope invariants do not become safe merely because the rows moved to separate shards.

Dedicated Postgres does not replace application isolation. Continue to bind every query and job to the identity tuple, current grants and placement epoch. ClickHouse, object storage and caches keep their own scoped access and placement contracts; a Postgres endpoint does not automatically isolate the rest of the product.

Evaluate Xata for dedicated-service provisioning, migration/CI environments and tenant sandboxes. Xata describes copy-on-write branches with independent compute ([branching](https://xata.io/postgres-branching)). That is a candidate capability, not a decision to replace ClickHouse Managed Postgres or a reason to create an instance for every tenant. Keep the first implementation path above until a provider comparison establishes the required guarantees.

Production services with interactive latency SLOs stay warm. Permit hibernation only for profiles whose declared SLO includes wake-up and cache warming; test reconnection storms and whether replication/background connections prevent idling ([scale-to-zero lifecycle](https://xata.io/scale-to-zero)). Copy-on-write reduces the cost of cloned unchanged blocks, not the compute and distinct data of thousands of independently active tenants.

Create new tenants from a clean schema/template. Never clone a shared multi-tenant production database into a new customer's security boundary. Data-bearing test branches stay within their tenant's authorized boundary, with anonymization or synthetic fixtures where required.

A Postgres branch is not a complete Loom fork. Register an environment/branch identity and pin a consistent baseline of database revisions, ClickHouse serving generations and artifact manifests. Use separate writable projection destinations, job claims and external-effect destinations. Cloned outbox rows, credentials or erasure jobs must not execute against production. An older copy of grants cannot restore revoked production access. Branch promotion uses the same fenced, reconciled cutover as any other authority change; do not assume automatic merging of business-state mutations.

Manage the fleet with bounded active-tenant connection pools, migration orchestration, credential rotation, per-source CDC progress, backups, failover and retirement. Budget source/replication connections, compute including HA, storage divergence and catch-up capacity at the expected number of concurrently active tenants. Database-per-tenant improves isolation and placement options; it does not remove a hot namespace's semantic coordination limit or establish better retrieval relevance.

Before changing the provider or placement default, qualify durability and failure-domain behavior, primary failover/fencing, PITR, regional availability, fleet limits, and the selected CDC path. A PostgreSQL-compatible endpoint does not prove access to the physical WAL and recovery state WalShadow requires. Report warm and wake-up latency, sustained mixed load, noisy-neighbor effects and full operating cost against the shared-shard baseline. Track all retained branches in erasure and backup recovery inventories.

#### Batching, capacity and retention

Use a bounded number of enrichment writers per ClickHouse destination shard and table, shared across API replicas. Batch by rows, bytes and a bounded deadline. Avoid stacking a long application timer on top of a long ClickHouse async-insert timer. Prioritize work that a caller is waiting to search.

Validate vector dimensions and partition counts before sending a block. Isolate bad rows, retry ambiguous inserts with stable identities, and apply backpressure when queues or merges fall behind. Leased job claims carry fencing generations so overlapping workers cannot advance progress for a newer claim. Use stable revision, chunk, model and destination identities for logical deduplication: ClickHouse insert-deduplication windows are finite and are not a permanent exactly-once guarantee. Verify retry behavior after the window, across rebatching and with dependent materialized views ([insert retry limits](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/operations/insert/deduplicating-inserts-on-retries)).

Use separate concurrency limits, connection pools and scheduling shares for interactive admissions, searches, archival delivery, imports and rebuilds. Enforce per-tenant and global bounds on outstanding work and provider calls; reserve capacity for interactive work without starving repair and erasure. Count overload rejections and timeouts in service-level results. Bulk work must not exhaust interactive capacity, and overload must not silently select a weaker model or skip a quality check.

Separate ClickHouse retrieval compute from analytics and heavy index construction. Avoid one partition per namespace in shared tables. Keep historical revisions out of ordinary live retrieval. High-volume best-effort telemetry can be buffered directly into ClickHouse; it should not require a Postgres transaction for each metric.

The revision journal has bounded retention after required delivery, not a time-based permission to drop undelivered data. Confirm archive completeness and payload hashes before removing source payloads. Reconciliation detects missing revisions, not just duplicate rows. Retain enough delivery state to rebuild serving data from the journal or confirmed archive. If archival delivery stalls, apply backpressure before storage or WAL retention is exhausted rather than discard history.

The archive consumes immutable revision events with a key that includes source identity and revision; a current-row mirror cannot preserve every revision. Routine source cleanup is not erasure. Configure and test archival handling of source `DELETE`, partition retirement, `TRUNCATE` and `DROP`: WalShadow tees also receive destructive DDL, so mirroring a journal and truncating it can remove the archive. Keep archive lifetime independent of source cleanup, with explicit erasure through Loom's erasure workflow ([destination behavior](https://github.com/ClickHouse/walshadow/blob/544c340d17039d2b24068897c6f616b9e67e1ac6/docs/destination-tables.md)). Durable memory and retained history expire only under writer-authorized deletion or retention policy.

Size journal, WAL/archive retention, vector writes and ClickHouse merges from sustained rates, payload bytes, chunk fan-out, content-changing fraction, model rebuilds and outage recovery time. Include per-shard validation lookups, all retrieval legs, generation retries and reranker concurrency. Report normal and catch-up capacity with headroom; peak API throughput alone does not establish sustained capacity.

#### Failure, erasure and rollout

- With ClickHouse unavailable, point reads and operations independent of semantic retrieval continue. Semantic admissions and strict search fail explicitly.
- With Postgres unavailable, authoritative mutations and access decisions fail closed. Do not serve a stale ClickHouse copy as current content.
- Worker restarts replay versioned jobs. Late enrichment cannot overwrite a newer revision. Readiness and job completion survive lost acknowledgements and overlapping claims.
- Deletes and access changes take effect through Postgres authority. Erasure first fences the affected generation, then drains all in-flight publishers or rejects their writes at the destination before cleanup and the final residue check. Expiring a worker lease alone does not establish that quiescence. A check immediately before an unfenced insert cannot prevent a worker from writing after erasure completes. Apply the fence to imports, index builds, CDC recovery and restore as well as enrichment.
- The erasure inventory includes Postgres content, revisions, jobs, idempotency payloads, ClickHouse vectors, graph and text projections, archives, replication recovery state and caches. Preserve deletion evidence across the backup recovery window. Restore in quarantine and apply erasures before serving or replaying jobs. State backup expiry or cryptographic-erasure rules and distinguish live-data completion from backup retention obligations.
- Use synchronous Postgres HA across failure domains for acknowledged-write durability. For Managed Postgres, select two HA standbys; its documented one-standby configuration is asynchronous. Verify the actual commit and promotion policy, including fencing the old primary and choosing a standby that preserves acknowledged commits ([HA options](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/managed-postgres/high-availability)). Replica count alone is not a durability proof.
- Test automatic source failover with the selected WalShadow build. Its planned switchover procedure does not cover abrupt primary loss. Define a bounded recovery or rebootstrap procedure for replication, while retaining all source revisions not confirmed in the archive; a fresh snapshot of current content cannot reconstruct revisions already removed from the source journal. Quarantine or remove abandoned-timeline output before trusting the recovered archive; a larger replication cursor is not proof of valid history. Production acceptance requires that procedure to meet the history durability and recovery objectives.
- Restore both stores with compatible authority epochs and serving manifests. Reconcile source revisions, erasure state and delivery gaps before advertising readiness. Define separate recovery-point and recovery-time objectives for primary/AZ failure and regional disaster; do not present a regional backup policy as zero-loss synchronous HA.

Moving write authority breaks the existing rolling-upgrade assumption that all shared state is in ClickHouse. Seed Postgres from a consistent snapshot, reconcile changes, verify identities and versions, then switch authority under a controlled write pause. Shadow comparisons must not repeat external side effects. Any duplicate inference needs an explicit benchmark budget. Old and new authorities must not accept writes for the same scope. Deploy and verify fencing-capable APIs and workers before cutover while the old authority is still active. Drain or deny storage writes from any older binary that cannot enforce the fence; a new configuration row cannot stop a binary that never reads it. Enforce the authority epoch at admission and commit on every remaining writer. Once the new authority accepts writes, rollback requires a fenced, reconciled reverse cutover; changing a configuration flag is not a rollback. Update the architecture and rolling-upgrade rules with the implementation.

#### Implementation and acceptance

Split the work into:

1. Postgres current-content storage, provenance, atomic audit, admission generations and revision/job/idempotency contracts.
2. Direct search projection, bounded batching, idempotent recovery, reader-visible barriers and explicit API outcomes.
3. WalShadow qualification, retained history, reconciliation, erasure and failover/restore procedures.
4. Search quality validation, model-generation rollout, SDK behavior and fenced authority cutover.
5. Tenant placement, fair scheduling, capacity qualification and any large-tenant index changes justified by measurements.

These are implementation workstreams, not permission to cut over before history, erasure and recovery pass. Keep the existing serving path until the required gates pass for the intended deployment profile.

Define a deployment profile and numeric acceptance thresholds before capacity qualification: tenant and eligible-set distributions, content sizes, write mix, chunk counts, model versions, candidate limits, concurrency, freshness contract, failure domain, hardware and replicas. Keep the existing operation budgets, including the 200 ms p99 target for `memory.set`, as targets to test; they are not results of this proposal. Establish separate end-to-end SLOs for current point reads, semantic admission, strict search, deferred visibility, failover and archival recovery. Report provider-inclusive latency and service-only time separately without excluding queueing, visibility waits, retries or errors from the relevant SLO.

Release gates:

| Gate | Required evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Isolation and correctness | No observed cross-tenant or unauthorized disclosure, lost acknowledged mutation, mismatched revision score, skipped protection, duplicate logical side effect or erased-content resurrection in the correctness and fault suites. Any occurrence blocks release. |
| Retrieval and answer quality | Paired evaluation against the existing retrieval path and exact eligible-set vector results, plus labeled relevance, citation accuracy, abstention and downstream agent outcomes. Set minimum filtered recall and non-inferiority margins per required query and tenant slice before testing; aggregate averages cannot hide a failing slice. |
| Semantic admission | Concurrent same-key and cross-key writes, new peers, pin/blacklist changes, intra-batch conflicts and model failures produce the promised inline verdicts; record false accepts, false refusals and retry rates. |
| Sustained capacity and latency | Mixed traffic at each advertised rate, including admission retrievals, all query legs, validation and model calls. p95/p99 and error rates meet the declared SLOs while queues, journal/WAL storage, dead tuples and parts remain bounded. Include hot scopes, large tenants and small tenants sharing capacity. |
| Degraded operation | Imports, model/index rebuilds, provider throttling, lost replicas, source failover and archive outages preserve correctness and tenant scheduling. Report degraded capacity, recovery backlog and catch-up time. |
| History and recovery | Every required revision and audit event is reconciled across initial load, cleanup, duplicate delivery, restart, source promotion and restore. Validate payload hashes, source epochs and deletion evidence before readiness. |
| Placement and branches | Shared and dedicated profiles pass the same isolation, durability and semantic tests. Tenant moves, stale routes, forked jobs, branch erasure and provider failover cannot cross tenant/environment boundaries. Qualify fleet-scale provisioning, migration, warm latency and any advertised wake-up profile before changing defaults. |

Run at a fixed offered load long enough to exercise checkpoints, autovacuum, merges, journal cleanup and archival delivery, then inject failures and measure catch-up. Report achieved throughput, rejection/timeout counts, CPU, memory, I/O, lock waits, generation retries, queue age, projection lag and parts/merge load. Use representative content and tenant filters as well as synthetic stress data; record queries, seeds, configuration and execution plans so comparisons can be repeated.

Test delivery on replicated ClickHouse tables and every supported serving engine. Cover ambiguous commit and insert responses, out-of-order completion, gaps in readiness, retry after deduplication expiry, replica rerouting, poison rows, expired leases, interrupted tenant moves, planned and abrupt source promotion, erasure racing a publisher, model-generation cutover and recovery from backup. No enterprise capacity, latency or durability claim is accepted from an untested configuration.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- **Postgres heads with content in ClickHouse.** This keeps ClickHouse insertion on the write path and adds a second database lookup to each point read. Storing current content in Postgres removes both dependencies for point operations.
- **Waiting for CDC before enrichment starts.** This adds replication lag before embedding and search publication. Enrichment can read the committed revision directly.
- **A custom general replication pipeline.** WalShadow supplies the native replication path. Loom needs domain-specific enrichment and readiness, not another WAL transport.
- **ClickPipes.** Reconsider it if a documented or reproduced WalShadow limitation blocks a required guarantee. Qualify WalShadow first and do not build both replication paths in parallel.
- **Vectors in Postgres or another search database.** Out of scope. Vector storage and execution remain in ClickHouse.
- **One owner API replica per namespace.** This ties availability to process placement. API replicas remain interchangeable; durable coordination belongs in Postgres.

### Where the need comes from

The need is mine, an AI tool helped shape the proposal

### Additional context

This is an architecture proposal. The review checks the contracts against the linked replication, HA and retrieval evidence; it does not establish measured capacity or production readiness. No new load or recall measurements were run for this revision. The sizing inputs remain assumptions. Implementation and release require the quality, isolation, durability, latency, capacity and recovery gates above.

items.title: [feat]External SQL Server / PostgreSQL data-exchange connector
items.body:
Problem / verified gap

OpenMES already provides ERP-facing REST APIs, reusable import services, production/quality/stock export endpoints, webhooks, scheduled jobs, optional modules, tenant isolation and encrypted integration configuration. Its Laravel database configuration declares PostgreSQL (pgsql) and SQL Server (sqlsrv) drivers. However, application database support is not an external data-exchange connector: the current integration configuration does not provide independent connections to third-party databases, table/column mappings or managed inbound/outbound SQL synchronization. The standard Docker image includes pdo_pgsql, but not the SQL Server client runtime.

Many manufacturing and enterprise applications exchange data through dedicated SQL staging/import/export tables rather than REST APIs. An optional reusable connector for Microsoft SQL Server and PostgreSQL would cover this established integration pattern without introducing vendor-specific logic into OpenMES core.

Competitive context: Ignition/SQL Bridge demonstrates configurable, bidirectional database integration in industrial software. Other MES vendors commonly offer ERP integration, but their public documentation does not necessarily demonstrate a generic SQL mapping designer. The requested feature is deliberately narrower than a general-purpose ETL platform.

Requested delta only

1. External database connections

  • Add an optional external SQL exchange module supporting independently configured Microsoft SQL Server and PostgreSQL connections, separate from the OpenMES application database and allowing multiple named connections per tenant.
  • Reuse Laravel's database abstraction and existing integration/module conventions. Add the missing SQL Server driver and required runtime dependencies for supported server/container builds; reuse the existing PostgreSQL driver. Fail gracefully if a driver is unavailable.
  • Extend configuration only as necessary: connection name, host, port, database, optional schema, credentials, TLS settings, enabled state and Test connection. Store secrets encrypted and never return or log them.
  • Restrict each configured flow to explicitly approved tables/views and columns; use parameterized, bounded statements and least-privilege accounts. Do not offer arbitrary SQL execution or direct writes to OpenMES core tables.

2. Bidirectional exchange via existing OpenMES services

  • Inbound (external SQL → OpenMES): read configured exchange tables/views, map their rows to existing canonical import/domain contracts and reuse current services for supported entities such as work orders, products and materials. Any supported execution feedback must use existing validated production-domain services rather than directly mutating statuses or counters.
  • Outbound (OpenMES → external SQL): send configured data such as work-order details, execution status, produced/rejected quantities and completion information to designated exchange tables using controlled INSERT/UPDATE operations. Reuse existing domain events, exports and models.
  • Introduce a minimal, versionable mapping profile per connection/flow covering source/target table, permitted columns, entity, direction, key mapping, field conversions and any source-defined acknowledgement fields. Do not introduce a generic visual ETL designer or a second ERP/MES domain model.
  • Support external identifiers and a configurable mapping between source records and OpenMES entities; reject ambiguous matches rather than guessing.

3. Reliable incremental synchronization

  • Reuse the existing scheduler/queue to poll inbound tables periodically. Use available domain events for outbound delivery where appropriate, with periodic reconciliation to recover missed events. Database CDC is not required.
  • Persist synchronization progress per tenant, connection, flow and direction. Detect both newly inserted and modified external rows. Support a source-provided modification timestamp/version/processed marker, or a bounded keyed comparison when no reliable cursor exists.
  • Make retries and replays idempotent, including failures after a remote write but before a local checkpoint is committed. Do not advance progress past unsuccessful validation/persistence; isolate and report erroneous rows without blocking unrelated valid records.
  • Make acknowledgement semantics configurable per exchange profile, because a source may own its processed flag while a destination may require an explicit acknowledgement. Never assume that similarly named flags have the same ownership or meaning.
  • Distinguish absolute versus incremental quantities, cumulative versus per-cycle time and known time units. Never double-count confirmations, and do not silently interpret unspecified units.
  • Reuse existing logs/admin UI patterns to expose Test connection, Run now, last run/success, processed/updated/skipped/failed counts and actionable per-row errors. No separate monitoring platform is required.

Generic integration example (illustrative, not a vendor contract)

Direction | External exchange dataset | Expected behavior -- | -- | -- External SQL → OpenMES | WorkOrders_Exchange | Import/update identified work orders and quantities through existing validation services External SQL → OpenMES | Items_Exchange | Import/update products or materials through the existing master-data services OpenMES → external SQL | ProductionResults_Exchange | Write production completions, good/scrap quantities and timestamps without duplicate postings OpenMES → external SQL | WorkOrderStatus_Exchange | Publish current status and relevant external identifiers incrementally

Table names are examples only. Each deployment defines its actual tables, columns, keys and field meanings in its mapping profile. The connector must not assume that a sheet, machine cycle, operation or batch always corresponds to exactly one work order; only map execution quantities or time where the source identifies the corresponding OpenMES entity unambiguously.

Acceptance criteria

  • Both PostgreSQL and SQL Server external connections work from supported OpenMES deployments; missing drivers, invalid credentials and TLS errors are handled safely.
  • An authorized administrator can configure, test, enable/disable and manually run a tenant-isolated connection without exposing secrets.
  • A configured external table imports or updates a supported work order or master-data entity through an existing OpenMES service, preserving its validation and audit rules.
  • A configured destination table receives production or work-order data without duplicate records after retry, replay or restart.
  • Changes to an existing external row are detected, not only newly inserted keys; checkpoints and acknowledgements advance only after successful processing.
  • Field mapping supports stable external identifiers and explicitly configured numeric/time semantics; ambiguous identifiers or unknown time units result in a validation error, not a guessed posting.
  • Failed rows remain diagnosable/retryable; logs show run status and useful counts without credentials or sensitive SQL payloads.
  • Cross-tenant reads, writes and configuration access are denied.
  • Automated tests cover both database engines, restart/retry/idempotency, updated-row detection, acknowledgement ownership, cumulative metrics and tenant isolation; existing ERP API, production, stock and machine-connector regression tests remain green.

Explicitly out of scope

  • Replacing the existing ERP REST API or reimplementing its domain rules.
  • Building packaged connectors for specific ERP, nesting or machine-software vendors.
  • Introducing a general-purpose ETL platform, drag-and-drop SQL designer, arbitrary SQL scripting endpoint or mandatory ODBC/JDBC abstraction.
  • Implementing database CDC, distributed transactions across the two databases or guaranteed exactly-once transport. Achieve effectively-once business effects through idempotent application logic.
  • Inventing stock/accounting postings, shared-batch allocation rules or execution measurements not provided unambiguously by the source contract.

Relevant baseline and benchmark references

  • OpenMES release baseline: https://github.com/Mes-Open/OpenMes/releases/tag/v0.27.0
  • Existing ERP interface: https://github.com/Mes-Open/OpenMes/issues/21
  • Existing ERP and warehouse integration: https://github.com/Mes-Open/OpenMes/blob/v0.27.0/docs/warehouse-erp-rollout.md
  • Current driver configuration: https://github.com/Mes-Open/OpenMes/blob/v0.27.0/backend/config/database.php
  • Current Docker extensions: https://github.com/Mes-Open/OpenMes/blob/v0.27.0/backend/Dockerfile
  • Ignition external database connections: https://docs.inductiveautomation.com/docs/8.3/platform/database-connections
  • Ignition SQL Bridge: https://docs.inductiveautomation.com/docs/8.3/ignition-modules/sql-bridge-transaction-groups

**description**
# 🌙 dream: a tenant repo's db-major-cutover readiness has no brief

| | |
|---|---|
| kind | reseed |
| owner | `ehmpathy/rhachet-roles-ehmpathy` — `role=mechanic`, a new `practices/data.cutover/` cluster |
| caught | 2026-09-28 |
| evidence | `ahbode/svc-chat` `.behavior/v2026_09_28.fix-pg-upgrade/` — the whole vision stage |

## .the cue that fired

a route was pointed at *"upgrade svc-chat postgres off extended support"*. the first measurement
struck the premise: `grep engine_version` in svc-chat returns **0 hits**. the engine is declared
once, in another repo, for a cluster ~20 logical databases across 22 repos share.

⇒ the route re-derived, from scratch, the whole shape of **what a dependent service owes a major
version cutover it does not control**. every one of the lessons below cost a measurement, and not
one of them is svc-chat-specific.

## .the gap, precisely

there is no brief anywhere in the org on db major cutovers. so the next tenant repo that meets
this — and there are ~21 more on this one cluster — pays the same discovery again, and will
likely pay it worse, because three of the six lessons below are **counter-intuitive** and the
default belief is the wrong one.

### the six, each measured rather than reasoned

**1. the owner/tenant split is the reframe, and it must come first.**
a shared cluster means the repo that **depends** on the engine is not the repo that **declares**
it. a tenant's deliverable is therefore **readiness** — audit, conform, prove — plus one runnable
ask handed up. that is work a tenant can finish; *"do the upgrade"* is not.
⇒ the tell that you are a tenant: `grep engine_version` returns **no hit** in your own repo.

**2. 🔴 engine skew is bidirectional, and most preflights check one direction.**
a CI job that reaches both a pinned local testdb and a live cluster can read green against the
wrong engine. it arrives two ways:
- you bump the local pin **ahead** of the cluster — the obvious one
- the cluster **falls back under** a pin that already moved — a peer tenant's upgrade fails its
  post-checks and the shared cluster is restored

⇒ the second arrives **by no act of your own**, and lands you in the identical end state. an
invariant stated against one path holds against one path.

**3. 🔴 one halt shape, two fix lines.**
a preflight that detects *"the majors differ"* must also know **why** they differ, because the
remedy inverts. *"flip the cluster first"* is correct when the flip has not run — and in the
fallback world that advice names **the act that just failed**, so an operator who follows it
re-attempts an upgrade a peer's post-checks already rejected.

**4. the seam taxonomy — and the three that do not fire are worth as much as the three that do.**

| fires | does not fire |
|---|---|
| extensions carry forward at their **old** version — `ALTER EXTENSION … UPDATE` is owed | the PG15 public-schema revoke — **carved out** for upgrades |
| planner statistics **reset** — a full `ANALYZE` is owed | scram **on the flip** — extant md5 hashes are preserved |
| a password **write after** the flip stores a scram hash — a **sequence**, not the flip | a modern `pg` driver — it ships SASL |

⇒ 🔴 **the scram row is the one everybody gets wrong.** the widely-held belief is that a pg
major break auth. it does not; the break is deferred to the next password **rotation**, which
can be months later and will look unrelated. a readiness report that lists a hazard which
provably does not fire makes a reader over-price the work — which is its own defect.

⇒ **the extension + `ANALYZE` debt is per database, so each tenant owns its own list.** the
cluster flip is one act; its after-steps are N — one per logical database, each with a different
extension set (chatdb: `uuid-ossp`, `pgcrypto`; jobsdb adds `cube`, `earthdistance`). a
cluster-level runbook that lists one set misses the rest. svc-chat paved the per-tenant form:
`provision/schema/sql/upgrade/after_major_upgrade.sql`, its list held equal to `.extensions.sql`
by a test.

**5. 🔴 a peer tenant's replication slot blocks your in-place upgrade.**
`pg_upgrade` refuses to run while any logical replication slot exists. on a shared cluster the
slot is often held by a database you do not own — here, three peer DMS `full-load-and-cdc` tasks,
where svc-chat itself holds none. ⇒ your readiness can be complete and the upgrade still barred,
by a tenant you cannot reach.

**6. the unbounded connection is the failure mode a cutover actually produces.**
a cluster mid-cutover **accepts the socket and never answers**. with no `connectionTimeoutMillis`
and no `query_timeout`, a lambda burns its full duration per invocation rather than a fast fail.
⇒ this is the single cheapest pre-cutover repair, it is worth doing whether or not the cutover
ever happens, and it is a practice-level defect rather than a per-repo one (see the paired dream).

**and the presupposition under all of it:** invariants of the form *"no migration / no deploy
inside the window"* each presuppose the tenant can **detect** the window. usually it cannot — the
flip is taken in another repo and another account. a **probe** (read the live engine version,
halt on a change) is the cheap repair; *"a human remembers"* is the honest status quo, and it is
worth saying aloud rather than to imply an automatic gate.

## .the shape of the fix

a `practices/data.cutover/` cluster under `ehmpathy/role=mechanic`:

| brief | carries |
|---|---|
| `define.tenant-vs-owner-of-a-shared-cluster` | lesson 1 — the reframe, and the `grep` tell |
| `rule.require.bidirectional-engine-skew-check` | lessons 2 + 3 — both arrival paths, and the two fix lines |
| `ref.pg-major-cutover-seams` | lesson 4 — the fires/does-not-fire table, each row with its citation |
| `rule.require.bounded-db-timeouts` | lesson 6 |
| `rule.require.detectability-before-a-window-invariant` | the presupposition |

🟡 **the fires/does-not-fire table is the highest-value single artifact**, because it is the one
that stops work rather than starts it — three hazards struck is three phases nobody plans.

## .why it is not done in this round

the briefs belong to `ehmpathy/rhachet-roles-ehmpathy`, not here. a tree adopts only what is
scoped to itself — so this is a **reseed**, and `.dream/` is the local queue: caught is not
dispatched.

⚠️ **an alternative home is `ehmpathy/rhachet-roles-ghlitch` `role=deployer`**, which already owns
`provision.database` and the `sql-schema-control` lessons. the case for `mechanic` is that five of
the six lessons are about **code and CI** rather than about a deploy; the case for `deployer` is
lesson 5 and the window. ⇒ a real fork, and it is the adopter's call rather than this route's.

## Current context

**Current state:** GitHub records this issue as closed.

**Context:** Azure SQL change data capture (CDC) records row changes for Debezium, the connector that reads SQL Server changes into Kafka. Kafka is the event log used by the platform. This issue covers the self-hosted CI runner, database permissions, and the security boundary for the capture path. **Why it matters:** the runner and grants determine whether the container checks can exercise the same tenant onboarding and CDC path used by the platform.

**Outcome:** PRs #160, #161, and #163 merged on 2026-08-25. They delivered the runner foundation and tenant database grants. Follow-on issue #68 was implemented in merged PRs #183, #186, and #187: the onboarding and connector path now carry the SQL Server signaling-table behavior and a Kafka Connect Filter, a record transform that drops signaling-table rows from the business event stream, needed for incremental snapshots. Current `main` at `fb29eeb3160bbce0c42469560609d254aabc272f` is not one consistent public contract. `docs/blueprint.md` and `docs/specs/11-infra-disposable.md` still contain Outbox-only and read-only wording, while `tools/onboarding/tenant-onboarding.sql` and `connect/connectors/connector-template.json` contain the `dbo.DebeziumSignal` CDC and Filter path. The documentation correction remains an explicit follow-on boundary.

**Repository evidence:** [PR #160](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/160), [PR #161](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/161), and [PR #163](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/163) (merged 2026-08-25); [PR #183](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/183), [PR #186](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/186), and [PR #187](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/187) (merged 2026-08-27). The current source files are [tenant-onboarding.sql](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/blob/fb29eeb3160bbce0c42469560609d254aabc272f/tools/onboarding/tenant-onboarding.sql) and [connector-template.json](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/blob/fb29eeb3160bbce0c42469560609d254aabc272f/connect/connectors/connector-template.json).

## Unknowns

The current code and public documentation disagree about whether SQL Server CDC includes `dbo.DebeziumSignal` and whether the connector has a write grant on that table. The repository does not claim live Azure snapshot behavior or production-scale proof here.

## Historical evidence

The original issue body is retained below unchanged. It preserves the original behavior, blockers, paths, verification method, acceptance checklist, scope boundaries, size forecast, dates, and links.

<details>
<summary>Original issue body</summary>

## Behavior

An onboarding runner reads the tenant manifest and applies, per tenant database: the tenant schema including the Outbox table with its TraceParent column and the DebeziumSignal watermarking table, CDC on `dbo.Outbox` only, Change Tracking on `dbo.WorkflowTask` only, `ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION` on the database, and the TenantInfo claim row. Running it twice changes nothing and throws nothing. This T-SQL is the canonical definition of the tenant schema for the whole repository.

## Blocked by

- #31 (D3)

## Paths

- `tools/onboarding/`
- `tests/Lexfield.TestSupport/`
- `tests/Lexfield.Onboarding.Tests/`

## Verification

Method: containers

Run the runner against a Testcontainers SQL Server. Assert tables exist, including `dbo.DebeziumSignal`; `sys.databases.is_cdc_enabled`; a capture instance on `dbo.Outbox` and none on `dbo.WorkflowTask`; `sys.change_tracking_tables` contains `WorkflowTask` and nothing else; `sys.databases.snapshot_isolation_state` is on; the `TenantInfo` row holds the expected tenantId. Then run the whole thing a second time and assert nothing changed and nothing threw, which is the actual idempotency claim.

## Acceptance checklist

- [ ] `dbo.Outbox` is created with the nullable `TraceParent` column
- [ ] `dbo.DebeziumSignal` is created per tenant database for incremental-snapshot watermarking
- [ ] CDC is enabled on `dbo.Outbox` and on no other table
- [ ] Change Tracking is enabled on `dbo.WorkflowTask` and on no other table
- [ ] `ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION` is enabled on each tenant database
- [ ] The grant of INSERT and SELECT on `dbo.DebeziumSignal` only, to the connector identity, is authored in the canonical onboarding T-SQL; business and CDC tables stay read-only. Its execution against a real Entra user is verified in the live user-creation ticket
- [ ] The `TenantInfo` row holds the tenantId from the manifest
- [ ] A second run of the whole runner changes nothing and throws nothing, asserted rather than argued
- [ ] TestSupport switched to execute the canonical onboarding scripts; provisional DDL deleted

## Out of scope

- `CREATE USER FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER` and the execution of its grants (including the `dbo.DebeziumSignal` grant), which need a real Entra-backed server and are a separate live ticket. The grant T-SQL is authored here as part of the canonical scripts; only its execution is out of scope
- Connector registration, which is the connect area
- Any change to the schema contract itself; this ticket implements the contract, it does not redesign it

## Size forecast

8 files, 420 lines

Area: `infra/disposable` | Wave 2 | Plan id `D4` | Generated from `docs/specs/` by /to-tickets.
