* `architectural-styles.adoc` — **Monolith, modular monolith, microservices: what each style actually is.**
  Software architecture as decisions about quality attributes, not functional requirements; an architectural
  style constrains the *implementation view* (Richardson): the monolith as one deployable, microservices as many
  loosely coupled independently deployable services; the **modular monolith** as one deployable with enforced
  module boundaries (Spring Modulith, Java modules/packages, .NET projects) — the middle ground the rest of the
  section keeps coming back to; layered (three-tier) vs. **hexagonal** logical views and why hexagonal is the
  natural shape of each service (link to the SpringBoot and Architectural Patterns pages); the **scale cube**
  (X cloning, Z partitioning, Y functional decomposition) as the vocabulary for "scaling"; microservices vs.
  SOA; the **distributed monolith** anti-pattern. 📊 SVG `architecture-scale-cube.svg`; 📊 Mermaid
  three-column figure of the same Bookshop as monolith / modular monolith / microservices.
* `benefits-and-drawbacks.adoc` — **What microservices give you and what they cost you.** The benefits of the
  monolithic architecture while the application is small (simple to develop, easy radical changes, simple
  testing and deployment, easy X-axis scaling) and the symptoms of **monolithic hell** as it grows (complexity
  intimidates developers, slow edit-build-run-test loop, long commit-to-deploy path with manual testing and
  monthly releases, conflicting resource requirements make scaling hard, no fault isolation, locked into an
  obsolete stack). The **benefits of microservices**, each explained with the Bookshop example: continuous
  delivery/deployment, small easily maintained services, **independent deployability**, **independent
  scalability** (CPU-hungry search vs. memory-hungry catalogue), **autonomous "two-pizza" teams** owning services
  end to end, easy experimentation with and adoption of new technologies, fault isolation. The **inconveniences**:
  finding the right set of services is hard and getting it wrong produces a distributed monolith; distributed
  systems are complex (IPC instead of method calls, partial failure, latency, retries, circuit breakers); **loss
  of ACID transactionality** — sagas, eventual consistency, no cross-service joins (API composition / CQRS) —
  linking to the Architectural Patterns pages for the mechanics; **higher complexity and much more code and
  infrastructure to maintain** (service chassis, observability, service discovery, gateways, per-service
  pipelines, contract tests, security tokens, distributed IDs — each linked to the existing page that documents
  it); features spanning services need coordinated rollouts; higher operational and skills bar; deciding when to
  adopt is itself hard. 📊 side-by-side comparison table; 📊 SVG `architecture-monolithic-hell.svg` (the
  downward spiral: growth → complexity → slower delivery → more pressure).
* `choosing-monolith-or-microservices.adoc` — **When a monolith is the better choice and when microservices
  are.** A plain-language decision guide: a monolith (modular from day one) for small projects, small teams (one
  team that fits around a table), one-shot deliveries and prototypes, applications that will not need to evolve
  much, startups still searching for their business model ("a startup should almost certainly begin with a
  monolithic application" — Richardson; MonolithFirst — Fowler), strict transactional domains, and anywhere the
  operational prerequisites (automated deployment pipeline, monitoring, rapid provisioning — Fowler's
  MicroservicePrerequisites) are missing; microservices for large, complex, long-lived systems developed by
  several autonomous teams, for **performance and scale** reasons when components have very different resource
  and scaling profiles, when fault isolation or independent release cadence is a business requirement, when
  parts of the system need a different technology stack, and for consumer-facing or SaaS products at scale. The
  "is it really the architecture?" check: slow delivery and buggy releases are often a **process** problem
  (manual testing, no CI/CD) — fix that first (Richardson 13.1.1). Signals that it is time to split (the
  monolithic-hell symptoms as a checklist) and signals that it is time to **merge back** (the Prime Video
  monitoring case study: chatty services and per-call infrastructure cost). 📊 Mermaid decision flowchart; 📊
  table "project profile → recommended style" that the new-project guide later expands.

### Layering the architecture

* `layering-backend-and-frontend.adoc` — **Isolating backend and frontend so they evolve independently.**
  From the classic monolith that renders HTML pages to a **backend that exposes only an API** (REST by default;
  GraphQL/gRPC where the existing comparison pages say so) **behind a gateway**, consumed by **completely
  separate web frontends** (React, Angular, Vue — each linked) and by **native mobile apps** (Android/Kotlin,
  iOS/Swift, or cross-platform) that use the very same API; why this lets the frontend team iterate, A/B-test
  and release without touching the backend, lets several UIs share one backend, and opens the door to native
  apps and partner integrations; what it costs (CORS, two deployables, API versioning, contract-first with
  OpenAPI — link to `api-first-rest-and-grpc.adoc` —, SEO/SSR, authentication via the **BFF** — link to the
  OAuth browser-based-apps page); when **server-rendered UIs** (Thymeleaf, Vaadin, Blazor Server, JSF) are still
  the right, simpler choice (internal tools, small teams, content sites, one-shot projects); server-side rendering
  frameworks (Next.js/Nuxt/Angular SSR) as the hybrid; **micro-frontends** named in one paragraph with links, not
  documented. The Bookshop example: one Spring Boot API, one React web app, one Android app. 📊 SVG
  `architecture-layered-target.svg` (browser SPA + native apps → gateway/BFF → API → services/database); 📊
  Mermaid sequence diagram of one "place order" request crossing the layers; 📊 table "UI approach → when to use".
* `api-gateway-and-bff.adoc` — **API gateway and backends for frontends.** Why clients should not call services
  directly (many round-trips, no encapsulation, unsuitable protocols); the API gateway as the single entry point
  — request routing, API composition, edge functions (authentication, rate limiting, TLS, logging), protocol
  translation —, its benefits and drawbacks (one more highly available component, risk of becoming a development
  bottleneck); the **backends-for-frontends** variant (one gateway per client type owned by the client team, the
  Netflix story), and when one gateway is enough; **implementation options** with links: off-the-shelf (AWS API
  Gateway, Kong, Traefik, Envoy / Kubernetes Gateway API, NGINX) vs. building your own (Spring Cloud Gateway,
  YARP), GraphQL as a gateway (link to the GraphQL federation / when-to-use pages); the gateway during a
  migration as the **strangler's routing seam**. 📊 Mermaid figure of gateway vs. BFF topologies; a ~20-line
  Spring Cloud Gateway route example routing `/api/orders/**` to the extracted Order service and everything else
  to the monolith.

### Migration paths

* `migration-overview.adoc` — **How to approach any migration.** The **balancing act** between business
  motivators (competition, operational cost, new markets, customer demand) and technical desires (erase technical
  debt, shiny new stack) — the strategy must be driven by the business (Golding); **timing**: "modernize first"
  vs. "deliver now, modernize incrementally", and why early customer feedback usually wins; the **fish model** of
  costs and revenue during a transformation; **no big bang rewrite** ("the only thing a Big Bang rewrite
  guarantees is a Big Bang"), the **strangler fig** as the universal shape of every path in this section;
  **demonstrate value early and often**; **minimize changes to the legacy system**; **don't build the deployment
  infrastructure up front** — an automated deployment pipeline with automated tests is the only thing you can't
  live without; a **time-boxed target-architecture definition** (a couple of weeks) as the destination; and the
  five **pitfalls** every path warns about (big bang, distributed monolith, shared database, premature
  infrastructure, forgetting the organisation and process side). Ends with a **"where are you? → which page"**
  table that maps the reader's current situation (legacy stack monolith / healthy monolith that has outgrown
  itself / modular monolith / partially extracted / single-tenant installs) to the following four pages. 📊 SVG
  `architecture-strangler-over-time.svg` (the monolith shrinking while the strangler application grows); 📊
  Mermaid figure of the fish model; 📊 Mermaid flowchart "which migration path".
* `migration-path-legacy-to-modern-stack.adoc` — **From a legacy technology stack to a modern one** (without
  necessarily changing the architectural style). Typical starting points and their modern targets, as a table
  with links to the existing references: Java EE / Struts / JSP / Spring 3-4 XML → **Spring Boot** or
  **Quarkus**; .NET Framework Web Forms / MVC 5 → **ASP.NET Core** (link to the existing Web Forms migration
  page); jQuery/server-templated UI → **React / Angular / Vue** SPA or a server-rendered modern framework;
  SOAP/ESB → **REST / gRPC + messaging**; stored-procedure business logic → application-layer domain model;
  legacy ORM/JDBC → **Hibernate / Spring Data**; ad-hoc deployment → containers and a pipeline. The techniques,
  each explained simply with the Bookshop example: the **strangler fig with a reverse proxy / gateway** in front
  of the legacy app (route by path, header, or user cohort; YARP, NGINX, Spring Cloud Gateway), **separate the
  presentation tier from the backend first** (Richardson's second strategy: expose the business logic as an
  API, then rebuild the UI as a SPA against it — the seam every later step reuses), **branch by abstraction**
  and **parallel run** (legacy-displacement patterns), the **anti-corruption layer** between old and new models,
  **data synchronisation** during the overlap (dual writes vs. CDC with Debezium — link), **incremental
  framework upgrades** when the stack is upgradable (Spring's backward compatibility) vs. strangling when it is
  not, feature flags and cohort-based cut-over, and the **exit criteria** for decommissioning the legacy system.
  📊 Mermaid flowchart of the strangler routing (proxy → legacy vs. new); 📊 SVG
  `architecture-presentation-backend-split.svg` (monolith with UI → API backend + SPA); 📊 step-by-step table
  "week 0 → week N" for the Bookshop UI migration.
* `migration-path-monolith-to-modular-monolith.adoc` — **From a big-ball-of-mud monolith to a modular
  monolith** — the safest first step of any microservices migration and, for many teams, the final destination.
  Identify modules by business capability / subdomain (link to Strategic Design), draw the **target module map**,
  enforce boundaries (packages + **Spring Modulith** `@ApplicationModule` and its verification tests; ArchUnit;
  .NET projects), replace cross-module object references and shared tables with **module APIs and in-process
  domain events** (Spring Modulith events — the outbox in a single database), give each module its own schema
  or table prefix so the database can later be split, kill **god classes** by splitting them per module, and
  measure coupling. Why this already buys most of the maintainability benefits at none of the distributed cost,
  and the **signal to go further**: a module needs its own release cadence, scaling profile, team, or stack.
  📊 Mermaid module-dependency graph of the Bookshop before/after; a ~25-line Spring Modulith module + event
  example; 📊 table "monolith → modular monolith → microservices: what you gain at each step".
* `migration-path-monolith-to-microservices.adoc` — **From a (modular) monolith to microservices** — the
  centrepiece of the section, written as a step-by-step guide with the Bookshop example. Richardson's **three
  strategies**: (1) **implement new features as services** ("stop digging" — the Bookshop's new
  recommendations feature is born as a service; when a feature is too small or too coupled to be a service);
  (2) **separate presentation tier and backend** (link back to the legacy page); (3) **extract business
  capabilities into services** — the vertical slice (inbound adapters, domain logic, outbound adapters, schema),
  **splitting the domain model** (object references → ids, extracting `Shipment` out of the `Order` god class),
  **refactoring the database** (split table, move table), **replicating data back to the monolith** to avoid
  widespread changes, and **what to extract first** (rank by: accelerates development, solves a
  performance/scaling/reliability problem, unblocks other extractions; "freeze the monolith and extract on
  demand" vs. the planned backlog). **Designing how the service and the monolith collaborate**: the integration
  glue (repository-style interface for queries, service-style interface for commands), querying the monolith via
  REST vs. keeping a **replica fed by events**, updates via **transactional messaging**, the **anti-corruption
  layer** in both directions, **how the monolith publishes domain events** (inserting publish calls vs.
  transaction-log tailing/CDC when the monolith can't be changed — link to Kafka Connect / outbox) and subscribes
  to them (helper application when it can't). **Data consistency between monolith and service**: why splitting
  an ACID transaction forces a saga, why the monolith is often an unwilling saga participant (compensating
  transactions need semantic-lock states scattered across the monolith), the rule "**keep the monolith's
  transactions pivot or retriable**", and **sequencing the extractions** so the monolith never needs a
  compensating transaction (the Bookshop sequence: Order → Customer → Catalogue/Inventory → Payment, each shown
  as the resulting saga) — linking to the Architectural Patterns saga page for the saga mechanics themselves.
  **Security**: from session cookies to a user-info cookie/token propagated by the gateway (link to OAuth
  pages). **Deployment**: a service at a time, containerised, on whatever the team already runs; Kubernetes only
  when there are enough services to justify it (link). Closing checklist per extracted service. 📊 SVG
  `architecture-extract-service.svg` (vertical slice leaving the monolith, gateway routing, integration glue); 📊
  Mermaid sequence diagrams for the Bookshop "place order" saga before and after extracting Payment (monolith as
  pivot); 📊 Mermaid figure of query-by-API vs. replica-by-events; 📊 table of extraction order with the reason
  for each step.
* `migration-path-to-multi-tenant-saas.adoc` — **From single-tenant installed software to multi-tenant SaaS.**
  Why this is a distinct path (it changes the business, not only the code); the **control plane / application
  plane** split and why the control plane (onboarding, identity, tenant management, metrics, billing, admin) is
  built first — "**build your multi-tenant foundation on day one**"; **tenant context** flowing through every
  request (routing, logging, data access, isolation); the **silo / pool** vocabulary and the deployment models
  (full-stack silo, full-stack pool, hybrid with a premium siloed tier, mixed mode per service, pods); the three
  **migration patterns** with the Bookshop-as-a-SaaS example — **silo lift-and-shift** (fastest, least
  invasive, one version for everyone, automated per-tenant onboarding), **layered migration** (pool the web
  tier, then the application tier), **service-by-service migration** (strangle the application tier into
  pooled multi-tenant microservices, "don't compromise on the new microservices", integrating legacy code with
  the control plane) —, their pros and cons side by side, the **phased approach** that chains them, "**where you
  start matters**" (identity → onboarding → tenant authentication → tenant context in services → tenant-aware
  logs and metrics), and the guiding principles (**avoid the tech-first trap**, no one-size-fits-all, protect
  the multi-tenant principles). Links to the AWS SaaS Lens and the SaaS Architecture Fundamentals whitepaper as
  the primary online sources, and to the Hibernate multitenancy page for the data-partitioning mechanics. 📊 SVG
  `architecture-saas-migration-patterns.svg` (the three patterns side by side over control plane + application
  plane); 📊 Mermaid figure of the phased approach; 📊 table silo vs. pool vs. hybrid vs. mixed vs. pod with
  "when to use".

### Starting from scratch

* `starting-a-new-project.adoc` — **Which path and which technologies to use for a new project**, chosen among
  the technologies documented on this site. First the **profile questions** (expected size and domain
  complexity; expected traffic — low, high, bursty; lifetime — one-shot vs. long-term maintenance and evolution;
  number of teams; need for a public API, native apps, several UIs; need for multi-tenancy; compliance; team
  skills and budget), then the **default path**: start as a **modular monolith with a clean API layer** and a
  separate frontend when there will be more than one client, extract services only when a signal from the
  "choosing" page appears; then **scenario cards**, each with a one-paragraph story, the recommended
  architecture, a recommended stack drawn *only* from documented technologies with links to the existing
  comparison pages, and what to explicitly *not* do: (a) **small one-shot project / internal tool** (a
  monolith, server-rendered UI or a small SPA, one relational database, single JAR/container or PaaS, no
  Kafka, no Kubernetes); (b) **startup MVP that must evolve fast** (modular monolith, REST API + React/Angular/Vue
  from day one so native apps can follow, PostgreSQL, container on a managed platform, feature flags); (c)
  **long-lived line-of-business application for one organisation** (modular monolith with Spring Modulith or
  Quarkus, RabbitMQ for background work, OAuth/OIDC, observability from day one); (d) **high-traffic consumer
  application** (API gateway/BFF, microservices for the hot paths only — search on Elasticsearch/Solr, catalogue
  cache, order/payment sagas —, Kafka, Kubernetes, CQRS read models — links to the Architectural Patterns
  pages); (e) **large multi-team enterprise platform** (microservices by business capability, API-first
  contracts, gateway + BFF per client, event-driven integration, per-service databases, distributed tracing);
  (f) **multi-tenant SaaS product** (control plane first, pooled application plane, tiering; serverless for the
  control plane where traffic is low); (g) **batch / data-processing job** (Spring Batch, no web layer at all —
  link). Cross-cutting recommendation tables with links: backend framework (Spring Boot vs. Quarkus; Java vs.
  Kotlin; Python/FastAPI where the GraphQL section already documents it), API style (REST vs. GraphQL vs. gRPC),
  messaging (Kafka vs. RabbitMQ — or none), database (link to Choosing the Right Database), frontend
  (React/Angular/Vue vs. Vaadin/Blazor/Thymeleaf; Bootstrap vs. Tailwind), mobile (Kotlin/Android, Swift/iOS,
  cross-platform in one line), authentication (OAuth/OIDC, BFF for SPAs), deployment (single process → container
  → managed container platform → Kubernetes → serverless: what each is good for, with the serverless long-tail
  latency caveat for JVM services and Quarkus native as the mitigation). 📊 Mermaid decision flowchart
  (profile → style → deployment); 📊 SVG `architecture-project-profile-matrix.svg` (the scenario × concern matrix
  in one picture); 📊 one small Mermaid topology figure per scenario card.

### Reference

* `cheat-sheet.adoc` — describes the sheet and links every section page, plus
  `xref:attachment$architecture-cheat-sheet.pdf[Download the Architecture Cheat Sheet (PDF)]`.

## Cheat sheet (`modules/ROOT/attachments/architecture-cheat-sheet.pdf`)

Exactly **one A4 page**, landscape or portrait like the existing sheets, produced with the established
mechanism (hand-built HTML/CSS → headless Chromium → PDF, HTML not checked in), visually consistent with
`architectural-patterns-cheat-sheet.pdf` / `messaging-cheat-sheet.pdf` (same colour-coded boxes, fonts and
footer). Content, **built around "where are you now? → what to do"**:

* **Migration paths by current architecture** — one row per starting point: *legacy-stack monolith* (proxy +
  strangler; split presentation from backend first; ACL; CDC for data overlap), *healthy monolith that outgrew
  itself* (modularise first: modules by capability, Spring Modulith, in-process events, per-module schema),
  *modular monolith with a hot spot* (extract that capability: new features as services first; vertical slice;
  ids not references; replicate data back; gateway routes; keep the monolith pivot/retriable; extraction order),
  *partially extracted system* (sagas/outbox/CQRS per Architectural Patterns; consolidate the gateway/BFF; retire
  the monolith or keep it as one more service), *single-tenant installs* (control plane first → silo
  lift-and-shift → layered → service-by-service; silo/pool per service).
* **Monolith vs. microservices** signal box — choose a monolith when…, choose microservices when…, "is it really
  the architecture?" check, signals to split, signals to merge back.
* **Benefits / inconveniences** two-column box (microservices).
* **Layering** box — SPA + native apps → gateway/BFF → API → services; when server-rendered UI is fine.
* **New project → recommended stack** matrix — the seven scenario cards of `starting-a-new-project.adoc` in one
  compact table (architecture, backend, API, messaging, database, frontend, mobile, deployment), each cell
  naming documented technologies only.
* **Pitfalls** strip — big bang, distributed monolith, shared database, premature Kubernetes, tech-first SaaS.
* **Pointers** — the microservices.io, martinfowler.com, Azure/AWS/GCP guidance URLs, and the two books.

## Cross-links to add in existing pages

* `backend/index.adoc` — new "Architecture" bullet in `== Sections`; description/keywords updated.
* `backend/architectural-patterns/index.adoc` — one sentence in the intro pointing to
  `xref:backend/architecture/index.adoc` for the monolith-vs-microservices decision and the migration paths
  (that section explicitly declared "strangler migration" out of scope; this is where it now lives).
* `backend/springboot/architectural-patterns.adoc` — its *Where this section stops* paragraph gains a pointer to
  the new section for migration and layering.
* `web/aspnet/web-forms/migrating-to-modern-aspnet.adoc` — one sentence pointing to
  `xref:backend/architecture/migration-path-legacy-to-modern-stack.adoc` for the technology-neutral strangler
  strategy.
* `web/aspnet/core/architecture-and-patterns.adoc` — its modular-monolith bullet links to
  `xref:backend/architecture/migration-path-monolith-to-modular-monolith.adoc`.
* `backend/oauth/browser-based-apps.adoc` — one sentence pointing to `api-gateway-and-bff.adoc` for the BFF as an
  architectural (not only security) pattern.
* `database/choosing-the-right-database.adoc` and `backend/graphql/when-to-use-graphql-or-rest.adoc` — a
  "see also" line pointing to `starting-a-new-project.adoc`, which composes them.
* `modules/ROOT/pages/index.adoc` — keywords only.

## Bibliography additions

* The new `backend/architecture/index.adoc` gets its own `== Bibliography` following the Architectural
  Patterns format (*Pattern catalogues and canonical articles*, *Cloud-provider architecture guidance*,
  *Technology documentation*, *Consulted reference books*) listing **every** link in the "Online sources"
  section above plus the two books (Richardson — Manning page; Golding — O'Reilly page with the Amazon fallback
  and the free AWS whitepaper) and the further-reading titles (Newman; Ford et al.; Richards & Ford; Ambler &
  Sadalage), each with the note on how it was used, and the closing sentence that the books are consulted
  references only and the online catalogues are authoritative on any discrepancy.
* `backend/architectural-patterns/index.adoc#_bibliography` — under *Consulted reference books*, extend the
  Richardson entry's note to say that chapters 1, 2, 8, 12 and 13 are the narrative source for the sibling
  Architecture section, and add Golding's book with the same links as above (it is the source of the
  multi-tenancy angle that the Hibernate multitenancy page and the new SaaS page share). No other existing
  bibliography needs changes.

## Out of scope

* Re-documenting anything in the table above (DDD tactical patterns, sagas/outbox/CQRS mechanics, REST vs.
  GraphQL vs. gRPC, Kafka vs. RabbitMQ, database selection, OAuth flows, Kubernetes/serverless mechanics,
  Spring Boot vs. Quarkus) — all linked.
* Service discovery, circuit breakers, service mesh, distributed tracing, contract testing, the microservice
  chassis — named in one sentence with a link where a page touches them (the "what it costs you" page and the
  new-project deployment table), not documented.
* AWS-specific mechanics from Golding's chapters 4–12 and 14–16 (Cognito, EKS/Lambda implementations, tiering,
  SaaS Anywhere, GenAI) — only the deployment models, migration patterns and guiding principles are used.
* Micro-frontends beyond one paragraph with links; a full tutorial for any gateway product, Spring Modulith or
  YARP (each is shown in one short snippet at most and linked).
* Organisational/process transformation (team topologies, DevOps adoption) beyond the sentences the migration
  overview needs to say "this is not only a technology change".
* Cost modelling and cloud pricing.

## Task details

* **Importance**: important.
* **Estimated difficulty**: hard — 13 concept pages plus a landing page and a one-page PDF, of which the five
  migration/decision pages carry a hard "simple to understand, with worked examples, Mermaid and SVG figures"
  requirement and must stay mutually consistent on one running example; the material itself is stable and
  well-sourced, the cross-linking surface is large (nine existing sections are linked), and every recommended
  technology must be one this site already documents. No new tooling is needed; the Architectural Patterns and
  Messaging sections provide a complete precedent for structure, disclaimer, figures and the PDF pipeline.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `modules/ROOT/partials/architecture-disclaimer.adoc` exists, contains **only** the AI-assistance
      disclosure and the bibliography pointer, and no other admonition block
      (`NOTE`/`TIP`/`WARNING`/`CAUTION`/`IMPORTANT`) appears anywhere under `modules/ROOT/pages/backend/architecture/`
      other than that include.
- [ ] `modules/ROOT/nav.adoc` has the Architecture block under *Guides & References → Backend Development*,
      after the Architectural Patterns block; `backend/index.adoc` lists "Architecture" as a new bullet with
      updated `:description:`/`:keywords:`; the root `pages/index.adoc` keywords mention monolith, modular
      monolith, microservices, strangler fig, migration, API gateway, BFF and SaaS.
- [ ] All 13 concept pages + `index.adoc` + `cheat-sheet.adoc` exist under
      `modules/ROOT/pages/backend/architecture/`, each with `:description:`, `:keywords:`, the disclaimer include
      and a `== References` section linking only online documentation; every technology a page recommends is one
      already documented on this site and is linked to its existing reference page.
- [ ] The pages answer explicitly, with the arguments from the books and the linked online sources: **what**
      microservices give you (independent teams and services, small and fast-to-evolve independently deployable
      units, independent scaling, fault isolation, technology freedom), **what** they cost (loss of ACID
      transactionality and consistent queries, distributed-system complexity, more code and infrastructure to
      maintain, coordinated cross-service rollouts), **when** a monolith is better (small projects, small teams,
      one-shot, no need to evolve, missing prerequisites) and **when** microservices are (large, complex,
      multi-team, long-lived systems; performance/scaling of large systems), and **how** to layer backend and
      frontend so they evolve independently and native apps can share the API.
- [ ] The five migration/decision pages (`migration-overview.adoc`, the four `migration-path-*.adoc` pages) and
      `starting-a-new-project.adoc` are written in plain, step-by-step language, share the Bookshop running
      example, each contain at least the 📊 figures listed (Mermaid and SVG under
      `modules/ROOT/images/architecture-*.svg`), and each provide links to recommended external sites as proof
      and further reading for every migration technique and every technology recommendation.
- [ ] `starting-a-new-project.adoc` covers at least the seven scenario cards (small one-shot / startup MVP /
      long-lived line-of-business / high-traffic consumer / large multi-team platform / multi-tenant SaaS /
      batch job) and the cross-cutting recommendation tables, with every recommendation linked to the existing
      comparison page it derives from.
- [ ] `npm run validate:mermaid` passes for every Mermaid block in the section.
- [ ] `index.adoc` has a `== Bibliography` section listing and linking every source in the groups above,
      including both books with their publisher pages and the note on how they were used, and the Architectural
      Patterns bibliography is extended as described.
- [ ] `modules/ROOT/attachments/architecture-cheat-sheet.pdf` exists, is exactly one A4 page, covers every box
      listed under "Cheat sheet" — in particular the "migration path by current architecture" rows and the
      "new project → recommended stack" matrix —, is visually consistent with the existing cheat sheets, and is
      linked from `cheat-sheet.adoc` via `xref:attachment$…`.
- [ ] The cross-links listed under "Cross-links to add in existing pages" are in place.
- [ ] `npx antora antora-playbook.yml` builds with no `xref` or AsciiDoc errors and
      `build/site/backend/architecture/` renders every page, every SVG and the PDF download.

items.title: Production-readiness hardening for Taper (auth, graceful shutdown, TLS, index/constraint gaps, ops layer)

labels.name: ready-for-agent
labels.description: Fully specified, ready for an AFK agent

items.body:
## Problem Statement

Taper is a distributed, multi-tenant inventory system whose invariants (no overselling, exactly-once saga steps, tenant isolation via RLS, transactional outbox + CDC) are proven by chaos/load tests and CI. But running it in front of real traffic is blocked by gaps in the surrounding production casing:

- Services cannot be restarted or scaled without abruptly killing in-flight requests — no graceful shutdown or drain anywhere.
- The auth token is a private sandbox HMAC format with a hardcoded default secret and no roles — anyone who ships defaults can mint tokens for any tenant.
- All internal transport is plaintext (no TLS).
- Hot query paths do sequential scans for lack of lookup indexes.
- The most safety-critical business logic (order saga, reservation TTL sweeper, stock reconciliation) has zero unit tests.
- The database enforces no CHECK constraints, and idempotency records grow without a retention owner.
- Logging is unstructured `log.Printf` with no request correlation; `/healthz` is a blind 200.
- No operational layer: no K8s/Helm, no backup runbook for the single Postgres that holds every DB, no SLOs/alerting, no data-retention or tenant-offboarding story, no migration ledger, no config validation or `.env.example`.

## Solution

Harden Taper along fifteen work items grouped into four batches:

1. **Runtime resilience** — graceful shutdown + in-flight draining on every service and consumer; dependency-aware readiness probes; liveness on gRPC services.
2. **Security** — real JWT with roles (RBAC), no compile-time default secret in any path, TLS on all internal dials, rate-limit hygiene, config validation that fails fast instead of falling silent to dev defaults.
3. **Data integrity & query** — lookup indexes on the proven hot paths, CHECK constraints mirroring the domain invariants in CONTEXT.md, and a retention owner for idempotency records.
4. **Testability & operations** — unit coverage for the untested business logic, structured logging with request correlation, migration ledger, and the operational layer (K8s manifests, backup runbook, SLOs/alerting, incident runbook, GDPR/retention/offboarding policy).

## User Stories

**Runtime resilience**

1. As an operator, I want to send SIGTERM to any service and have it stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests, flush traces, and exit cleanly, so that deploys and scale-downs never drop a request mid-saga.
2. As an operator, I want Kafka consumers to cancel on shutdown after completing their current poll/commit, so that at-least-once offsets remain safe and no message sits uncommitted mid-write.
3. As an operator, I want background loops (reservation TTL sweeper, reconciliation scan, saga resume, outbox pruning) to stop promptly on shutdown, so that two instances never run the same sweep.
4. As an operator, I want the gateway's readiness probe to report the dependency state (Postgres reachable, each downstream gRPC service reachable, Kafka health where relevant), so that load balancers stop routing traffic to an instance that cannot serve.
5. As an operator, I want each gRPC service to expose a liveness endpoint independent of dependency state, so that a deadlocked process is clearly distinguishable from one merely waiting on a downstream.
6. As an operator, I want readiness to go unhealthy before a planned dependency maintenance, so that upstream traffic drains before the dependency drops.

**Security**

7. As an API consumer, I want the claims I present to be standard JWT-shaped and the secret to be required at boot (no default), so that a misconfiguration is loud rather than insecure by default.
8. As a tenant administrator, I want role claims so that a given token can be restricted to read-only or limited mutation, so that the blast radius of a leaked token is bounded.
9. As a tenant administrator, I want the gateway to reject tokens scoped beyond their granted operations, so that least-privilege is enforced at the surface.
10. As an operator, I want all internal gRPC dials to use TLS, so that tenant and order data is not observable on the wire between services.
11. As an operator, I want the gateway HTTP listener to support TLS termination, so that client traffic is encrypted end-to-end.
12. As an operator, I want the per-tenant rate-limit bucket map to evict idle tenants, so that the gateway's memory does not grow without bound with tenant churn.
13. As an operator, I want config validation to fail startup on a missing required value or an unparseable one, so that a wrong `GATEWAY_RATE_PER_TENANT` cannot silently apply a default.
14. As an operator, I want a `.env.example` documenting every environment variable, so that provisioning a new environment is repeatable.

**Data integrity & query**

15. As an operator, I want lookups by order to use an index, so that per-order reads stop forcing sequential scans as the table grows.
16. As an operator, I want `stock_events` to be indexed for the reconciliation scans, so that drift detection stays cheap at scale.
17. As a tenant, I want the database to reject impossible stock arithmetic (negative available, negative quantities, out-of-enum states), so that a bug in any write path cannot silently corrupt the invariant the reconciliation scan exists to catch.
18. As an operator, I want `processed_idempotency_keys` to have a retention owner analogous to outbox pruning, so that the table cannot grow without bound.
19. As an operator, I want each migration to run against a ledger, so that a partial apply cannot silently replay and so rollback/forward is machine-verifiable.

**Testability & operations**

20. As a developer, I want unit tests for the order saga step transitions and compensation, so that a regression in one step is caught in milliseconds, not after a full stack run.
21. As a developer, I want unit tests for the reservation TTL sweeper and stock reconciliation, so that the safety-critical background loops are exercised without the compose stack.
22. As an operator, I want structured JSON logs with a request/trace correlation, so that logs can be filtered and aggregated alongside traces.
23. As an operator, I want Kubernetes manifests (or Helm) mirroring the compose topology, so that the proven stack can be deployed on a container orchestrator.
24. As an operator, I want a backup/restore runbook for the shared Postgres, so that the single source of all service databases has a recoverability story.
25. As an operator, I want recorded SLOs with Prometheus alerting rules, so that error budget burn is paged rather than discovered.
26. As an operator, I want an incident-response runbook, so that a paged-on-call engineer has a fixed playbook.
27. As a compliance officer, I want documented data-retention rules per table and topic, so that records are pruned on policy rather than by accident.
28. As a compliance officer, I want a documented tenant-offboarding path that purges a tenant's rows RLS-scoped per database, so that leavers do not leave data behind.
29. As an operator, I want the containers profile to be able to run without a single dev secret default, so that the shipped images are safe even if a crawler finds them.

## Implementation Decisions

**B1 — Runtime resilience**

- Add a shared `pkg/closer`-style helper (or one per binary) that waits for SIGTERM/SIGINT, triggers `grpcServer.GracefulStop()` and `http.Server.Shutdown(ctx)` with a bounded drain window, cancels the root context for background loops, and flushes OTLP before exit. Consumers pass a cancellable context to their `Run` loop instead of `context.Background()`.
- Each service gains a dependency-aware readiness handler (Postgres ping, downstream gRPC health via the existing breakers, Kafka connectivity for consumers); liveness stays a static 200 on a separate port/path. The gateway grows `/readyz`; gRPC services expose the same via their admin/metrics listener.
- Background loops subscribe to the cancellable root context; idempotency + resume already make re-running safe, the goal is *prompt* stop, not exclusivity.

**B2 — Security**

- Replace the sandbox HMAC token in `pkg/auth` with a standards-shaped JWT (subject + claims: `tenant_id`, `role`, `scopes`, `exp`) verified with constant-time HMAC; keep the same `Issue`/`Verify` surface so gateway call sites change little. `role` maps to an allowed-operation set checked at the gateway core before dispatch.
- Remove the `"taper-sandbox-secret"` default: absent or blank `GATEWAY_JWT_SECRET` fails startup with a clear message (compose and load harness keep explicit overrides). DB credential defaults likewise fail-fast in the containers profile; dev defaults remain only where a non-container local run needs them, with a warning.
- All gRPC dials in `pkg/grpcx` move to TLS-capable credentials; a `GRPC_TLS_*` env surface (CA bundle, optional client cert) governs it, with insecure dial reserved for an explicit `GRPC_INSECURE=1` escape hatch for local dev.
- Rate-limit buckets gain idle eviction (map with last-used timestamp, evict under a small mutex beyond a floor), and the docs keep the honest "per-process, not global" note.
- `pkg/config` gains validating accessors that return errors; binaries compile an env checklist at boot and exit non-zero on missing/invalid required values.

**B3 — Data integrity & query**

- New migrations (up/down pairs): lookup indexes on `orders(order_id)`, `saga_instances(order_id)`, `order_lines(order_id)`, `stock_events(tenant_id, sku_id, warehouse_id)`; CHECK constraints for positive quantities, `available_qty >= 0`, and status-in-enum where the domain states in CONTEXT.md pin them; a retention sweep for `processed_idempotency_keys` mirroring the existing outbox prune approach.
- No new FKs — the aggregate-id string-key style in ADR-0001 stands; constraints are value-level only.

**B4 — Testability & operations**

- Unit tests for the untested `internal/` packages following the existing `internal/gateway/core_test.go` and `pkg/...` style (constructor-injected log/deps, table-driven).
- Logging moves to `log/slog` with a JSON handler and a correlation field carried from the trace context already propagated; stdout for pods, structured retainers appended to the runbooks.
- K8s manifests (Deployment/Service/ConfigMap/Secret wiring + PVC for Postgres, ServiceMonitor for the existing RED endpoints) under a `deploy/` dir; compose remains the dev path.
- Docs: backup/restore + PITR runbook, SLO definitions + alerting rules alongside `docs/runbooks`, incident runbook, data-retention matrix, tenant-offboarding procedure.
- Migration ledger: `schema_migrations` table applied via a small runner in `scripts/` that records each applied version per DB (replacing the raw glob in CI).

## Testing Decisions

A good test asserts **external behavior**: a request/state change observed through the public surface, never internals. For graceful shutdown, that means "process exits 0 after drain and the in-flight add/move completed and its events landed" — not "the handler ran". For auth, "a tenant-scoped read is rejected after its token's scope changes" — not hash internals.

- **Primary seam — integration harness (`integration/`)**: extends the existing suite (prior art: `chaos_test.go` kills real processes mid-saga and asserts `available + allocated == seeded`; `saga_test.go` drives the live stack). Add (a) a graceful-drain test that SIGTERMs each service under live traffic and asserts no request fails + invariant holds, (b) a readiness test that stops Postgres/Kafka/downstreams and asserts `/readyz` flips while `/healthz`/liveness stays up, (c) an RBAC test asserting scoped tokens are rejected (prior art: gateway tenant-injection assertions in `gateway_test.go`), (d) after the migration batch, the oversell-audit SQL and chaos invariants still pass (guards the indexes/constraints).
- **Secondary seam — unit (`pkg/...` and `internal/gateway`)**: auth mint/verify round-trips + expired/forged/scoped rejection; rate-limit eviction under churn; config fail-fast on missing/invalid values; `slog` writer emits expected JSON fields; saga step machine, reservation sweeper expiry, and reconciliation drift detection in table-driven unit tests per the existing `core_test.go` pattern.

## Out of Scope

- Distributed rate limiting (multi-gateway limiter / Redis) — currently justified as per-process; the spec only adds eviction hygiene and keeps the documented ceiling.
- Mutual TLS at the service mesh / sidecar layer — plain TLS on the dials is in scope; an injected sidecar or mTLS identity layer is not.
- Horizontal DB sharding / xDS service discovery — out of scope; client-side `round_robin` stays.
- Per-tenant data residency or multi-region deployment.
- Paid observability vendor integration — Prometheus/Jaeger wiring additions stay local-first.

## Further Notes

- The four batches are independent; Batch 1 (resilience) and Batch 3 (indexes/constraints) are the cheapest and highest-ROI, matching the containerized `--scale` story already in the repo.
- ADR-0001 (architecture foundations) and ADR-0002 (outbox pruning) are respected: outbox/event-sourcing style keying and pruning ownership are untouched; the idempotency retention owner mirrors ADR-0002's approach.
- The `ready-for-agent` label is applied. Where an item needs a human (e.g. choosing the SLO targets, GDPR review of the retention matrix), it should be split off with `ready-for-human` before an agent picks it up.

items.title: decision register: every open decision by workstream — plain language, recommendation, consequence (approve in batches)
items.body:
# Decision register — every open decision, by workstream

**What this is.** The problem map (#2820) found ~50 open decisions scattered across long design documents, and the risk is that they get lost or re-litigated rather than decided. This register puts every one in a single place, in plain language, each with a recommended answer and the cost of the alternatives, so they can be approved in batches instead of read one design doc at a time. Nothing here is scheduled or implemented; a row is only "decided" when the owner (or the engineer, for engineering rows) records an answer.

**How to use it.** Approve per workstream — each approval unlocks only the work that workstream gates and nothing else. **Owner-required** rows are bolded in the last column; everything marked *engineering* is an internal judgement call that does not need owner input and can be decided by whoever implements it. Reply with e.g. "approve A1, A2; amend C2 to X" and the rows move to `approved`.

**Counts:** 50 open decisions — **17 owner-required**, 33 engineering. Plus 1 already-approved row and 4 approved items listed at the end.

**Legend.** *Thing* = holds state and gets replaced as state changes. *Happening* = a dated occurrence. *Link* = a named relationship. *Detail* = a field on something else. *Pack* = a namespaced domain vocabulary (`venture:deal`). *ME00 — meRGE-by-name* = the graph identifies objects by their bare name, so two same-named things collapse into one node.

---

## A — Write-path integrity

*The five ways data enters the graph ("doors") disagree about which fields exist and what to do with unknown ones. Three filed bugs (#2813, #2795, #2814) are all the same class: declared ≠ stored.*

| ID | WS | Decision (plain language) | Recommendation | Options + what each costs/buys | Owner or engineering? | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A1** | A | Do we make all five write doors speak one existing contract, or just fix each door's private field list? | **Do both, staged.** Stage 1 (now): derive every door's field list from one shared declaration + add the parity test — kills the three filed bugs cheaply. Stage 2: route capture and the M2 lane through the existing `sdk.ingest` bundle contract so a sixth door can't reintroduce the drift. | Route-everything-now: strongest, but weeks of adapter work and it delays the bug fixes. Fix-lists-only: ships fastest, kills the filed bugs, but leaves the structural cause — a future field can again reach one door and not another, and #2813-style eval/product divergence stays possible. Staged: gets the fixes now and the prevention next. | **owner** | #2820 (newest decision, "route through `sdk.ingest` + parity test" vs "keep the doors, fix the lists"); #2813 | open |
| **A2** | A | Is the event journal the source of truth for durability — and does the hosted product get a journal at all? | **Give hosted a journal and make the journal authoritative.** The store is derived data; "props not in the journal are not durable by construction" is the correct framing, not a bug. | Journal-authoritative + hosted journal: correct event-sourced posture, real recovery; costs storage/config and a hosted change. Store-as-authority with FalkorDB AOF + backups: cheaper, but requires *stating* the store is the source of truth and killing the "derived" label — rigging a snapshot to look like replay is the worst of both. Note: the SDK already journals full point snapshots when `event_log_path` is set; hosted's `_make_sdk` sets none. | **owner** | #2820 §3 (highest-priority WS-A question); #2795 | open |
| A3 | A | How does graph configuration (pack installs, pipeline stages) survive `rebuild_all`? | **Classify node labels** as derived vs authoritative configuration, **preserve the authoritative ones**, and export/restore around any rebuild that must wipe them. Audit existing graphs for prior silent wipes. | Allow/deny list + preserve: correct, needs a label classification and a test. Export/restore: works without a classification but adds operator steps. Declarative config source outside the graph: cleanest long-term, biggest change. Today rebuild wipes `:PackManifest`/`:PackInstall`, and because "no marker ⇒ no restriction," a wipe silently *grants* packs a graph was restricted from. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2814; #2792 Q11 | open |
| A4 | A | What happens when a door or a relation hits a field/predicate it can't persist — reject, warn, or drop? | **Declare the policy per door, never silent.** External commit stays fail-closed (callers can retry); internal capture/M2 warn-and-record; SDK/eval persist. Add `prop_unknown`/`prop_dropped` to the existing 11-key warnings channel. Same rule for extraction-emitted relations with no write path: drop-with-audit, not silence. | Uniform reject-everywhere: safest but breaks in-loop capture (failing a whole session is worse than one drop). Uniform warn-everywhere: loses the fail-closed guarantee at the untrusted commit boundary. Per-door declared policy: matches RFC 9413 §5.1 ("virtuous intolerance") and RFC 6709 (ignore/require/reject as a declared choice). Merges the unknown-field question and #2766's relation drop/reject question. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2820 (c)/(d); #2766 Q2 | open |
| A5 | A | Does `:Batch` quarantine become the general sink for unknown props, or is a warnings-only channel enough? | **Warnings-only for internal doors.** Keep `:Batch` for its existing bundle-quarantine semantics; don't overload it as a props graveyard. | General sink: nothing is ever lost, but it becomes a second, unvalidated store that nobody reads. Warnings-only: honest and cheap; the contract test asserts nothing silently vanishes. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2820 open question 3 | open |

---

## B — Ontology substrate

*The vocabulary layer: what a pack is allowed to declare, what a declaration actually means at runtime, and where each kind lives. Most items here are mechanical bugs; three are real ontology decisions.*

| ID | WS | Decision (plain language) | Recommendation | Options + what each costs/buys | Owner or engineering? | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **B1** | B | When a pack declares a relationship (e.g. "a tranche is gated by a condition"), what does that declaration *mean* if the runtime has no write path for it? | **Declared mapping table per pack** — each domain predicate must map to a writable structural predicate (e.g. `gatedBy → dependsOn`), and `tortoise pack validate` prints a per-relation verdict (`writable` / `declaration-only` / `predicate-not-in-allowlist`). Do not extend the writable allowlist until a mapping proves insufficient. | Extend the allowlist with new predicates: most expressive, but each new predicate needs EP semantics and is an ontology change. Mapping table: cheap, honest, keeps the structural vocabulary small. Accept declaration-only + warn: cheapest, but means the pack's relation graph is documentation, not behaviour — today 9 of the venture pack's 11 relations and `pm`'s `blocks` have no write path. | **owner** | #2766 Q1; #2725 relation draft | open |
| **B2** | B | Can a relation declare IMPL/NAND between two Objects, or must operators only connect epistemic targets (Points/Events)? | **Enforce the §8 rule** (error, not warning): operators connect epistemic targets only. Object→Object relationships get a structural predicate (reuse `dependsOn`), not a faked IMPL. | Enforce §8: coherent, but a probe shows `{gatedBy, mechanism: IMPL, Object→Object}` currently validates clean, so real packs may already rely on the loophole. Allow Object→Object under a new non-operator mechanism: more expressive, more surface. Today the validator does no bucket check at all, which invites the exact modelling error the ontology forbids. | **owner** | #2787 Q1; ONTOLOGY §8 | open |
| B3 | B | Is the `extractable` flag a real extractor contract, and do same-kind self-relations need a cardinality? | **Rename `extractable` to declaration-only metadata** unless a consumer is written (it has zero production consumers today); **exempt self-relations** from an explicit cardinality unless the relation carries real semantics. | Wire `extractable`: makes manifests meaningful, needs extractor work. Remove/rename: honest, documents that it is inert. Cardinality on self-relations: more precise, more authoring burden. Merges two #2787 mechanics. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2787 Q2–Q3 | open |
| B4 | B | Which layer is the source of truth for kind vocabularies — the pack-facing `CANONICAL_*` lists or the runtime registries? | **`CANONICAL_*` is the declared source; runtime registries derive from it**, with a consistency-guard test. Today both exist and diverge (4 event kinds, 5 object kinds, and the source-type lists disagree). | Widen the pack validator to match runtime: packs can use more kinds, but the declared set keeps drifting. Narrow runtime: consistent, but removes capability. Declared-source + derived: one place to change, needs a build/test guard. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2786 Q1 | open |
| B5 | B | Documented aliases (`AgentSession`/`sessionCaptured`): one canonical entry plus an alias map, or duplicate entries? | **One canonical entry + alias map.** Duplicates are what let the two vocabularies drift apart in the first place. | Alias map: one identity per concept, small resolver change. Duplicates as today: no code change, but the divergence bug recurs. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2786 Q2 | open |
| B6 | B | The CRM bridge writes an undeclared `commitment` point kind. Promote it to a canonical kind, or remap it? | **Remap the bridge** to the renamed `actionItem` Object and retire the point kind, consistent with the already-approved rename. | Promote: keeps the bridge untouched, adds a kind to close the gap. Remap: one fewer undeclared vocabulary, but a bridge change. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2786 Q3; #2725 renames | open |
| B7 | B | Consistency guard: a test-only assertion or a generated/built set? | **Generated set + test** — regenerate the runtime registries from the canonical constants so drift is impossible by construction, and keep a test as the backstop. | Test-only: cheapest, catches drift after the fact. Generated: prevents it, small build step. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2786 Q4 | open |
| **B8** | B | When a pack references a kind from a pack that isn't installed, should the load hard-fail, degrade gracefully, and should `depends_on` force-install the dependency or stay advisory? | **Hard-fail the load with a precise message on self-hosted, and make `depends_on` force-install (with an explicit opt-out).** Today an unresolved reference **silently deletes the entire referring pack** — dropping one starter pack kills up to three others. A refused load is recoverable; a silently missing vocabulary is not. | Hard-fail + force-install: correct and predictable; enterprise tenants get a cascade unless they opt out. Graceful-degradation + advisory `depends_on`: maximum availability, but recreates the silent-loss failure mode and leaves `depends_on` dead code (it has zero consumers today). Merges #2781 Q1+Q2. | **owner** | #2781 Q1–Q2; #2820 pattern 3 | open |
| B9 | B | Do cross-pack references need per-graph enablement (a graph may not have the referenced pack installed)? | **Yes — resolve cross-pack refs against the graph's installed pack set**, not the catalog, once #2714/#2728 land. | Per-graph resolution: consistent with per-graph pack selection, requires the enforcement work. Catalog-only: simpler, but a graph can reference a pack it doesn't have. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2781 Q3; #2728/#2714 | open |
| B10 | B | How does a pack declare which *value* fields a kind carries (e.g. `fundingTranche` has `committedAmountMinor`/`currency`)? | **Add a declared `values`/`valueFields` key to `kindDefs`** (closed vocabulary, validated, unknown keys still rejected). Do not hardcode value fields in code — that is the hardcoded-map anti-pattern #2729 exists to remove. | Declared key: one clean surface, touches manifest schema + prompt render. Hardcode in Python: no schema change, but #2782's value model would have nowhere to be declared per kind and every new kind is a code change. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2818 | open |
| B11 | B | Should value schemas feed the classification index text (which rotates the cached index) or stay out of it? | **Keep them out** so `compile_kind_index_spec` output stays byte-identical and the npz cache key doesn't rotate on every pack install. If rotation is wanted, make it an explicit decision, not a side effect. | Out: stable cache, value fields still reach the extraction prompts. In: richer classifier signal, but every pack install silently forces an index rebuild. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2818 fix step 3 | open |
| B12 | B | Resolve the `milestone` three-way collision (Object kind + legacy point kind + miner event kind)? | **Reuse `pm:milestone`** and keep namespaced references; defer any semantic change to #2767. Redeclaring it fails cross-pack near-miss validation and blocks installs. | Redeclare: strictly worse (ambiguous name, blocking validation). Reuse: no new vocabulary, needs the pack to reference the pm kind. Mechanical. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2767; #2725 revised draft | open |
| B13 | B | Add `strategy`/`plan`/`goal`/`target` to the canonical object kinds so packs can subclass them, or document why they're excluded? | **Add them** (they are documented core kinds in ONTOLOGY §5 but rejected by the registry, which blocks the `commitment`-state family). | Add: aligns doc and code, lets packs subclass. Document-exclusion: cheaper, but contradicts ONTOLOGY §5 and blocks pack authoring. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2727; #2820 finding AF-2 | open |
| B14 | B | What credibility tier do the meeting source kinds get (`meeting_transcript`, `meeting_minutes`)? | **Transcript = T1 (primary record), minutes = T2 (derived artifact)**; decide with evidence from the corpus and add a named decision if it disagrees. | Tiers encode trust in downstream EP weighting, so they matter; NEUTRAL defers the question and makes every meeting equally trusted. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2726 | open |

---

## C — State & value model

*The largest workstream: giving things a lifecycle that a graph can customize, and giving money/numbers a real representation. #2792's design already carries a recommendation for each row.*

| ID | WS | Decision (plain language) | Recommendation | Options + what each costs/buys | Owner or engineering? | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | C | Give money a first-class representation (amount + currency) instead of prose or an untyped prop? | **Yes — approved.** Shared value object, stored **flat** as scalar props on the entity that owns the claim (`committedAmountMinor` on the tranche, `releasedAmountMinor` on the disbursement), `values[]` array on Points; integer minor units, never floats; currency explicit per amount. | Flat scalars: range-indexable and `SUM()`-able, which is why the feature exists. Nested JSON: **not storable** — FalkorDB cannot persist maps, and a JSON string is unindexable. Prose-only: cheapest, but forces re-extraction of every historical number later. | **approved** (owner, #2782) | #2782 | approved |
| **C2** | C | What makes an entity's identity — is a name unique globally, or only within a scope (a graph, a portfolio company, a meeting)? | **Scope-first: identity becomes `(scope, kind, name)`**, with persons staying global (a partner legitimately sits on three boards) and Objects scope-qualified. Only build graph-per-startup if the pilot needs a single cross-portfolio ranked query. | In-graph scope key: fixes collision by construction, needs a backfill and fold/`about*` join updates. Graph-per-startup with app-layer fan-out: simpler key, breaks single cross-portfolio queries. Name-only (today): no work, but two same-named tranches collapse and one company's status fold flips the other's object. | **owner** | #2730 Q1; #2782 Q2; #2820 pattern 1 | open |
| C3 | C | Is a meeting's `scope` authoritative (safe to auto-scope from) or advisory (a hypothesis to be confirmed)? | **Authoritative when asserted by the Envelope; never infer a scope from a filename** — an inferred scope must be marked as a hypothesis. Today startup is filename-convention only. | Authoritative: enables auto-scoping, needs the Envelope to carry it. Advisory-only: safe, but leaves auto-scoping unavailable. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2730 Q2 | open |
| **C4** | C | Do `scope`, `isPlaceholder`, and `sameAs` live in the core ontology or in the `venture` pack? | **Core.** Identity and scoping are domain-neutral, and cross-pack referencing is currently broken (#2781), so a pack-owned identity concept would make core behaviour depend on pack installation. | Core: available everywhere, adds ONTOLOGY §5 vocabulary + a changelog entry. Venture-pack: keeps core small, but identity is not a venture concept and the dependency is unsafe. | **owner** | #2730 Q3 | open |
| C5 | C | For legitimately cross-scope entities (a joint venture), one node with several scopes or one canonical node plus membership links? | **One canonical node + explicit membership links.** Multi-scope nodes make "which scope is this query in?" ambiguous. | Canonical + memberships: queryable per scope, one extra link type. Multi-scope: fewer nodes, ambiguous resolution. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2730 Q4 | open |
| C6 | C | How do existing entities get their new identity key, and does replay produce the same graph as live? | Backfill `entityKey` with `scope = graph`, and require `live == journal == replay` (tracked in #2296) as part of the change, not an afterthought. | Backfill + parity: migration work, but without it a rebuild re-mints different identities. Map-on-read only: cheaper, leaves two identity systems in the graph. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2730 Q5; #2296 | open |
| C7 | C | Is a pipeline tied to exactly one kind, or is it a named definition several kinds can share? | **Named pipeline with one default per kind** (the HubSpot/Salesforce shape); add an optional `pipelineId` on the object later without reworking the model. | One-per-kind: simplest, blocks two deal types sharing a pipeline. Named: slightly more model, no later migration. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2792 Q1 | open |
| **C8** | C | Do the canonical stage *slots* (the fixed meanings stages map onto) live in core or in the pack? | **Core** — slots, outcome vocabulary and the terminal invariant are core; packs and graphs own only the labels/bindings. Otherwise comparable lifecycles can't be compared across packs. | Core slots: cross-pack comparability, one more core concept. Pack slots: keeps core small, but the same lifecycle means different things per pack. | **owner** | #2792 Q2 | open |
| **C9** | C | Is the terminal outcome set `{won, lost, withdrawn, completed}` right? | **Yes**, with `denied`/`rejected`/`waived` mapped to `lost`/`withdrawn` at the binding level rather than added as new canonical outcomes. | Fixed canonical outcomes: comparable and queryable. Free-form outcomes: flexible, unqueryable. | **owner** | #2792 Q3 | open |
| C10 | C | When a later meeting mentions an older stage (out of order, or a step backwards), apply it or just record it? | **Valid-time ordering: record stale transitions but don't apply them; backward transitions are record-only unless explicitly marked a correction.** | Apply-everything: latest-writer wins, but a retrospective mention resurrects a closed deal. Record-only: history retained, needs a "current stage" derivation rule. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2792 Q5–Q6 | open |
| C11 | C | Retiring a stage that objects currently sit in: block it or migrate them? | **Allow + flag the occupants + provide a bulk-map tool.** Never silently migrate. | Block: no orphaned objects, but blocks cleanup. Allow + flag + tool: operator-driven, auditable. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2792 Q7 | open |
| C12 | C | Does the pilot need a UI for unknown stage values, or is a tool + flagged list enough? | **Tool + flagged list for the pilot**; the Settings queue lands with #2728. | Tool-only: ships sooner. UI: nicer, couples the pilot to #2728. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2792 Q8 | open |
| **C13** | C | When a stage transition is blocked by an unmet gate, warn or refuse? | **Warn by default; `block` is opt-in per pipeline.** A memory system should record reality even when reality violates a rule. | Warn: never loses a real-world transition, relies on the flag being seen. Block: enforces process, but silently drops data when extraction is wrong. | **owner** | #2792 Q9; #2725 gate decision | open |
| **C14** | C | Keep `Object.status` as the existence axis and add a separate `pipelineStageId` for domain stage? | **Yes**, with dual-write for the compatibility kinds for one deprecation cycle. Today `status` already conflates existence ("superseded") with domain stage ("in_progress"), and the fold vocabulary collides across domains (`open`→`in_progress`, `closed`→`completed`). | Two axes: clean separation, one additive property + dual-write. One axis: no schema change, but the collision persists. | **owner** | #2792 Q10 | open |
| C15 | C | Does #2729 (pack-declared status folds) land first as the mechanism, or are #2729 and #2792 one design? | **One design.** #2792 generalizes exactly the mechanism #2729 introduces; merging avoids building the declaration surface twice (and absorbs #2729's four sub-questions). | One design: one mechanism, larger single change. Two: #2729 lands sooner for github/pm parity, but the declaration surface is reworked. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2792 Q12; #2729 | open |
| **C16** | C | Who may edit a graph's pipeline stages, and who may reopen a closed entity? | **Graph-scoped admin** for both — the same role as pack installation — with a full config audit trail. Reopen by extraction only with an explicit quoted reopen utterance + confidence gate; never an ordinary mention. | Graph-admin: consistent governance, needs an admin role check. Open-to-members: convenient, unaudited. | **owner** | #2792 Q13 + Q4 | open |
| C17 | C | After a graph overrides a pack's default stages, what happens when the pack's defaults change? | **Override = full snapshot; no auto-merge; an explicit "reset to default" that shows a diff.** | Snapshot: graph config is predictable, pack improvements don't reach overridden graphs. Auto-merge: keeps graphs current, silently changes stages under live objects. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2792 Q14 | open |
| C18 | C | How does a gate interact with a stage transition — an attribute of the transition, or an independent thing that governs it? | **Independent kind that references the transition/thing it governs** (consistent with the approved "a gate IS a thing" decision); the transition records whether the gate was met. | Independent: reusable across tranches, stage gates, milestones; one more concept. Transition-attribute: cheaper, but duplicates gate semantics per transition type. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2792 Q6; #2725 gate decision | open |
| C19 | C | Events have an undocumented arbitrary-prop lane that nothing reads. Remove it or formalize it? | **Remove it** (Events strictly fixed-field) unless #2729/#2792 needs event-carried props, in which case declare them explicitly. Today it advertises event-carried state that no code reads and the commit path forbids — a trap. | Remove: strict, may block a future need. Keep + document: cheaper, preserves an unused escape hatch. Declare explicitly: most work, most honest. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2788 Q1–Q2 | open |
| C20 | C | What is the minimum extraction-side contract for typed values to actually reach the graph? | The four coordinated changes: `values[]` in the output contract, a deterministic normalizer, a Point extras pass in the projection (so values survive rebuild), and the capture-seam passthrough. **Watch the highest-risk coupling:** changing `compute_client_commit_id`'s canonical form makes pre-change payloads fail with `commit_id_mismatch`. | Partial (schema only): the field is accepted, then dropped by capture/M2 and invisible to benchmarks. Full contract: more work, but otherwise #2782's feature is unobservable on the product path. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2782 extractor-intersection report; #2813 | open |

---

## D — Venture pack delivery

*The actual product: the `venture` pack's vocabulary. #2725 is an explicit owner-approval gate — no authoring until the owner signs off.*

| ID | WS | Decision (plain language) | Recommendation | Options + what each costs/buys | Owner or engineering? | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **D1** | D | Is `gate` a core kind or declared in the `venture` pack? | **Core.** "Gate" is a broad cross-domain term (funding, product, deployment), and cross-pack referencing is broken (#2781), so a venture-owned gate could not be reused safely. | Core: reusable, one more core concept. Venture pack: keeps core small, but gates in other domains would fork the vocabulary. | **owner** | #2725 open 1 (D6 sub-decision) | open |
| D2 | D | Is `fundingAgreement` a subtype of the existing core `agreement`, or core `agreement` plus a round-type attribute? | **Fix #2783 (the lowercase-parent bug) and declare `venture:fundingAgreement ⊂ agreement`.** The attribute fallback loses classifier precision. | Subtype: precise classification, needs a one-line validator fix. Attribute: no validator change, but a grant and a SAFE look alike to the extractor. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2725 open 2; #2783 | open |
| **D3** | D | Does the pilot ship *with* the value layer (#2782), or author valuation fields now and land values second? | **Land the write-path fixes (A) and the value layer (#2782) first, then author the pack.** Do not author value fields against a write path that silently drops them — every valuation would be recorded as prose and need re-extraction. | Values first: delays the pack, but the corpus's best-grounded requirement (tranche gates, valuation) works. Pack first: ships sooner, but valuation is prose-only and #2813/#2795 would eat the fields anyway. | **owner** | #2725 open 3 | open |
| **D4** | D | Which gates exist in the pilot — tranche gates only, or programme stage-gates too? | **Tranche gates only.** They are the single best-grounded state requirement in the corpus; programme stage-gates need the configurable pipelines (#2792) and should be added there. | Tranche-only: grounded, ships sooner. Add stage-gates: more complete, blocked on #2792 and partly extrapolated from a 4-meeting corpus. | **owner** | #2725 open 4 | open |
| **D5** | D | Does `asset` duplicate the existing `product-strategy:product`? | **Declare `asset` as the general parent in the `venture` pack and leave `product` alone** (cross-pack reference is unsafe per #2781); record `equivalentTo` where they overlap. | General `asset` + `product` subtype: clean taxonomy, would require a cross-pack subtype that #2781 blocks. Reuse `product`: no duplication, but "product" does not cover IP/datasets, and it welds a venture concept to another pack. | **owner** | #2725 earlier D3 | open |
| **D6** | D | Are the 8 uncovered corpus concepts (risk/blocker, board decision, budget rubrica, experiment result, procurement, competitor, document/artifact, patent lifecycle) in scope now or parked? | **Park all except risk/blocker and board decision/resolution** (highest recurrence in the corpus); decide the rest after the pilot's first cycle. | All-in-now: more complete, more unvalidated vocabulary and a slower gate. Park-all: smallest surface, but the two recurring concepts get recorded as free-text statements. | **owner** | #2725 earlier D4 | open |
| D7 | D | Vertical vocabulary (biotech, agritech): an overlay pack convention (`venture-biotech`) or broad kind definitions inside the base pack? | **Overlay pack convention** (per the issue's own indicator 4), so the base pack stays vertical-neutral. | Overlay: reusable and clean, needs the overlay mechanism to work (relation/cross-pack caveats). Broad kindDefs: no new mechanism, but bakes verticals into the general pack. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2725 O/I/T indicator 4 | open |

---

## E — Repo / CI hygiene

*Pre-existing breakage blocking merges. All mechanical; no owner decisions. **E first — one red check on `main` blocks the only PR in flight.***

| ID | WS | Decision (plain language) | Recommendation | Options + what each costs/buys | Owner or engineering? | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | E | What do we do about `main` being red (test (b) fails on clean `origin/main`), which blocks PR #2747? | **Fix first, before any workstream work.** Cheap and it unblocks the only in-flight PR. | Fix now: hours; everything else stays blocked. Work around: not an option — it blocks the CI gate for every PR. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2749; #2820 (E first) | open |
| E2 | E | MCP tool tests patch a dead `mcp_server.sdk` global and fail. | Repoint the tests at `_get_team_sdk()`. | Test-only change; no product impact. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2734 | open |
| E3 | E | `CORE_SOURCE_KINDS` snapshots the source registry at import, so runtime registrations are invisible to the Layer-1 gate. | Make the constant read-through (or rebuild it), plus a test that a runtime registration is visible to the gate. | Read-through: fixes the class; snapshot stays a latent trap. This is the same declared≠enforced class as A4. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2742 | open |
| E4 | E | `rebuild_all` drops live-only Point props (`search_keys`, `quote`, `when`, `source_turn_id`) because Point is the only label with no extras lane in the replay fold. | **One-lane fix:** add the extras pass to `_upsert_point_props` (the journal already carries the data — this is not a journal rewrite). | One-lane: small, fixes #2795 and repairs the existing E3 fields. Journal rewrite: unnecessary per the corrected research. | engineering — no owner input needed | #2795; #2820 §4 | open |
| E5 | E | The `subclassOf` gate rejects lowercase canonical parents (`agreement`, `standard`, `document`), blocking `fundingAgreement ⊂ agreement`. | Fix the gate to accept canonical core parents (it currently contradicts its own error message). | One-line validator fix; unblocks D2 and the `commitment`-state family (B13). | engineering — no owner input needed | #2783; #2820 finding AF-3 | open |

---

## Already decided (recorded approvals)

| Decision | Answer | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Value layer exists — money is a value object, not prose | Flat scalar props on the owning entity, `values[]` on Points, integer minor units, explicit currency | #2782 (owner-approved) |
| Venture pack name | `venture` (namespace `venture`) | #2725 owner decision 2026-09-09 |
| Hiring in the venture pack | **No** — HR is its own domain; the CEO search is an `actionItem` for now | #2725 owner decision |
| Kind renames | `commitment`→`actionItem`, `opportunity`→`deal`, `holding`→`investment`, `instrument`→`fundingAgreement` | #2725 owner decision |
| Gate semantics | A gate **is** a Thing (Object) with status pending → criteria-met → passed/failed/waived. Sub-decision (core vs venture) is D1. | #2725 owner decision |
| Lifecycles must be configurable, not hardcoded | Filed as #2792 (pack defaults + per-graph add/rename/reorder; transitions dated; current stage derived) | #2725 owner decision |

---

## Why this order

```
E (#2749) ──► unblocks PR #2747 (#2727, #2726)

A (write contract + silent-loss bugs) ─┐
                                       ├──► C (state & value model) ──► D (venture pack)
B (ontology substrate, mechanical) ────┘
```

- **E first:** one red check blocks everything.
- **A and B in parallel:** A is a decision plus three fixes; B is mostly mechanical.
- **A before C:** the value layer must not be built on a write path that silently drops props, or every new field inherits the loss.
- **B before C:** value fields need somewhere to be declared (#2818).
- **C before D:** the pack's kinds need lifecycles (#2792) and values (#2782) to exist. The pack *sheet* can still be reviewed now.
- **D1–D6 are independent** of the rest and can be decided immediately.
