items.body:
<!-- local-draft: none, reason: local model switched off; template rewrite drafted by a Claude agent and reviewed by the orchestrator -->
## Summary

Add persistent `IDeadLetterStore` implementations for the 10 providers of the database matrix: ADO.NET, Dapper and EF Core on SQL Server, PostgreSQL and MySQL, plus MongoDB. Today only the in-memory `FakeDeadLetterStore` (`src/Encina.Testing.Fakes/Stores/FakeDeadLetterStore.cs`) exists, so a production application cannot keep dead letters across restarts, list, count, replay or expire them.

Scope and status:

- The maintainer decided on 2026-10-07 that the dead letter queue (DLQ) enters 1.0 complete (milestone v0.19.0, p0; SPEC-000 DEC-008, #2008). Oracle and SQLite are out of the matrix (ADR-009, ADR-024), so the 10 providers replace the "13 providers" of the original text and title.
- Implementation plan (merged): `docs/plans/dead-letter-stores-implementation-plan-583.md` (12 phases). Its Design Choices 1-9 and items B1-B10 were decided on 2026-10-09 (see Alternatives Considered).
- One PR, `Fixes #583, #2012`: #2012 (manager errors, replay exclusivity, plaintext replay outcome) is folded in. #2011 (health check) lands first as its own PR.

What changed versus the original body: 13 providers became 10 (SQLite removed); the proposed schema is replaced by the reshaped record of the plan (PascalCase `DeadLetterMessages`, `ErrorCode`, `SourceMessageId`, `TenantId`, replay claim); the cross-cutting rows for locks, resilience, idempotency and module isolation were corrected to match the plan and today's code; the 85% coverage line is replaced by the per-flag manifest targets (AGENTS.md section 9).

## Motivation

The `IDeadLetterStore` interface is defined in `src/Encina.Messaging/DeadLetter/IDeadLetterStore.cs` but has no persistent implementation. Dead letter queues are needed for:

- Storing messages that failed processing after all retries.
- Manual inspection and reprocessing.
- Compliance and audit requirements (storage limitation through `RetentionPeriod` and `DeleteExpiredAsync`).
- Debugging production issues.

Verified against `main` (2026-10-09) while writing the plan, the current state is worse than "no store":

1. None of the 8 provider packages has a `DeadLetter/` folder or a dead letter script (highest script is `028_CreateOperationAuditEntriesTable.sql`).
2. `MessagingConfiguration.UseDeadLetterQueue` registers nothing; only `PatternFlags()` reads it. `AddEncinaDeadLetterQueue<TStore, TFactory>` is called by no production code.
3. `IDeadLetterMessage.IsExpired` forces a wall-clock read (AGENTS.md section 3, `TimeProvider`).
4. `ExceptionMessage` is never written (it can carry personal data) and `ErrorMessage` holds an error code, not a message.
5. The order of results is undefined; `GetStatisticsAsync` assumes two opposite orders and reads the whole queue (`take: int.MaxValue`); `DeleteAllAsync` loads the queue and swallows `Left` results.
6. There is no tenant and no idempotency key: the same source message can be dead-lettered twice (SPEC-002 REQ-017 keeps dead-lettered outbox rows requeueable), and SPEC-000 section 2 forbids retrofitting a tenant key after 1.0.

A persistent store makes each of these observable in production, so the plan fixes the contract defects together with the stores.

Strategic context: #1991 (wire the five `IntegrateWith*` sources to the DLQ, option (a)) depends on this issue; #584-#589 (Marten, EventStoreDB, Elasticsearch, Kafka, Azure, DynamoDB) stay post-1.0 and implement the contract fixed here.

## Proposed Solution

Full detail, SQL per dialect and AI-agent prompts are in the merged plan. Summary:

1. **Reshaped record** (Choice 1): `ErrorMessage` renamed `ErrorCode`; `ExceptionMessage` and `IsExpired` removed; `SourceMessageId`, `TenantId` and nullable `ReplayClaimedAtUtc` added; `bool IsExpiredAt(DateTime utcNow)` with the rule `ExpiresAtUtc <= now` (Choice 2).
2. **Store contract** (Choices 5, 6): `AddAsync -> Either<EncinaError, bool>` (false = source message already captured); `GetMessagesAsync` oldest first by `(DeadLetteredAtUtc, Id)` with `newestFirst`; conditional `MarkAsReplayedAsync -> bool`; atomic replay claim before dispatch with claim expiry; set-based `DeleteManyAsync`; `DeadLetterFilter` gains `TenantId`, `SourceMessageId`, `ExpiresAtOrBeforeUtc`, `AllTenants`.
3. **Table** `DeadLetterMessages` (script `029_CreateDeadLetterMessagesTable.sql` in the six ADO.NET and Dapper packages, EF `DeadLetterMessageConfiguration`, MongoDB collection `dead_letter_messages`) with six indexes, including unique `(SourcePattern, SourceMessageId)`. PostgreSQL uses quoted PascalCase and `TIMESTAMPTZ` for every `*AtUtc` column (Choice 9, B4). No `ModuleId` (#747), no `ActorId` / `CausationId` (#2013).
4. **Stores**: `DeadLetterStoreADO`, `DeadLetterStoreDapper` (x3 each), `DeadLetterStoreEF`, `DeadLetterStoreMongoDB`, each in a `DeadLetter/` folder of the existing provider package (Choice 3).
5. **Core components**: orchestrator stamps tenant and source id and handles duplicates; manager propagates every store `Left`, defaults to the ambient `IRequestContext.TenantId` with an explicit all-tenants option (B7), stores a replay outcome code only (max 256, B3); statistics from counts instead of a full read.
6. **Opt-in registration** (Choice 4): `UseDeadLetterQueue` drives a new public `AddDeadLetterQueueServices<TStore, TFactory>(bool, DeadLetterOptions)` from every provider registration (including `AddEncinaADOWithTenancy`, B5); `TryAdd` so the application's own store or the fake wins.

```csharp
services.AddEncinaADO(config =>
{
    config.UseDeadLetterQueue = true;                         // finally registers store, manager, orchestrator, cleanup
    config.DeadLetterOptions.RetentionPeriod = TimeSpan.FromDays(7);
    config.DeadLetterOptions.ReplayClaimTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5);
});
```

```csharp
public interface IDeadLetterStore
{
    Task<Either<EncinaError, bool>> AddAsync(IDeadLetterMessage message, CancellationToken ct = default);
    Task<Either<EncinaError, IEnumerable<IDeadLetterMessage>>> GetMessagesAsync(
        DeadLetterFilter? filter, int skip, int take, bool newestFirst = false, CancellationToken ct = default);
    Task<Either<EncinaError, int>> DeleteManyAsync(DeadLetterFilter filter, CancellationToken ct = default);
    // MarkAsReplayedAsync -> bool, atomic replay claim, DeleteExpiredAsync, GetCountAsync, SaveChangesAsync: see the plan
}
```

## Alternatives Considered

The alternatives to this feature's design were decided by the maintainer on 2026-10-09 and are not re-opened here: see [`docs/plans/dead-letter-stores-implementation-plan-583.md#maintainer-decisions`](https://github.com/dlrivada/Encina/blob/main/docs/plans/dead-letter-stores-implementation-plan-583.md#maintainer-decisions) (Design Choices 1-9 and B1-B11, each with its options and rationale in the plan's Design Choices section).

Decided summary (all option A): reshape then persist (1); `IsExpiredAt(utcNow)` (2); `DeadLetter/` folder in the 8 existing packages (3); flag-driven `AddDeadLetterQueueServices` (4); oldest-first, set-based store contract (5); unique `(SourcePattern, SourceMessageId)` with `AddAsync -> bool` (6); stamped `TenantId` column with explicit store filter and ambient-tenant default in the manager (7); application cleanup loop on MongoDB, no TTL index (8); quoted PascalCase on PostgreSQL (9). Storage is the 10 usual providers only; there is no Marten store (ADR-019) and no follow-up issue for it.

Alternatives of the original body, kept because they still hold (they argue for a database store at all):

1. **Use message broker dead letter queues only**: broker DLQs (RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus) are transport-specific; database storage gives a unified view across all transports.
2. **Use logging instead of dedicated storage**: logs are hard to query and reprocess from.
3. **Store in a separate microservice**: a centralized dead letter service adds complexity; per-service storage is simpler and keeps data locality.

## Affected Packages

- [ ] Encina (core)
- [x] Encina.EntityFrameworkCore
- [x] Encina.Dapper.*
- [x] Encina.ADO.*
- [ ] Encina.AspNetCore
- [x] Encina.MongoDB
- [x] Encina.OpenTelemetry
- [ ] Encina.Caching.*
- [x] Encina.Messaging
- [ ] Encina.Polly
- [ ] Encina.Cdc
- [x] Other: Encina.Testing.Fakes (fake store and message follow the new contract)

## Provider Implementation Matrix

Database feature: all 10 providers of the AGENTS.md section 5 matrix (SQLite and Oracle are out of the matrix, ADR-009/ADR-024). Every provider registers through `AddDeadLetterQueueServices`.

| Provider | Store | `029` script / config | Unique source key | Replay claim | Notes |
|----------|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|-------|
| ADO-SqlServer | `DeadLetterStoreADO` | script | yes | yes | `OFFSET/FETCH`; error 2627/2601 -> `false` |
| ADO-PostgreSQL | `DeadLetterStoreADO` | script | yes | yes | quoted PascalCase, `TIMESTAMPTZ`; `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` |
| ADO-MySQL | `DeadLetterStoreADO` | script | yes | yes | backticks, `DATETIME(6)`; error 1062 -> `false` |
| Dapper-SqlServer | `DeadLetterStoreDapper` | script | yes | yes | `CommandDefinition` with the token (#1418 not copied) |
| Dapper-PostgreSQL | `DeadLetterStoreDapper` | script | yes | yes | same SQL as ADO |
| Dapper-MySQL | `DeadLetterStoreDapper` | script | yes | yes | GUID type handler for `CHAR(36)` |
| EFCore-SqlServer | `DeadLetterStoreEF` | `DeadLetterMessageConfiguration` | yes | yes | no raw SQL, no `HasFilter`; `ExecuteUpdateAsync`/`ExecuteDeleteAsync` |
| EFCore-PostgreSQL | `DeadLetterStoreEF` | same configuration | yes | yes | Npgsql |
| EFCore-MySQL | `DeadLetterStoreEF` | same configuration | yes | yes | Pomelo; translation of `ExecuteUpdateAsync` verified at implementation |
| MongoDB | `DeadLetterStoreMongoDB` | `MongoDbIndexCreator` | yes | yes | camelCase elements, collection `dead_letter_messages`, ordinary index on `ExpiresAtUtc`, no TTL index |

## Cross-Cutting Integration

Evaluated per AGENTS.md section 6 / ADR-018, as recorded in the plan's matrix. Legend: Included, Deferred (issue), N/A (reason).

| # | Function | Status | Notes |
|---|----------|--------|-------|
| 1 | **Caching** (`ICacheProvider`, decorator, `[Cache]`) | N/A | Write-once records read by operators and the health check; a cached count or page would hide new dead letters |
| 2 | **OpenTelemetry** (`ActivitySource`, `Meter`) | Included | `InstrumentedDeadLetterStore` (`ActivitySource("Encina.Messaging.DeadLetter")`) and `DeadLetterMetrics`; no tenant id, payload or error message in telemetry (SPEC-002 REQ-062) |
| 3 | **Structured Logging** (`[LoggerMessage]`, `Log.cs`) | Included | EventIds 2990-2992 (`EventIdRanges.Messaging`) and 3165-3166 (`EventIdRanges.MongoDB`); re-check they are free when work starts |
| 4 | **Health Checks** (`IEncinaHealthCheck`) | Included | `DeadLetterHealthCheck` fails closed on a store `Left` and registers through `TryAddEnumerable`: delivered by #2011, which lands first |
| 5 | **Validation** (`IValidationProvider`, pipeline) | Included | Store argument rules, `DeadLetterOptions` setter validation, source key lengths checked before I/O (internal validation, not a validation provider) |
| 6 | **Resilience** (retry, circuit breaker, timeout) | N/A | Calls only the application's own database; a failed capture returns `Left` to the source, which owns retries (#1991); cleanup retries at its next interval |
| 7 | **Distributed Locks** (`IDistributedLockProvider`) | Included | No distributed lock; two concurrent replays of one message are prevented by the atomic replay claim (`ReplayClaimedAtUtc`, with expiry), folded in from #2012 |
| 8 | **Transactions** (`IUnitOfWork`, atomicity) | Included | One statement per write; ADO.NET/Dapper enlist through #718's accessor if it has landed; the EF store's shared-`DbContext` rule is documented for failure-path callers (#1991 uses a new scope) |
| 9 | **Idempotency** (`InboxPipelineBehavior`, dedup) | Included | Unique `(SourcePattern, SourceMessageId)`, `AddAsync -> bool`, `OnDeadLetter` once per source message |
| 10 | **Multi-Tenancy** (`TenantId`, `ITenantContext`) | Included | `TenantId` column stamped at capture, filter and index; manager defaults to the ambient tenant with an explicit all-tenants option; replay under the persisted tenant is #2013 |
| 11 | **Module Isolation** (`ModuleId`, `IModuleContext`) | Deferred (#747) | No column now; `DeadLetterMessages` added to #747's scope. The original claim "Source field enables module filtering" does not hold: `SourcePattern` names a messaging pattern, not a module |
| 12 | **Audit Trail** (`IOperationAuditStore`, audit events) | Deferred (#2013) | Operator audit of replay and delete, with `ActorId` / `CausationId` columns, is #2013 (p0, follows this issue) |

Corrections versus the original matrix: Distributed Locks N/A became Included (replay claim); Resilience Deferred became N/A; Idempotency Deferred became Included; Module Isolation Included became Deferred (#747); Audit Trail Deferred now points at #2013.

### Observability Details

| Metric Name | Type | Description |
|-------------|------|-------------|
| `encina.dlq.messages_added_total` | Counter | Dead letters stored (tag `source_pattern`) |
| `encina.dlq.duplicates_ignored_total` | Counter | Captures ignored by the unique source key (`source_pattern`) |
| `encina.dlq.messages_replayed_total` | Counter | Replays (`outcome` = succeeded/failed) |
| `encina.dlq.messages_deleted_total` | Counter | Deletions (`reason` = manual/expired) |
| `encina.dlq.store_failures_total` | Counter | Store failures (`operation`, `error_code`) |

| Span Name | Attributes | Description |
|-----------|------------|-------------|
| `encina.dlq.add`, `.query`, `.count`, `.replay_mark`, `.delete`, `.delete_many`, `.delete_expired` | `dlq.source_pattern`, `dlq.message_id`, `dlq.count`, `encina.error_code` on failure | One activity per store operation; never `EncinaError.Message` (#1788), never a tenant id |

## Test Matrix

| Test Type | Required? | Scope | Notes |
|-----------|:---------:|-------|-------|
| **UnitTests** | Required | Orchestrator, manager (tenant default, claim expiry, propagated `Left`), `AddDeadLetterQueueServices`, fake, decorator, telemetry | `FakeTimeProvider`; stores justify unit 0 in the manifest (real SQL is exercised by integration) |
| **GuardTests** | Required | Constructors and public methods of the 10 stores, 8 factories, decorator, manager, orchestrator; `skip`/`take`/`Guid.Empty`/blank outcome; options setters | |
| **ContractTests** | Required | `DeadLetterStoreContract` abstract base run against the fake and reused by all 10 integration classes | Order, filters, duplicate key, conditional mark, claim won once, `DeleteAllAsync(All)`, `ExpiresAtUtc == now` boundary, PostgreSQL non-UTC session time zone |
| **PropertyTests** | Required | FsCheck sequences of add, mark, delete, clock advance: sorted disjoint pages, expiry never removes live rows, idempotent adds | Complex ordering and expiry logic |
| **IntegrationTests** | Required | All 10 providers on real databases, shared `[Collection("<Family>-<Db>")]` fixtures; concurrent duplicate insert, two-tenant filter, one end-to-end test per family | Schema scripts `029` checked in the PostgreSQL/MySQL schema script tests; no `.md` justification allowed |
| **LoadTests** | Justified | `tests/Encina.LoadTests/Messaging/DeadLetter/DeadLetterStore.md` | Written only on terminal failure; concurrency covered by the duplicate-insert test and the idempotency property |
| **BenchmarkTests** | Justified | `tests/Encina.BenchmarkTests/Encina.Benchmarks/Messaging/DeadLetter/DeadLetterStore.md` | Not a hot path |

## Implementation Tasks

### Core Abstractions

- [ ] Phase 1: reshape `IDeadLetterMessage`, `DeadLetterData`, `DeadLetterContext`, `DeadLetterFilter`, `IDeadLetterStore`; add `DeadLetterStoreLimits` and error codes; update `PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt`
- [ ] Phase 2: orchestrator (tenant, source id, duplicates, count-based statistics), manager (propagated `Left`, outcome code, claim before dispatch, ambient tenant), fake store and message
- [ ] Phase 3: `AddDeadLetterQueueServices`, `DeadLetterOptions` validation and `ReplayClaimTimeout`, provider registrations (including `AddEncinaADOWithTenancy`), MongoDB options
- [ ] Phase 4: entities, factories, `029` scripts (and `000_CreateAllTables.sql`), `DeadLetterMessageConfiguration`, MongoDB indexes, integration test schemas

### Provider Implementations (if applicable)

- [ ] ADO.NET providers (3): `DeadLetterStoreADO` for SqlServer, PostgreSQL, MySQL
- [ ] Dapper providers (3): `DeadLetterStoreDapper` for SqlServer, PostgreSQL, MySQL
- [ ] EF Core provider (1 package, 3 databases): `DeadLetterStoreEF`
- [ ] MongoDB provider (1): `DeadLetterStoreMongoDB`

### Observability

- [ ] OpenTelemetry metrics (`DeadLetterMetrics`)
- [ ] Traces / spans (`InstrumentedDeadLetterStore`, source added to `WithEncina`)
- [ ] Health checks: fail-closed `DeadLetterHealthCheck` (delivered by #2011, lands first)
- [ ] `[LoggerMessage]` 2990-2992 and 3165-3166

### Testing

- [ ] UnitTests
- [ ] GuardTests
- [ ] ContractTests
- [ ] PropertyTests
- [ ] IntegrationTests (Docker, 10 providers)
- [ ] LoadTests (justification file)
- [ ] BenchmarkTests (justification file)
- [ ] Coverage manifests: per-file targets and justifications; local CRAP table

### Documentation

- [ ] XML doc comments on all public APIs
- [ ] README updates (Messaging and the eight provider packages)
- [ ] Configuration guide (provider section of `docs/features/dead-letter-queue.md`)
- [ ] Architecture Decision Record: ADR-046 (number reserved)

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `IDeadLetterStore` is implemented and persists on all 10 providers; `UseDeadLetterQueue = true` registers store, factory, orchestrator, manager, health check and cleanup on each (DI test with `ValidateOnBuild` and `ValidateScopes`, also for `AddEncinaADOWithTenancy`)
- [ ] The reshaped record and store contract are applied to the fake and all 10 stores; the contract test passes on the fake and on the 10 real databases
- [ ] Capture is idempotent per `(SourcePattern, SourceMessageId)`; the tenant is stamped and filterable
- [ ] No store `Left` is swallowed; statistics and bulk deletes never load the whole queue
- [ ] `ReplayResult` holds an outcome code only (max 256); a replay is claimed atomically before dispatch (#2012)
- [ ] Unit, guard, contract, property and integration tests per the Test Matrix; load and benchmark justification files written
- [ ] Every coverage flag of every touched `src/` file reaches its target in the package manifests; `coverage-report.cs --check-justifications` and the CRAP gate (<= 10) pass
- [ ] OpenTelemetry instrumentation in place with no payload, `EncinaError.Message` or tenant id in telemetry
- [ ] Documentation complete (ADR-046, feature page, READMEs, changelog fragments `added`, `changed`, `fixed`)
- [ ] Zero build warnings; `PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt` clean (RS0016/RS0017) in all touched packages

items.title: Enhancement: Modernize /design-database-schema with 2025 best practices (RLS, specialized indexes, GDPR, zero-downtime migrations)
items.body:
# Enhancement: Modernize `/design-database-schema` with 2025 Database Best Practices

## Executive Summary

The `/design-database-schema` cascade command provides a **solid journey-driven foundation** for schema design, but lacks **critical 2025 database patterns** identified through validation against state-of-the-art practices. This issue documents gaps and provides implementation recommendations to bring the command to world-class standards.

**Overall Assessment: B+ → Target: A+**

### Key Strengths ✅
- Journey-first schema design philosophy prevents generic database modeling
- Multi-paradigm support (relational, document, graph, time-series, key-value)
- Excellent i18n and integration constraint propagation patterns
- Comprehensive migration file generation across ORMs

### Critical Gaps ❌
- Missing PostgreSQL 17 specialized index types (GIN, BRIN, GiST)
- No Row-Level Security (RLS) patterns for multi-tenancy (2025 SaaS standard)
- Missing GDPR "Right to Erasure" workflow (3-layer deletion: upstream → medallion → physical purge)
- No zero-downtime migration patterns (blue-green, CDC, expand-contract)
- Missing audit logging with JSONB deltas pattern
- No tail latency (p99) performance optimization guidance

---

## Validation Methodology

Conducted side-by-side comparison of:
1. **Current implementation**: `.claude/commands/design-database-schema.md`
2. **Best practices reference**: `reference-material/database-design-guide.md`
3. **Template**: `templates/07-database-schema-template.md`

Evaluated across 7 dimensions:
- A. Paradigm Selection Decision Tree
- B. Schema Design Patterns
- C. Performance Optimization
- D. Data Integrity & Constraints
- E. Multi-Tenancy Patterns
- F. Compliance & Security Patterns
- G. Migration Strategies

---

## Critical Priority Enhancements (Implement Immediately)

### 1. Add Specialized Index Types for PostgreSQL 17

**Current State**: Generic "index foreign keys and WHERE columns" guidance  
**Gap**: Missing index type specialization costs 10-100x query performance  
**Impact**: Slow JSONB queries, massive index bloat on time-series tables

**Recommendation**: Replace Step 5 "Design Indexes" (line 543) with specialized index type decision tree:

```markdown
### Step 5: Design Indexes with Specialized Types

**Index Type Decision Tree** (PostgreSQL 17):

1. **Is this a foreign key or equality/range query?**
   → Use **B-tree** (default): `CREATE INDEX idx_assessments_user_id ON assessments(user_id);`

2. **Is this a JSONB containment or full-text search query?**
   → Use **GIN** (Generalized Inverted Index):
   ```sql
   CREATE INDEX idx_assessments_results_gin ON assessments USING GIN (results);
   ```
   **Query pattern**: `SELECT * FROM assessments WHERE results @> '{"status": "passed"}';`
   **Performance**: 10-100x faster than B-tree on JSONB columns

3. **Is this a massive time-ordered table (>10M rows)?**
   → Use **BRIN** (Block Range Index):
   ```sql
   CREATE INDEX idx_usage_events_created_brin ON usage_events USING BRIN (created_at);
   ```
   **Performance**: 99% smaller than B-tree, ideal for `usage_events`, `audit_log`, `webhook_events`

4. **Is this geometric/spatial data?**
   → Use **GiST**: `CREATE INDEX idx_locations_geom ON locations USING GiST (geom);`

**Validation Checklist**:
- [ ] All JSONB columns have GIN indexes if queried with `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&` operators
- [ ] Time-ordered tables >1M rows use BRIN indexes on timestamp columns
- [ ] All foreign keys have B-tree indexes
- [ ] Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on critical queries to verify index usage (no Seq Scan on large tables)
```

**Files to Update**:
- `.claude/commands/design-database-schema.md` (line 543-619)
- `templates/07-database-schema-template.md` (Indexes Strategy section)

---

### 2. Add Row-Level Security (RLS) for Multi-Tenant Isolation

**Current State**: Mentions RLS concept, no implementation pattern  
**Gap**: Missing 2025 SaaS security standard for tenant isolation  
**Impact**: Catastrophic data leakage risk if application filters fail

**Recommendation**: Add new Step 2c after i18n section (line 229):

```markdown
### Step 2c: Implement Row-Level Security (RLS) for Multi-Tenancy

**IF** architecture uses multi-tenant pattern (shared schema), implement RLS:

**Why RLS is the 2025 standard**:
- ✅ Defense-in-depth: Prevents data leakage from coding errors
- ✅ Database-level enforcement: Cannot be bypassed by application bugs
- ✅ Compliance-ready: Required for SOC2, ISO 27001 certification

**Step 1: Enable RLS on tenant-scoped tables**
```sql
ALTER TABLE documents ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE assessments ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE usage_events ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
```

**Step 2: Create tenant isolation policy using session variable**
```sql
-- Policy: Users can only see their team's data
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation_policy ON documents
  FOR ALL
  USING (team_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::UUID);

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation_policy ON assessments
  FOR ALL
  USING (team_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::UUID);
```

**Step 3: Force policy for all roles (prevents superuser bypass)**
```sql
ALTER TABLE documents FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE assessments FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
```

**Application Integration** (Node.js example):
```typescript
// Set tenant context at request start (middleware)
await db.query('SET app.tenant_id = $1', [user.teamId]);

// All subsequent queries automatically filtered by RLS
const docs = await db.query('SELECT * FROM documents'); 
// ↑ Only returns current tenant's docs, even with SELECT *
```

**Security Validation**:
```sql
-- Test tenant isolation
SET app.tenant_id = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001';
SELECT * FROM documents; -- Should only see Team 1 docs

SET app.tenant_id = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002';
SELECT * FROM documents; -- Should only see Team 2 docs
```

**When to use RLS**:
- ✅ Multi-tenant SaaS with shared schema (team_id on every table)
- ✅ Compliance requirements (HIPAA, SOC2, GDPR)
- ✅ High-risk data (financial, healthcare, PII)

**When NOT to use RLS**:
- ❌ Separate database per tenant (physical isolation)
- ❌ Single-tenant applications
- ❌ Performance-critical systems (adds ~5-10% query overhead)
```

**Files to Update**:
- `.claude/commands/design-database-schema.md` (new section after line 229)
- `templates/07-database-schema-template.md` (add Multi-Tenancy section)

**References**:
- [PostgreSQL RLS Documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html)
- Reference guide: "Underrated Postgres: Build Multi-Tenancy with Row-Level Security"

---

### 3. Add GDPR Right to Erasure Workflow

**Current State**: No data deletion compliance patterns  
**Gap**: Missing legally-required GDPR Article 17 implementation  
**Impact**: Legal risk (up to 4% global revenue fines), incomplete user data deletion

**Recommendation**: Add new section after Integration Schema (line 515):

```markdown
## GDPR Compliance Patterns

**IF** Session 2a marks GDPR compliance as required OR product serves EU users:

### Right to Erasure Workflow (GDPR Article 17)

**The Problem**: Standard `DELETE` leaves data in backups, replicas, event logs, and cloud storage time-travel snapshots.

**Multi-Layer Deletion Pattern** (required for complete data removal):

```sql
-- PHASE 1: Soft Delete (30-day safety period)
UPDATE users 
SET deleted_at = NOW(), 
    deletion_requested_by = 'user_request'
WHERE id = $user_id;

-- Notify external integrations immediately
-- POST to Stripe API: DELETE /customers/{id}
-- POST to SendGrid API: DELETE /contacts/{id}

-- PHASE 2: Upstream Deletion (event streams)
-- Remove from Kafka topics, Redis cache, message queues
DELETE FROM kafka_offset_tracking WHERE user_id = $user_id;
REDIS DEL user:session:{user_id};

-- PHASE 3: Hard Delete After Verification (30 days later)
BEGIN;
  -- Delete user-owned data (CASCADE handles relationships)
  DELETE FROM users 
  WHERE id = $user_id 
    AND deleted_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days';
  
  -- Anonymize audit logs (retain compliance records but remove PII)
  UPDATE audit_log
  SET old_data = jsonb_set(old_data, '{email}', '"[REDACTED]"'::jsonb),
      new_data = jsonb_set(new_data, '{email}', '"[REDACTED]"'::jsonb)
  WHERE user_id = $user_id;
  
  -- Anonymize analytics events (preserve metrics, remove identity)
  UPDATE analytics_events
  SET user_id = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000',
      properties = properties - 'email' - 'name' - 'phone'
  WHERE user_id = $user_id;
COMMIT;

-- PHASE 4: Physical Purge (reclaim disk space)
VACUUM FULL users; -- PostgreSQL: Physically removes deleted rows
```

**For Cloud Data Warehouses** (Snowflake, Databricks):
```sql
-- Override 30-day time travel retention (critical for GDPR)
DELETE FROM bronze.user_events WHERE user_id = $user_id;
VACUUM TABLE bronze.user_events; -- Snowflake
-- or
PURGE TABLE bronze.user_events; -- Databricks

-- Verify time-travel snapshots deleted
SELECT * FROM bronze.user_events AT (TIMESTAMP => DATEADD(day, -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()))
WHERE user_id = $user_id; -- Should return 0 rows
```

**GDPR Deletion Validation Checklist**:
- [ ] User data deleted from all application tables (via CASCADE)
- [ ] Audit logs anonymized (PII replaced with `[REDACTED]`)
- [ ] External integrations notified (webhooks sent to Stripe, SendGrid, etc.)
- [ ] Event streams purged (Kafka topics, Redis cache)
- [ ] Data warehouse time-travel snapshots purged
- [ ] Backups older than retention period excluded from restores
- [ ] Deletion logged in compliance audit trail with timestamp

**Retention Exceptions** (do NOT delete):
- Financial records required by law (invoices, tax records) - 7 years
- Fraud prevention data (hashed identifiers only)
- Aggregated analytics with no PII (metric totals)

### PII Data Masking for Dev/Test Environments

**Pattern**: Hash/scramble PII in non-production environments to prevent leaks:

```sql
-- Anonymize production snapshot for dev/staging (run after DB restore)
UPDATE users SET
  email = md5(email::text) || '@example.com',
  first_name = 'User',
  last_name = substring(md5(id::text), 1, 8),
  phone = NULL,
  address = NULL
WHERE TRUE; -- Apply to all rows

-- Verify no real PII remains
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email NOT LIKE '%@example.com'; -- Should be empty
```

**Automation**: Add to CI/CD pipeline for staging database refreshes.
```

**Files to Update**:
- `.claude/commands/design-database-schema.md` (new section after line 515)
- `templates/07-database-schema-template.md` (add Compliance Patterns section)

**References**:
- [GDPR Article 17 - Right to Erasure](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/)
- Reference guide: "Best Practices For Protecting PII Data"

---

### 4. Add Zero-Downtime Migration Patterns

**Current State**: Basic migration files (Prisma, Alembic), no deployment patterns  
**Gap**: Missing production-grade migration strategies  
**Impact**: Cannot deploy schema changes without user-facing downtime

**Recommendation**: Add new section before Migration Files (line 609):

```markdown
## Zero-Downtime Migration Strategies

**For production deployments with <1 minute downtime tolerance:**

### Pattern 1: Expand-Contract (Backward-Compatible Changes)

**Use case**: Renaming column `name` → `full_name` in `users` table with 10M rows

**Traditional approach** (5+ minutes downtime):
```sql
-- ❌ BAD: ALTER TABLE locks table, blocks all writes
ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;
```

**Zero-downtime approach** (3-phase deployment):

**Phase 1 - Expand** (Deploy v1 application + migration):
```sql
-- Add new column (doesn't lock table)
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name TEXT;

-- Backfill in batches (avoids lock escalation)
UPDATE users SET full_name = name WHERE full_name IS NULL LIMIT 1000;
-- Repeat until backfill complete

-- Add index without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_full_name ON users(full_name);
```

**Application code v1** (writes to BOTH columns):
```typescript
await db.query(
  'UPDATE users SET name = $1, full_name = $1 WHERE id = $2',
  [newName, userId]
);
```

**Phase 2 - Migrate** (Wait 1 week, monitor for issues):
- All reads now use `full_name`
- Writes still go to both columns
- Monitor for any remaining `name` column usage

**Phase 3 - Contract** (Deploy v2 application + migration):
```sql
-- Safe to drop old column (no readers/writers remain)
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN name;
```

**Downtime**: 0 seconds (old and new schemas coexist during migration)

---

### Pattern 2: Online Index Creation (PostgreSQL)

**Use case**: Adding index to 100M row `assessments` table

```sql
-- ❌ WRONG: Locks table for writes (5+ minutes downtime)
CREATE INDEX idx_assessments_created ON assessments(created_at);

-- ✅ CORRECT: Builds index without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_assessments_created ON assessments(created_at);
```

**Tradeoffs**:
- CONCURRENTLY takes 2-3x longer to build (acceptable for zero downtime)
- If build fails mid-way, leaves INVALID index (must DROP and retry)

**Validation**:
```sql
-- Check for invalid indexes
SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS index_name, indisvalid
FROM pg_index
WHERE NOT indisvalid;

-- Drop invalid indexes and retry
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_assessments_created; -- if invalid
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_assessments_created ON assessments(created_at);
```

---

### Pattern 3: Blue-Green Database Migration

**Use case**: Migrating PostgreSQL RDS → Aurora (different database engine)

**Architecture**:
1. **Blue** (current production): PostgreSQL RDS
2. **Green** (new): Aurora cluster
3. **Replication**: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) - continuous sync Blue → Green

**Migration Steps**:

```bash
# Day 1: Start replication
aws dms create-replication-task \
  --source=postgresql-rds \
  --target=aurora-cluster \
  --mode=full-load-and-cdc # Full copy + ongoing changes

# Days 2-7: Monitor replication lag
aws dms describe-replication-tasks | jq '.ReplicationLag'
# Target: <1 second lag

# Day 8: Cutover (maintenance window)
# 1. Stop application writes (maintenance mode) - 10 seconds
# 2. Wait for replication lag = 0
# 3. Update application DATABASE_URL → Aurora
# 4. Resume application writes

# Day 9-14: Monitor Green performance
# Keep Blue running as hot standby

# Day 15: Decommission Blue (if no issues)
```

**Rollback Plan**:
- If issues detected on Green: Update DATABASE_URL → Blue (10 second switch)
- Keep Blue for 2 weeks minimum before deletion

**Downtime**: ~10-30 seconds (application restart with new connection string)

---

### Pattern 4: Change Data Capture (CDC) for Large Migrations

**Use case**: 500GB database migration with <5 minute cutover

**Tools**:
- **Debezium** (Kafka-based CDC)
- **AWS DMS** (managed service)
- **pg_logical** (PostgreSQL native)

**Pattern**:
```bash
# 1. Initial snapshot (runs in background, days/weeks)
debezium capture --mode=snapshot --source=prod-db --target=new-db

# 2. Continuous replication (captures ongoing changes)
debezium capture --mode=cdc --source=prod-db --target=new-db

# 3. Monitor lag until <1 second
debezium lag-monitor

# 4. Cutover (short maintenance window)
# - Stop writes to source
# - Wait for lag = 0
# - Switch application to target
# - Resume writes
```

**Validation**: Run queries on both databases, compare results:
```sql
-- Source DB
SELECT COUNT(*), MAX(created_at) FROM users;

-- Target DB (should match exactly)
SELECT COUNT(*), MAX(created_at) FROM users;
```

---

### Pattern 5: Shadow Testing for Risky Migrations

**Use case**: Major schema refactor (e.g., splitting monolithic table)

**Pattern**:
1. Deploy new schema alongside old schema
2. Write to BOTH schemas (old + new) for 1 week
3. Compare results: `SELECT * FROM old_table EXCEPT SELECT * FROM new_table_view`
4. Switch reads to new schema if validation passes
5. Drop old schema after 2 weeks

**Example** (splitting `users` table):
```sql
-- Old schema
CREATE TABLE users (id, email, name, address, phone, ...); -- 50 columns

-- New schema (normalized)
CREATE TABLE users (id, email, name);
CREATE TABLE user_profiles (user_id, address, phone, ...);

-- Write to both (application layer)
BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO users (id, email, name) VALUES (...);
  INSERT INTO user_profiles (user_id, address, phone) VALUES (...);
COMMIT;

-- Validation query
SELECT old.id FROM users_old old
LEFT JOIN users new ON old.id = new.id
LEFT JOIN user_profiles prof ON old.id = prof.user_id
WHERE new.id IS NULL OR prof.user_id IS NULL;
-- Should return 0 rows
```

---

### Migration Validation Checklist

Before deploying ANY schema change to production:

- [ ] **Tested on staging** with production-size dataset (not empty database)
- [ ] **Rollback plan documented** with exact commands to revert
- [ ] **Monitoring alerts configured** (replication lag, error rate, query latency)
- [ ] **Lock timeout set** to prevent indefinite blocking:
  ```sql
  SET lock_timeout = '5s'; -- Fail fast if lock unavailable
  ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN ...;
  ```
- [ ] **Index creation uses CONCURRENTLY** (PostgreSQL)
- [ ] **Large updates batched** (1000-10000 rows per transaction)
- [ ] **Customer communication sent** (if any user-facing impact)
```

**Files to Update**:
- `.claude/commands/design-database-schema.md` (new section before line 609)
- `templates/07-database-schema-template.md` (add Migration Strategies section)

**References**:
- [PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html#SQL-CREATEINDEX-CONCURRENTLY)
- Reference guide: "3 strategies for zero downtime database migration"

---

## High Priority Enhancements (Implement Soon)

### 5. Add Audit Logging with JSONB Deltas

**Current State**: Mentions audit columns (created_at, updated_at)  
**Gap**: Missing complete audit trail for compliance  
**Impact**: Cannot answer "who changed what when" for regulatory audits

**Recommendation**: Add after Step 6 "Add Data Constraints" (line 686):

```markdown
### Step 6a: Implement Audit Logging (if compliance required)

**Check Session 2a**: If regulatory compliance (HIPAA, SOC2, GDPR) marked as required:

**Pattern**: Immutable audit trail with row-level change tracking

```sql
CREATE TABLE audit_log (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  table_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  action_type TEXT NOT NULL, -- 'INSERT', 'UPDATE', 'DELETE'
  record_id UUID NOT NULL,    -- ID of affected row
  
  -- Full row snapshots
  old_data JSONB,             -- Row state before change
  new_data JSONB,             -- Row state after change
  
  -- Delta (what actually changed)
  changed_fields JSONB,       -- {"email": {"old": "a@x.com", "new": "b@x.com"}}
  
  -- Context
  user_id UUID,               -- Who made the change
  user_ip INET,               -- IP address (for fraud detection)
  user_agent TEXT,            -- Browser/API client
  
  -- Timing
  action_timestamp TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_audit_log_table_action ON audit_log(table_name, action_timestamp DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_audit_log_record ON audit_log(table_name, record_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_audit_log_user ON audit_log(user_id);

-- Trigger function to capture changes automatically
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION log_audit_changes() RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
DECLARE
  old_json JSONB;
  new_json JSONB;
  delta JSONB;
BEGIN
  -- Convert rows to JSONB
  old_json := CASE WHEN TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN row_to_json(OLD)::jsonb ELSE NULL END;
  new_json := CASE WHEN TG_OP IN ('INSERT', 'UPDATE') THEN row_to_json(NEW)::jsonb ELSE NULL END;
  
  -- Calculate delta (only for UPDATEs)
  IF TG_OP = 'UPDATE' THEN
    SELECT jsonb_object_agg(key, jsonb_build_object('old', old_val, 'new', new_val))
    INTO delta
    FROM jsonb_each(old_json) o(key, old_val)
    JOIN jsonb_each(new_json) n(key, new_val) USING (key)
    WHERE old_val IS DISTINCT FROM new_val;
  END IF;
  
  -- Insert audit record
  INSERT INTO audit_log (
    table_name, 
    action_type, 
    record_id,
    old_data, 
    new_data, 
    changed_fields,
    user_id
  ) VALUES (
    TG_TABLE_NAME,
    TG_OP,
    COALESCE(NEW.id, OLD.id),
    old_json,
    new_json,
    delta,
    current_setting('app.user_id', true)::UUID -- Set by application
  );
  
  RETURN COALESCE(NEW, OLD);
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Apply to sensitive tables
CREATE TRIGGER users_audit 
  AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON users
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION log_audit_changes();

CREATE TRIGGER assessments_audit 
  AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON assessments
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION log_audit_changes();
```

**Why Triggers Over Application Code**:
- ✅ **100% coverage**: Captures direct SQL, CLI, migrations, manual updates
- ✅ **Tamper-proof**: Application cannot bypass (compliance requirement)
- ✅ **Automatic**: No developer action required for new tables

**Query Examples**:

```sql
-- Who deleted this user?
SELECT user_id, action_timestamp, old_data->>'email'
FROM audit_log
WHERE table_name = 'users' 
  AND record_id = '...'
  AND action_type = 'DELETE';

-- What changed in last 24 hours?
SELECT table_name, action_type, changed_fields
FROM audit_log
WHERE action_timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours'
ORDER BY action_timestamp DESC;

-- Track specific user's changes
SELECT table_name, action_type, changed_fields, action_timestamp
FROM audit_log
WHERE user_id = '...'
ORDER BY action_timestamp DESC;
```

**Retention**: Archive audit_log older than 7 years to cold storage (compliance requirement).
```

**Files to Update**:
- `.claude/commands/design-database-schema.md` (new section after line 686)

---

### 6. Add Temporal Tables Pattern

**Current State**: No point-in-time data reconstruction patterns  
**Gap**: Cannot answer "what did this record look like on 2025-01-15?"  
**Impact**: Missing compliance audit capability for regulated industries

**Recommendation**: Add to "Data Integrity & Constraints" section:

```markdown
### Temporal Tables for Point-in-Time Forensics

**When to use**: Financial services, healthcare, legal (Session 2a compliance requirements)

**Pattern** (PostgreSQL with temporal_tables extension):

```sql
-- Install extension
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS temporal_tables;

-- Main table with system versioning columns
CREATE TABLE users (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  
  -- System versioning (managed automatically)
  valid_from TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
  valid_to TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT 'infinity'
);

-- History table (exact copy of structure)
CREATE TABLE users_history (LIKE users);

-- Trigger to automatically version changes
CREATE TRIGGER users_versioning
  BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ON users
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION versioning(
    'valid_from', 'valid_to', 'users_history', true
  );
```

**How it works**:
- Every UPDATE/DELETE copies old row to `users_history` with `valid_to = NOW()`
- New row gets `valid_from = NOW()`, `valid_to = 'infinity'`
- Full history of every change preserved

**Point-in-time queries**:

```sql
-- What was this user's email on 2025-01-15?
SELECT email FROM users_history
WHERE id = '...'
  AND valid_from <= '2025-01-15'
  AND valid_to > '2025-01-15';

-- Reconstruct entire table as of specific date
SELECT * FROM users_history
WHERE valid_from <= '2025-01-15'
  AND valid_to > '2025-01-15'
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM users
WHERE valid_from <= '2025-01-15';
```

**Compliance use case**: Regulator asks "prove this user consented to terms on 2024-06-01"
```sql
SELECT consented_to_terms, valid_from
FROM users_history
WHERE id = '...'
  AND valid_from <= '2024-06-01'
  AND valid_to > '2024-06-01';
-- Returns: consented_to_terms = true, valid_from = 2024-05-28
```

**Storage cost**: ~2-3x main table size (acceptable for compliance)
```

**Files to Update**:
- `.claude/commands/design-database-schema.md` (Data Integrity section)

---

### 7. Add Hybrid/Polyglot Architecture Decision Tree

**Current State**: Assumes single database paradigm  
**Gap**: 2025 reality is PostgreSQL + Redis + TimescaleDB for most systems  
**Impact**: Users choose wrong "one database for everything" approach

**Recommendation**: Add to Paradigm Selection section:

```markdown
### Hybrid Architecture Decision Tree (Polyglot Persistence)

**Modern Pattern**: Combine specialized databases for optimal performance

**When to use multiple databases**:

```
IF >80% of queries hit cache layer (sessions, rate limits)
  → Add Redis (in-memory, sub-millisecond latency)

IF >1M timestamped events per day (metrics, logs, IoT)
  → Add TimescaleDB/InfluxDB (10-20x better compression)

IF complex graph traversals (social network, fraud detection)
  → Add Neo4j (O(1) relationship queries vs O(n²) in SQL)

IF full-text search required (product search, documentation)
  → Add Elasticsearch (inverted indexes, fuzzy matching)
```

**Example Architecture** (SaaS application):

```
┌──────────────┐
│ PostgreSQL   │ ← Primary data store (users, billing, transactions)
└──────┬───────┘   - ACID guarantees
       │           - Complex relationships
       │           - Source of truth
       ↓
┌──────────────┐
│ Redis        │ ← Cache layer (sessions, rate limits, leaderboards)
└──────┬───────┘   - TTL-based eviction
       │           - Pub/sub for real-time
       │           - 10-100x faster than PostgreSQL
       ↓
┌──────────────┐
│ TimescaleDB  │ ← Observability (metrics, logs, traces)
└──────────────┘   - Time-bucketed storage
                    - Continuous aggregates
                    - 90-day retention → archive
```

**Data Flow**:
1. Write to PostgreSQL (source of truth)
2. Cache in Redis (read-through pattern)
3. Stream metrics to TimescaleDB (async)

**Trade-offs**:
- ✅ Optimal performance per use case
- ❌ Operational complexity (3 databases to maintain)
- ❌ Data consistency challenges (eventual consistency across stores)

**When NOT to use polyglot**:
- Team <3 engineers (operational burden too high)
- MVP stage (premature optimization)
- Simple CRUD app (PostgreSQL sufficient)
```

**Files to Update**:
- `.claude/commands/design-database-schema.md` (Paradigm Selection section)

---

## Medium Priority Enhancements

### 8. Add Tail Latency (p99) Monitoring Guidance

**Current State**: No performance SLO validation patterns  
**Recommendation**: Add to Performance Optimization section

```markdown
### Tail Latency Optimization (p99)

**The Problem**: Average latency hides slow queries affecting real users

**Metrics to track**:
- **p50** (median): 50% of queries faster than this
- **p95**: 95% of queries faster than this
- **p99**: 99% of queries faster than this ← **Most important for UX**

**Formula**: `Throughput (X) = Concurrency (NC) / Latency (R)`

**Example**:
- p50 latency: 20ms
- p99 latency: 500ms ← 1% of users wait 25x longer!

**Optimization**:
```sql
-- Find slow queries (p99)
SELECT query, mean_exec_time, max_exec_time
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY max_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

**SLO Target**: p99 latency <200ms for critical path queries (journey steps 1-3)
```

---

### 9. Add N+1 Query Prevention Validation

**Current State**: No ORM anti-pattern warnings  
**Recommendation**: Add to Query Examples section

```markdown
### N+1 Query Prevention

**The Problem**: ORM fetches related records in loop (1 + N queries instead of 1 query with JOIN)

**Example** (BAD - N+1):
```typescript
// 1 query to get users
const users = await db.query('SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100');

// 100 queries to get each user's documents (N+1!)
for (const user of users) {
  user.documents = await db.query('SELECT * FROM documents WHERE user_id = $1', [user.id]);
}
```

**Fixed** (GOOD - 1 query with JOIN):
```typescript
const usersWithDocs = await db.query(`
  SELECT 
    u.*,
    json_agg(d.*) AS documents
  FROM users u
  LEFT JOIN documents d ON u.id = d.user_id
  GROUP BY u.id
  LIMIT 100
`);
```

**Validation**:
- [ ] All list endpoints use JOINs, not loops
- [ ] ORM configured with eager loading for relationships
- [ ] Query count logged in development (warn if >5 queries per request)
```

---

### 10. Add Schema Anti-Patterns Section

**Recommendation**: Add to template and command:

```markdown
## Schema Anti-Patterns to Avoid

### ❌ Anti-Pattern 1: Missing Foreign Key Indexes
**Problem**: PostgreSQL does NOT automatically index foreign keys (unlike MySQL).

```sql
-- ❌ BAD: Foreign key without index = slow JOINs
ALTER TABLE documents ADD COLUMN user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id);

-- ✅ GOOD: Always index foreign keys
CREATE INDEX idx_documents_user_id ON documents(user_id);
```

**Impact**: 100-1000x slower JOINs on tables >10K rows.

---

### ❌ Anti-Pattern 2: UUID Primary Keys Without Default
**Problem**: Application must generate UUIDs (error-prone, inconsistent).

```sql
-- ❌ BAD: No default = application burden
id UUID PRIMARY KEY

-- ✅ GOOD: Database generates UUIDs
id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()
```

---

### ❌ Anti-Pattern 3: TIMESTAMP Instead of TIMESTAMPTZ
**Problem**: Timezone bugs when users span multiple regions.

```sql
-- ❌ BAD: Stores local time (ambiguous)
created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()

-- ✅ GOOD: Stores UTC with timezone
created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
```

**Real bug**: User in NYC creates record at "2025-03-09 02:30 AM" during DST transition → time doesn't exist!

---

### ❌ Anti-Pattern 4: Indexing Low-Cardinality Columns
**Problem**: Indexes on boolean/enum rarely used by query planner.

```sql
-- ❌ BAD: Only 2 values (true/false), index rarely helps
CREATE INDEX idx_users_is_active ON users(is_active);

-- ✅ GOOD: Use partial index for specific value
CREATE INDEX idx_users_active ON users(id) WHERE is_active = true;
```

---

### ❌ Anti-Pattern 5: No Unique Constraint on Natural Keys
**Problem**: Duplicate emails/usernames cause auth bugs.

```sql
-- ❌ BAD: Email can be duplicated
email TEXT NOT NULL

-- ✅ GOOD: Enforce uniqueness at database level
email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
```

**Defense-in-depth**: Application validation + database constraint.
```

---

## Implementation Plan

### Phase 1: Critical Security & Compliance (Week 1)
- [ ] Add Row-Level Security (RLS) pattern (#2)
- [ ] Add GDPR Right to Erasure workflow (#3)
- [ ] Add specialized index types (GIN, BRIN) (#1)

### Phase 2: Production Readiness (Week 2)
- [ ] Add zero-downtime migration patterns (#4)
- [ ] Add audit logging with JSONB deltas (#5)
- [ ] Add schema anti-patterns section (#10)

### Phase 3: Advanced Patterns (Week 3)
- [ ] Add temporal tables pattern (#6)
- [ ] Add hybrid/polyglot architecture guide (#7)
- [ ] Add tail latency monitoring (#8)
- [ ] Add N+1 query prevention (#9)

---

## Success Metrics

**Before**:
- Generic index guidance ("index WHERE columns")
- No multi-tenant security patterns
- Missing GDPR compliance workflows
- No production migration strategies

**After**:
- ✅ Specialized index types with 10-100x performance gains
- ✅ Row-Level Security preventing data leakage
- ✅ GDPR-compliant deletion workflows
- ✅ Zero-downtime migration patterns (expand-contract, blue-green, CDC)
- ✅ Complete audit trail for compliance
- ✅ Schema anti-patterns prevention

**Validation**:
- [ ] Test schemas generated with new patterns on staging databases
- [ ] Verify RLS prevents cross-tenant queries
- [ ] Benchmark GIN indexes vs B-tree on JSONB columns (target: 10x faster)
- [ ] Execute expand-contract migration on test table (verify 0 downtime)

---

## References

**Internal**:
- Current: `.claude/commands/design-database-schema.md`
- Template: `templates/07-database-schema-template.md`
- Best practices: `reference-material/database-design-guide.md`

**External**:
- [PostgreSQL RLS Documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html)
- [GDPR Article 17 - Right to Erasure](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/)
- [PostgreSQL Index Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-types.html)
- [Zero Downtime Migrations - New Relic](https://newrelic.com/blog/infrastructure-monitoring/migrating-data-to-cloud-avoid-downtime-strategies)

---

## Labels

`enhancement` `database` `schema-design` `security` `compliance` `performance` `documentation`

---

**Validation Date**: 2026-02-01  
**Reviewer**: Claude Code (Sonnet 4.5)  
**Methodology**: Side-by-side comparison against 2025 database best practices reference guide

items.title: Feature: @happyvertical/smrt-web — browser client data runtime (cached collections, offline writes, live updates, version awareness) + core sync surfaces
items.body:
## Problem Statement

SMRT application response time is dominated by network round trips, multiplied across two hops:

1. **Server → database.** Every `SmrtCollection` read is a network round trip to the database (~130ms/query measured in-cluster against CNPG, #1498). The opt-in server-side read-through collection cache (#1499) addressed this hop for SSR-rendered reads.
2. **Client → server.** Nothing addresses this hop. The generated client is a bare `fetch` wrapper with no caching, no request dedup, and no state. The reference templates fetch on component mount without SvelteKit server loads, so pages render empty, then fetch, on **every** navigation — and a page composing many collections (24 on the #1498 homepage) pays the full fan-out every time.

Beyond raw latency, three product needs have no answer today:

- **Offline capture is a planned requirement** (ergot ingestor): field work must survive connectivity gaps and page reloads, then sync automatically. There is no client-side write queue, and the generated REST layer deliberately strips client-supplied ids (mass-assignment guard, #1540), which blocks idempotent offline creates.
- **Public smrt-sites must be as fast as possible**, but generated routes emit no ETag/Last-Modified/Cache-Control, so neither browsers nor CDNs can cache anything — every anonymous page view hits the origin and the database.
- **Deployed clients cannot detect that they are stale.** After a deploy, running browser tabs keep executing the old bundle against a possibly changed API contract, and nothing tells them. Once client data is persisted locally, this graduates from annoyance to correctness bug: a cache written under an old manifest shape must never hydrate into new code.

The KMP mobile foundation (ADR 0001, epic #1745) is independently building the same machinery for mobile — offline write queue, delta sync, manifest-projected contract. Without a shared server contract, web and mobile will diverge into two bespoke sync protocols against the same framework.

## Solution

A new package, **`@happyvertical/smrt-web`** — the browser-side client data runtime, deliberate twin of `smrt-mobile` — plus the server-side sync surfaces it consumes, generated in core alongside the existing REST/CLI/MCP generators.

For a SMRT developer it looks like this: the build emits **typed client collections** for your `@smrt()` classes (wrapping TanStack DB). Components read them through live queries; reads are served instantly from a local stale-while-revalidate cache and revalidated in the background. Mutations apply optimistically, write through on success, and — for models that opt in — queue durably in an offline outbox that replays idempotently when connectivity returns, with `pending/uploading/synced/failed` state you can render. A server-sent-events channel pushes coarse invalidation signals so caches stay honest without polling, backed by an adapter-agnostic change feed written by the interceptors that already observe every framework mutation. The runtime is version-aware: persisted caches are keyed by the manifest hash, and a reactive `updateAvailable` signal fires when either the bundle or the API contract changes. Generated GET routes gain ETag/304 semantics, and `api: { public: true }` models emit CDN-cacheable headers — the smrt-sites speed answer.

Requests the client never makes are database queries that never happen: the client half completes what #1499 started on the server half.

## User Stories

1. As a SMRT app developer, I want generated, typed client collections for my `@smrt()` classes, so that I never hand-write fetch calls and state management per entity.
2. As a SMRT app developer, I want reads served from a local cache with stale-while-revalidate semantics, so that navigations render instantly instead of waiting on network round trips.
3. As a SMRT app developer, I want concurrent identical reads deduplicated into one request, so that composing many components over the same collection doesn't multiply load.
4. As a SMRT app developer, I want cache invalidation edges derived from the manifest's relationships, so that saving one entity refreshes dependent lists and joins without hand-wired cache keys.
5. As a SMRT app developer, I want optimistic mutations with automatic rollback on failure, so that the UI feels instant while the server stays authoritative.
6. As a SMRT app developer, I want mutation responses written through into the cache, so that a user always reads their own writes immediately.
7. As a SMRT app developer, I want live queries over cached collections (filters, joins, projections), so that components update reactively when any underlying row changes.
8. As a SMRT app developer, I want SvelteKit server-load data to seed the client cache on hydration, so that the first client render never double-fetches what SSR already fetched.
9. As a SMRT app developer, I want a durable offline write queue for opted-in models, so that user work survives page reloads and connectivity loss.
10. As a SMRT app developer, I want per-mutation sync state (`pending/uploading/synced/failed`), so that I can render outbox indicators and retry affordances.
11. As a SMRT app developer, I want the client to detect when its API contract (manifest) is stale, so that persisted caches never hydrate old-schema rows into new code.
12. As a SMRT app developer, I want a reactive `updateAvailable` signal covering both bundle and contract versions, so that I can prompt users to reload after a deploy.
13. As a SMRT app developer, I want ETag/If-None-Match handling on generated GET routes, so that unavoidable refetches cost a 304 instead of a body and a query.
14. As a SMRT app developer building public sites, I want `api: { public: true }` models to emit CDN-cacheable headers, so that anonymous traffic is served from the edge instead of my origin.
15. As a SMRT app developer, I want server-pushed invalidation over SSE, so that dashboards reflect other users' writes without manual refresh or aggressive polling.
16. As a SMRT app developer, I want the same generated collections to work across npm, federation, and standalone consumption modes, so that the data layer doesn't fork per deployment shape.
17. As a SMRT app developer using SQLite in development, I want the entire sync stack to work without Postgres, so that my dev loop is unchanged from today.
18. As a Svelte developer, I want first-class Svelte 5 bindings for live queries and sync state, so that the runtime feels native to runes-based components.
19. As a SaaS end user, I want previously visited pages to render instantly from cache, so that navigating the app feels native rather than web-slow.
20. As a SaaS end user, I want my own edits reflected immediately everywhere in the app, so that I never see a stale version of something I just changed.
21. As a field worker using the ingestor, I want to capture records while offline, so that connectivity gaps never block or lose my work.
22. As a field worker, I want queued captures to sync automatically with retries when connectivity returns, so that I never manually resubmit anything.
23. As a field worker, I want to see which captures are pending versus synced, so that I can trust the system with work I can't redo.
24. As a field worker with multiple tabs open, I want exactly one tab to replay the queue, so that flaky connectivity never produces duplicate submissions.
25. As a returning user, I want the app to warm-start from persisted local data, so that content appears before the network responds even on a cold load.
26. As an end user on a shared device, I want logout to wipe locally persisted data, so that the next user cannot read my rows out of browser storage.
27. As an end user, I want a clear prompt when a new version is deployed, so that I don't keep working in a stale and possibly incompatible client.
28. As a site visitor, I want content pages served from CDN/browser cache with correct revalidation, so that browsing is instant and always current after edits.
29. As the framework maintainer, I want the web write contract shared with the mobile write queue, so that offline replay semantics are designed once and drift is impossible.
30. As a mobile developer on the KMP foundation, I want a server change feed and an idempotent batch apply endpoint, so that the mobile client syncs against the same contract as the web.
31. As an operator running multiple replicas, I want invalidation to fan out across processes, so that scaling out never serves stale data past the configured bounds.
32. As an operator, I want client caching, persistence, and sync to be opt-in per model, so that sensitive models never reach client storage unless deliberately enabled.
33. As a security reviewer, I want queued client writes to flow through the same auth, interceptor, and writable-policy stack as normal CRUD, so that offline sync cannot become a privilege escalation or mass-assignment path.
34. As a security reviewer, I want change-feed reads, SSE subscriptions, and persisted caches scoped by tenant and identity, so that multi-tenant data cannot leak across tenants or across users of one device.
35. As a security reviewer, I want push events to carry no row payloads, so that authorization stays entirely on the read path.

## Implementation Decisions

**Package placement and shape**

- New package `@happyvertical/smrt-web`: framework-agnostic browser runtime (usable from any UI framework). `@happyvertical/smrt-svelte` gains the Svelte bindings on top — mirroring the core/smrt-svelte split. Name chosen as the deliberate twin of `smrt-mobile`; `client` was rejected as ambiguous, capability names (`sync`/`replica`/`local`) rejected as not signaling frontend.
- Server halves — change feed, sync-apply endpoint, SSE events route, conditional-GET support — are generated surfaces and live in core with the existing REST/CLI/MCP generators. The browser bundle must never drag server dependencies.

**Client store: wrap TanStack DB**

- TanStack DB (0.6, beta) provides collections, differential live queries, transactional optimistic mutations, durable persistence, and — via its offline-transactions package — a durable outbox with backoff retry, multi-tab leader election, and FIFO replay. Its collection model maps one-to-one onto SmrtCollection.
- Consumers never import TanStack directly: they import generated smrt-web collections. Beta churn is absorbed inside one wrapper package, and the documented fallback shape (same generated fetchers over TanStack Query) exists if the bet sours.
- Codegen: the vite plugin emits typed collection definitions as a virtual module alongside the existing generated REST client, for all three consumption modes (npm/federation/standalone). The manifest supplies types, relationships (invalidation edges), tenant scoping, and STI discriminators.
- Cached values are plain serialized DTOs (the public JSON projection), never hydrated SmrtObject instances — matching the mobile contract's DTO decision.

**Change feed (adapter-agnostic CDC)**

- A `_smrt_changes` system table (append-only: monotonic per-database sequence, table name, row id, operation, tenant, timestamp) written by the existing afterSave/afterDelete interceptor layer — the same mechanism the reports package and tenancy already use to observe every framework mutation. Delete entries double as tombstones.
- One read interface — changes since a cursor, optionally filtered by table and tenant — serves three consumers: delta pull for clients, the SSE push channel, and the per-table version source backing ETags.
- Explicitly adapter-agnostic: works identically on SQLite, Postgres, and DuckDB because it sits above the adapter. WAL-based external engines (ElectricSQL, PowerSync) were evaluated and rejected as the foundation due to Postgres-only coupling; they remain possible future accelerators behind the same interfaces.
- Accepted, documented gap (same as the #1499 collection cache): writes that bypass SMRT mutation paths (raw SQL) are invisible to the feed; a manual bump API is the escape hatch. Retention/compaction policy is owned by the module.
- Cross-replica fan-out reuses the adapter's optional notification capability (Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY) exactly as the collection cache does today; adapters without it fall back to polling the feed, and single-process deployments need neither.

**Write contract (shared with mobile #1739)**

- A dedicated idempotent batch apply endpoint — not a relaxation of the id-stripping mass-assignment guard on plain CRUD, which stays intact (#1540).
- Client-generated UUIDs (validated server-side) plus the ORM's existing upsert-on-id save semantics make replay idempotent by construction. FIFO per client; per-item results (`applied`/`conflict`/`rejected`); every item flows through the full interceptor, tenant, auth, and writable-policy stack.
- Conflict policy v1: server-authoritative last-write-wins with an updated-at guard — a losing write is applied or rejected per policy and always *reported* as a conflict in the item result so clients can surface it. Field-level merge is explicitly out of scope.
- This endpoint is the mobile foundation's write path too — one contract, two client runtimes.

**Push channel**

- Server-sent events (not WebSocket): works over plain HTTP, generated as a route like any other, trivially proxied. Client falls back to polling the change feed cursor where SSE is unavailable.
- Events are coarse invalidation signals — table, operation, row id — never row payloads. Authorization stays entirely on the read path; subscriptions are tenant- and identity-scoped.

**HTTP caching**

- Generated GET routes gain ETag (derived from the change feed's per-table version, stable across replicas) and If-None-Match → 304 handling. Default Cache-Control stays private.
- `api: { public: true }` models may emit public, s-maxage CDN headers — the v1 answer for smrt-sites speed.

**Version awareness**

- Two version signals: bundle version (integrates SvelteKit's native updated store) and API contract version (the manifest hash — only SMRT knows this).
- Persisted caches are keyed by (API base, tenant, identity, manifest hash); a hash change drops them rather than migrating. A reactive `updateAvailable` state covers both signals; deploy events may additionally ride the SSE channel. Presentation (toast, reload prompt) lives in the Svelte bindings.
- An explicit wipe API clears all persisted data on logout.

**Defaults and opt-in**

- Everything client-side is opt-in per model via decorator config, consistent with the #1499 cache philosophy: caching defaults on for generated collections (memory only), persistence and offline writes default off. Sensitive models never persist unless deliberately enabled.

## Testing Decisions

A good test asserts **external behavior**, never implementation details: HTTP semantics observed through real requests (a 304 with an unchanged ETag; a rejected item in an apply-batch result), feed behavior observed through its read interface (cursor monotonicity, tombstones present after delete, tenant filtering), replay idempotency observed through resulting database state, and collection behavior observed through the public collection API with only the network mocked.

All nine modules get tests:

- **Server modules (change feed, sync-apply, generator routes):** real in-memory SQLite per the repo's testing rules — never mock the database. Isolated per-test databases via the existing test-db helpers. Prior art: the collection-cache test suite from #1499 (TTL, invalidation, cross-process interest) and the tenancy/reports interceptor tests (observing afterSave/afterDelete side effects).
- **smrt-web runtime (collections, outbox, live-updates subscriber, version awareness):** mock only the external boundary (fetch, EventSource) per the mocking policy — never business logic. Behaviors under test: stale-while-revalidate and relationship-edge invalidation, outbox replay after simulated offline (including duplicate-replay idempotency against a scripted server), multi-tab single-replayer semantics, and version-keyed persistence dropping on manifest-hash change.
- **Svelte bindings:** component-level tests for live-query reactivity and update-available UX; package typecheck must include svelte-check per the repo convention for packages with Svelte subpaths.
- **Codegen:** test the generator, not the generated output — fixture manifest in, assert the emitted virtual-module shape, matching how existing generator tests work.

Regression discipline applies: every bug found during implementation lands with a regression test. New packages are subject to the Coverage Gate.

## Out of Scope

- **Full local-first database replica in the browser** (SQLite-WASM mirroring of whole tables, CRDTs, peer-to-peer). The change feed and tombstones deliberately make this possible later; v1 ships query-shaped caching plus targeted offline writes.
- **External sync engines** (ElectricSQL, PowerSync, Zero) as the foundation — evaluated and rejected for Postgres-only source coupling; revisit only if the native feed hits scale limits.
- **Field-level conflict merge / operational transforms** — v1 is server-authoritative LWW with conflict reporting.
- **The mobile client itself** — the KMP epic (#1745/#1739) owns the mobile queue and runtime; this PRD only supplies the shared server contract.
- **Content packs / ISR-style prerendered site exports** — future smrt-sites work; v1 sites speed comes from ETag/CDN headers.
- **Service workers and PWA installability.**
- **WebSocket transport.**
- **Template overhauls** — fixing the reference templates to use server loads + hydration is a small, independent lead-in tracked separately from this package.

## Further Notes

- Origin: measured ~130ms/query database round trips (#1498) led to the server-side read-through cache (#1499). This PRD is the client half of the same problem; the two share one invalidation philosophy (framework owns all mutation paths) and, after this lands, one change-observation spine.
- Alignment with ADR 0001 (KMP mobile foundation) is a design constraint throughout: DTO-projected contracts, durable queue state machine (`pending → uploading → synced → failed`), and the shared apply endpoint. Web and mobile are two runtimes over one server contract.
- TanStack DB status at writing: 0.6 (March 2026), beta; offline-transactions package provides the durable outbox. The wrapper-package strategy exists precisely because of the beta risk.
- Sequencing intent for implementation issues: a spike validating manifest-generated TanStack DB collections against the products reference package gates the deeper phases; the offline write contract lands before live push (the ergot ingestor needs the outbox sooner than dashboards need SSE); ETag/CDN work can proceed in parallel on the sites track.

items.title: [FEATURE] Add Encina.Audit.Marten — event-sourced IAuditStore with temporal crypto-shredding for compliance-grade audit trails

labels.name: area-compliance
labels.description: GDPR, EU Laws, and Regulatory Compliance patterns

milestone.title: Post-1.0: Security Core Completion (deferred items)
milestone.description: Security core: Core abstractions, ABAC, PII masking, field-level encryption, audit trail, anti-tampering, sanitization, secrets management (ISecretProvider + 4 cloud providers), XACML policy serialization, persistent PAP, and Attestation framework.

items.body:
## Feature Description
Add `Encina.Audit.Marten` as an **additional provider** for `IAuditStore` and `IReadAuditStore`, implementing event-sourced audit trails with temporal crypto-shredding via Marten (PostgreSQL).
This follows the Encina "pay-for-what-you-use" philosophy:
- **Simple apps** ÔÇö `InMemoryAuditStore` (dev) or DB provider (production)
- **Compliance-heavy apps** (SOX, NIS2) ÔÇö `MartenAuditStore` with immutable events + crypto-shredding
The existing `IAuditStore` interface does NOT change ÔÇö this is a new implementation, not a migration.
## Motivation
- **SOX 404**: Requires immutable audit trail of internal controls. Current mutable stores allow tampering.
- **NIS2 Art. 10**: Requires logging with integrity guarantees. Append-only event store provides this.
- **GDPR Art. 5(1)(e)**: Data minimization requires purging old audit data. Crypto-shredding achieves this without breaking immutability.
- **Forensics**: Temporal queries ("what happened at time X?") are natural with event sourcing.
## Design (Option C from architectural review)
```
IAuditStore (unchanged interface)
|-- InMemoryAuditStore          ÔÇö development/testing (existing)
|-- DB providers (13)           ÔÇö production simple (existing)
+-- MartenAuditStore (NEW)      ÔÇö production compliance-grade
    |-- Events encrypted with temporal keys (monthly/yearly)
    |-- PurgeEntriesAsync() destroys temporal keys (crypto-shredding)
    |-- Marten projections for efficient querying
    +-- ITemporalKeyProvider for key lifecycle management
```
### Key Behaviors
| Operation | DB Provider (current) | MartenAuditStore (new) |
|-----------|----------------------|----------------------|
| `RecordAsync` | INSERT row | Append encrypted event |
| `QueryAsync` | SELECT with filters | Project from decrypted events |
| `PurgeEntriesAsync` | DELETE rows | Destroy temporal encryption keys |
| Immutability | Rows can be UPDATE/DELETE'd | Events are append-only |
| Tamper evidence | None | Event stream integrity |
### Configuration
```csharp
// Simple app ÔÇö existing DB provider (no change)
services.AddEncinaAudit(options => { ... });
// Compliance-grade ÔÇö opt-in to Marten ES provider
services.AddEncinaAuditMarten(options =>
{
    options.KeyRotationPeriod = TimeSpan.FromDays(365); // yearly keys
    options.EncryptionScope = AuditEncryptionScope.PiiFieldsOnly;
    options.RetentionPeriod = TimeSpan.FromDays(2555); // 7 years (SOX)
    options.EnableAutoPurge = true;
});
```
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `MartenAuditStore` implements `IAuditStore` with event-sourced persistence
- [ ] `MartenReadAuditStore` implements `IReadAuditStore` with event-sourced persistence
- [ ] Audit events are encrypted with temporal keys via `ITemporalKeyProvider`
- [ ] `PurgeEntriesAsync()` destroys temporal keys (crypto-shredding), does NOT delete events
- [ ] Marten projections enable efficient `QueryAsync` with filtering and pagination
- [ ] Shredded entries are handled gracefully in query results (placeholder or skip)
- [ ] `ServiceCollectionExtensions.AddEncinaAuditMarten()` registers all components
- [ ] Existing `IAuditStore` implementations are NOT affected
- [ ] Unit tests with mocked `IAggregateRepository<T>`
- [ ] Integration tests against real Marten/PostgreSQL (Docker)
## Cross-Cutting Integration Checklist
- [x] OpenTelemetry ÔÇö inherit from Security.Audit diagnostics
- [x] Structured Logging ÔÇö inherit from Security.Audit logging
- [x] Health Checks ÔÇö verify Marten/PostgreSQL connectivity
- [x] Audit Trail ÔÇö this IS the audit trail implementation
- [ ] Caching ÔÇö evaluate caching projections for read-heavy queries
- N/A: Validation, Resilience (local DB), Distributed Locks, Transactions (Marten session), Idempotency (event versioning), Module Isolation
- Deferred: Multi-Tenancy (#798)
## Dependencies
- **Blocked by**: SPIKE issue for temporal crypto-shredding design (must be completed first)
- **Depends on**: #395 (Audit Trail Logging) ÔÇö `IAuditStore` interface
- **Depends on**: Encina.Marten.GDPR ÔÇö crypto-shredding reference pattern
- **Related**: #797 (Security module testing) ÔÇö integration tests for this provider
## Package Structure
```
src/
+-- Encina.Audit.Marten/
    |-- MartenAuditStore.cs           ÔÇö IAuditStore implementation
    |-- MartenReadAuditStore.cs       ÔÇö IReadAuditStore implementation
    |-- Events/
    |   |-- AuditEntryRecorded.cs     ÔÇö ES event
    |   +-- ReadAuditEntryRecorded.cs ÔÇö ES event
    |-- Projections/
    |   |-- AuditEntryProjection.cs   ÔÇö Read model for queries
    |   +-- ReadAuditProjection.cs    ÔÇö Read model for read audit
    |-- Crypto/
    |   |-- ITemporalKeyProvider.cs   ÔÇö Temporal key lifecycle
    |   +-- TemporalKeyProvider.cs    ÔÇö Marten-backed implementation
    |-- ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs
    |-- MartenAuditOptions.cs
    +-- Diagnostics/
        +-- MartenAuditDiagnostics.cs
```
